title: *S&P Affirms Ratings On Israel At 'A+/A-1'; Outlook Stable
text:
28 Mar 2014 01:02 EDT  Press Release: S&P Affirms Ratings On Israel At 'A+/A-1'; Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from Standard & Poor's: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- In our opinion, Israel's fiscal consolidation is on track, bolstered 
by extra one-off revenues in 2013 and upward revisions to GDP due to new 
calculation methodologies. We expect a modest decline in the gross general 
government debt ratio as a result. 
     -- We are therefore affirming our long- and short-term foreign and local 
currency sovereign credit ratings on Israel at 'A+/A-1'. 
     -- The stable outlook reflects our view that the government will continue 
to consolidate the public finances and that the effect of security risks on 
the Israeli economy will be contained. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On March 28, 2014, Standard & Poor's Ratings Services affirmed its long- and 
short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on the State of 
Israel at 'A+/A-1'. The outlook is stable. 
 
RATIONALE 
The affirmation reflects our view of Israel's prosperous and diverse economy 
as well as the positive medium-term impact of natural gas production on the 
external account. The fiscal profile is improving but remains a rating 
weakness, while geopolitical risks are the biggest rating constraint. 
 
We project real GDP growth of 3.2% in 2014, which is similar to the past two 
years. This includes the contribution of natural gas (about 0.4% of growth in 
2014). For 2015-2017, we forecast growth to remain stable at about 3.4% 
annually, suggesting a modest upswing due to the impending recovery in 
Israel's key export markets. In GDP per capita terms, this equates to trend 
growth of close to 1.5% annually. At above $38,000, we now view Israel as a 
high-income economy, with trend growth at the higher end of its peer income 
group. 
 
Public finances are improving due to stable growth, as well as last year's 
revisions to the national income accounts by the statistical office in line 
with OECD standards--notably the methodology for calculating GDP, which 
increased 2012 GDP by 6.9%. In combination with one-off revenues from 
corporate transactions of 0.6% of GDP, the general government deficit in 2013 
amounted to 3.2% of GDP. Since the bulk of fiscal consolidation has been 
scheduled for 2013-2014, we expect an average annual increase in the nominal 
level of general government debt of 2.6% of GDP in the medium term 
(2014-2017). This should enable Israel's net government debt burden to 
modestly decline over the 2014-2017 forecast horizon to 61% of GDP by 2017 
from 63% currently. This will largely be due to the increase in nominal 
general government debt over the period being slightly lower than the increase 
in GDP. Notably, the favorable interest rate environment is also helping lower 
the government's interest payments, which we expect to average about 10% of 
government revenues. 
 
Israel's external fundamentals remain strong; it continues to improve its net 
creditor position vis-a-vis the rest of the world. We project its narrow net 
external asset position will strengthen to 42% of current account receipts 
(CARs) over the forecast horizon. We forecast the current account will remain 
narrowly positive again in 2014 at 0.8% of GDP before gradually increasing 
thereafter. We estimate that the country's gross financing needs will continue 
to decline and stand at 77% of CARs and usable reserves in 2014. 
 
We consider monetary policy flexibility to be a rating strength. However, we 
no longer view the shekel as a free-floating currency and we expect the Bank 
of Israel (BoI, the central bank) to become increasingly interventionist. This 
is over and above its commitment to purchase foreign exchange in line with its 
assessment of the effect of natural gas production on the balance of payments 
and therefore to ward off appreciation pressures on the shekel. Further, a 
largely balanced current account, very strong foreign direct investment, and 
capital inflows on the financial account have added to appreciation pressures 
on the shekel, which is complicating the BoI's policy mix. Macro-prudential 
measures have failed to stem rapid price appreciation in the housing sector, 
but they do appear to have contained systemic risks. 
 
We consider Israel's institutions to be generally effective with a 
satisfactory degree of transparency and accountability. Recent electoral 
reforms could address the weakest element in Israel's governance, namely a 
lack of stability and limited policy predictability. Nonetheless, we believe 
the effects will only be seen at the earliest in the next electoral cycle. 
Meanwhile, external security threats and territorial disputes weaken political 
stability by inserting another dividing line in the electorate and distorting 
policy debates. 
 
Geopolitical risks are a rating constraint. In this respect, 
Israeli-Palestinian relations continue to be prone to violent outbreaks and 
also risk inviting other international repercussions. The war in Syria and 
instability in Sinai pose medium-term risks for deterioration, though recent 
trends have been favorable to Israel. Any significant armed conflict with 
Israel could further constrain the ratings if it significantly deters 
investment, weakens the economy's growth potential, or strains fiscal 
flexibility. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook reflects our opinion that consensus within the Israeli 
government to consolidate the public finances will continue to anchor fiscal 
planning and reduce government debt. We also expect the impact of security 
risks on the Israeli economy to remain contained. 
 
We could consider raising our ratings on Israel if it makes material progress 
in defusing external security risks. In our view, such progress would have 
positive implications for domestic stability, economic growth, and investor 
confidence. We could also consider an upgrade if fiscal consolidation 
continues to be successfully implemented, leading to declines in Israel's debt 
and interest burden. 
 
Conversely, we believe that a significant setback in the government's fiscal 
position, a significant decline in growth prospects, or a substantial 
deterioration of the security situation in Israel could put downward pressure 
on the rating. 
 
KEY STATISTICS 
 
RELATED CRITERIA AND RESEARCH

Corporate, Insurance, And Sovereign Issuers, May 7, 2013.

In accordance with our relevant policies and procedures, the Rating Committee 
was composed of analysts that are qualified to vote in the committee, with 
sufficient experience to convey the appropriate level of knowledge and 
understanding of the methodology applicable (see 'Related Criteria And 
Research'). At the onset of the committee, the chair confirmed that the 
information provided to the Rating Committee by the primary analyst had been 
distributed in a timely manner and was sufficient for Committee members to 
make an informed decision. 
 
After the primary analyst gave opening remarks and explained the 
recommendation, the Committee discussed key rating factors and critical issues 
in accordance with the relevant criteria. Qualitative and quantitative risk 
factors were considered and discussed, looking at track-record and forecasts. 
The chair ensured every voting member was given the opportunity to articulate 
his/her opinion. The chair or designee reviewed the draft report to ensure 
consistency with the Committee decision. The views and the decision of the 
rating committee are summarized in the above rationale and outlook.

title: Bank of Israel Members See Stronger Shekel Threatening Exports
text:
The Bank of Israel warned that a further appreciation of the shekel could slow a recovery in exports, a signal that it may once again intervene in the foreign exchange markets to weaken the currency.

According to the minutes of their late-February meeting released Monday, members of the Monetary Policy Committee agreed that at a time of sluggish world demand, the exchange rate threatens exports, a key driver of economic growth. At their meeting, MPC members agreed to cut the benchmark interest rate to 0.75% from 1.0%, the first reduction since September.

"Most Committee members agreed that if an additional appreciation occurs, it would be liable to undermine the recent trend of improvement in Israel's exports," the minutes said.

The central bank intervened heavily in the currency markets during January, buying a record $1.73 billion, and the currency weakened 0.8% against the dollar during that month.

With the shekel hitting a fresh, 30-month high against the dollar on Friday, Israeli foreign currency traders say they expect further central bank intervention in coming days.

"I wouldn't be surprised at all if we see another bank intervention," said Eytan Admoni, manager of financial markets at Bank of Jerusalem. "I was astonished the bank didn't intervene on Friday."

The central bank has a policy of intervening in currency markets when the shekel moves out of line with economic developments. Over the past year, factors pushing the shekel higher have included an increase in natural gas production, relatively strong economic growth, and interest rates that have been high relative to those of central banks in the U.S. and other large, developed economies.

To counter the specific impact on the shekel from higher gas production, the central bank has a program under which it will buy about $3.5 billion in 2014. But it can make additional purchases to control currency moves.

MPC members also cited slower inflation and rising unemployment as reasons for cutting the benchmark interest rate. They said signs of a cooling in the housing market opened the way for the cut, noting surveys that point to waning demand for home purchases and measures restricting mortgages as evidence of lower risk in the sector.

House prices have risen about 80% in Israel since 2007, prompting many economists and the International Monetary Fund to warn of a bubble in the market.

title: Israel 's  Forex  Reserves Rise on Revaluation,  Central Bank  Feb  Intervention  Waned
text:
JERUSALEM--Israel's foreign currency reserves grew by $811 million in February to total $83.98 billion, mainly due to an upward revaluation of the reserves as the dollar strengthened last month, the Bank of Israel said Thursday.

The central bank only bought about $350 million in foreign currency in February, after a record purchase of $1.73 billion during January in an attempt to offset a strong shekel and protect the competitiveness of Israel's exports.

The bank said all of the foreign currency purchases in February were made under an ongoing program to buy dollars to mitigate the strengthening effects on the shekel of Israel's increased natural gas production. That program calls for the bank to buy about $3.5 billion during 2014. In addition to that program, the bank also has a policy to intervene in the market, as it did very aggressively in January, when the shekel makes moves out of line with other economic or market conditions.

Partly due to the large purchases in January, and a decision at the end of February to lower the benchmark interest rate for the first time in several months by 25 basis points to 0.75%, the shekel was weaker against the dollar last month. But as many analysts predicted, the shekel has gained back some of that strength this week, as Israel's relatively higher interest rate and economic growth rate continue to make the shekel a safe haven for investors.

title: Governor of the Bank of Israel addresses the TheMarker Financial Conference
text:
Release date - 04032014

The following are the main points of the Governor of the Bank of Israel’s address at the TheMarker Financial Conference.

The Governor related to two issues: the macroeconomic situation and the stability of the financial system.

The macroeconomic situation

The global economy is continuing to grow at a moderate pace. Growth in the US continues to take root-even though the recent data has been weak, apparently due to the harsh weather. In Europe, the very moderate and fragile recovery is continuing, with some concern of deflation. In the emerging markets, there has been some improvement, although in some of the larger countries, mainly those that have current account deficits, there have been signs of weakness and fragility in recent months. Together with the moderate recovery, global trade is also expanding. Growth in Israel moves in line with, and higher than, that of the other advanced economies, and we expect that both the correlation and the gap will continue this year as well (slide 2).

However, looking at recent months, we see a further slowdown in growth in Israel, and the pace of growth declined from about 3 percent in the past year and a half to less than 2.5 percent in the past two quarters, while business output grew in those two quarters by just 1.6 percent (slide 3). Exports were the main factor in the slowdown in the third quarter, and there were signs of improvement in it in the fourth quarter., but at this stage, they are concentrated mainly in the pharmaceuticals industry and to a certain extent in the chemicals and electronics industries as well, and we have not yet seen the improvement expand to the other export industries.

The labor market continues to show a mixed trend: The unemployment rate declined and is at a historic low thanks to an increase in employment rates that took place together with stabilization of the participation rate at a very high level (slide 4). Our assessment is that the decline in the unemployment rate reflects, among other things, a structural decline in the unemployment rate due to processes increasing labor market elasticity in recent years that led to a decline in the frictional and the natural unemployment rates. Furthermore, most of the growth in employment in the past two years was in the public service industries-mainly in the non-governmental portion of the public services-while the number of Israeli employees in the business sector did not grow (slide 5). The number of work hours per employee in the business sector also declined, and the rate of those who are involuntarily in part-time employment increased. These reflect a certain weakness in the labor market.

Inflation in the past 12 months was 1.4 percent, and one year forward inflation expectations are anchored within the target range, below the center of the range (slide 6). Following the relatively rapid appreciation in the shekel exchange rate during the first half of 2013, there has been a moderation in the pace of appreciation (slide 7). It is important to note that the main forces acting for appreciation this year are the start of natural gas production and expectations of the effect it will have on the balance of payments in the next few years, as well as the relatively good position of the economy that is reflected in a current account surplus and in the flow of direct investments in innovative and attractive Israeli companies.

All of these factors formed the basis of monetary policy this year, including the background to the most recent interest rate reduction. It is important to mention that the monetary policy goals set in the law are, first of all, maintaining price stability, meaning keeping inflation within the range of 1-3 percent, and subject to that, support of growth and employment, and of financial stability. Therefore, the decline in inflation, together with expectations of moderation in inflation, enabled and even supported the reduction of the interest rate, which is intended to support activity and growth, both by lowering the cost of credit and by its effect on the exchange rate which mainly affects the commercial sector-the export industries and alternatives to imports.

As I have noted in the past, we are not indifferent to developments in the exchange rate, and we are aware of the effects it has on exports and on employment in the commercial industries. Therefore, in addition to the interest rate policy, the Bank of Israel also intervenes directly in the foreign exchange market-and we were active in the past year both in purchases to offset the effect of natural gas production on the current account of the balance of payments, and in order to moderate excess volatility in the exchange rate that is not in line with fundamental economic forces (slide 8). We must remember that the foreign exchange reserves are an important component of financial stability, and there are studies around the world that indicate that a high level of foreign exchange reserves reduce the likelihood of a financial crisis in the economy.

Regarding the housing market, home prices have continued to increase at a rapid pace, increasing by about 8 percent in 2013, together with a rapid increase in the number of new mortgages taken out. The Supervisor of Banks adopted measures intended to reduce the risks inherent in mortgages and in their rapid growth. The recent measures adopted-which restrict the payment-to-income ratio and set out that at least one-third of the mortgage should be at a fixed interest rate-are acting to reduce the risk that households that took out a mortgage will have difficulty in meeting their payments, for instance in a situation where one of the household members loses his job, or if the burden of repayment increases due to an increase in the interest rate. The decline in the share of mortgages with an loan-to-value (LTV) ratio above 60 percent, and the decline in the share of mortgages with a payment-to-income (PTI) ratio above 40 percent, indicate that the measures adopted have reduced the risk inherent in mortgages (slide 9). With that, the continued rapid growth in the number of mortgages and in their weight in the bank’s credit portfolio are a risk factor, and if additional measures are required, we will not hesitate to take them.

The increase in the number of building starts and completions that we witnessed in the past year, to almost 45,000 starts and more than 40,000 completions-higher than the basic demand for homes that is derived from growth in the number of households-is a positive development. If this trend continues-and we see that the government is making efforts in this direction-and if it includes areas of high demand, it will act to reduce the pressure and stabilize home prices.

Financial stability

The picture of the stability of the economy can be presented in multi-dimensional form by way of a radar chart that includes real data, accounting data and survey data, as well as data that show the risk philosophy of Israeli and global investors (slide 11). The diagram for the end of January 2014 indicates that the financial system and the economy are stable. The red diagram reflects the situation at the end of 2008, and shows a picture in which almost all risk indices, both global and domestic, were at record high levels at the height of the global financial crisis. The blue diagram, which shows the levels of the current risk indices, indicates relatively low levels, with most of the measured risks reflecting the global macroeconomic situation-moderate growth, high unemployment, and low indices reflecting consumer confidence and business confidence. These, of course, also have an effect on the domestic macroeconomic risk, which reflects moderate growth. In contrast, the market risk indices, both in Israel and globally, are at low levels, which creates a gap-both in Israel and abroad-between the real situation and the investors’ risk philosophy. This gap is apparently affected by the search for yields in a low interest-rate environment, but it is possible that expectations of an increase in corporate profits that will accompany the recovery also have an effect.

A view of the business sector’s sources of financing indicates that the trend of a decline in the weight of bank credit and an increase in the weight of domestic nonbank credit-through corporate bonds and recently through direct loans from institutional investors as well-that we witnessed since the beginning of the century continues even after the global crisis of 2008-9 (slide 12). This is obviously a positive process, in that it increases and variegates the sources of financing to the business sector, creates competition for the banks and acts to reduce the cost of financing, thereby supporting growth. However, the process is also accompanied by the creation of risks that must be addressed. Among other things, these reflect the fact that the nonbank credit market has developed rapidly, while its regulation is developing gradually. During the global crisis, most of the negative impact to the financial system in Israel was reflected in this market: Yields in the market skyrocketed and issuances froze. In total, more than 100 companies have entered debt restructuring proceedings thus far-representing bonds totaling about NIS 40 billion. It is important to emphasize that this number does not represent the scope of the loss absorbed by investors, which will naturally be lower (slide 13).

Since the global crisis, as a lesson from global developments as well as developments in Israel, in order to reduce the risks of a crisis and to reduce the damage of a crisis should one take place, many measures are being taken in the field of regulation that are intended to reinforce the durability of the financial institutions and system. Regulations have been updated in the field of corporate governance and risk management at the banks; the Basel III guidelines have been adopted in the area of capital requirements, and rules in the area of liquidity and leverage will be adopted; the use of stress tests to identify risks in institutions and in the system as a whole has been increased; the Business Concentration Law has been passed to reduce the risks derived from complex and leveraged business groups and to separate control of real corporation from financial corporations; the recommendations of the Hudak committee to strengthen control of investments by financial entities in corporate bonds have been adopted; the supervision of the payments and settlement systems has been strengthened; and the Banking Supervision Department has taken a series of measures to reduce the risks in the mortgage market (slide 14).

Beyond these changes, which have already been implemented or are in the process of implementation or assessment, there is also a series of committee recommendations or recommendations that are still being formulated, that are meant to complement the improvement of regulation: the Goldschmidt committee to arrange the management of direct loans by institutions; the Andoran committee, which is handling debt restructuring proceedings in the economy. There is also a bill in advanced stages of legislation to handle a failing bank, similar to legislation enacted in this area following the crisis in other advanced countries.

Even though much has been done in the field of financial regulation since the crisis, and there are steps still being taken, there remains much work to do. One of the important lessons taken out of the development of the financial crisis in various countries is the fact that while the institutions themselves were, in most cases, subject to supervision, there were parts of the system that are not supervised or are less supervised, which expanded rapidly. It also became clear that the connections between the various institutions, and the interfaces between them, which led to the rapid transfer of risks between parts of the system and increased its fragility, were neglected by regulators around the world. Therefore, the issue of an overall view of the financial system, and the issue of coordination and joint work by the various regulators is at the center of the recommendations of the various international bodies on an issue that is at the heart of the required reforms in the field of financial regulation.

In terms of Israel, it is desired, as the International Monetary Fund has recommended in this regard, to establish a financial stability committee that will entrench the coordination and cooperation between all of the financial regulatory authorities, with the aim of identifying, preventing and reducing systemic risks. This committee is supposed to define, monitor and assess systemic risks; examine risks and exposures in the financial system in order to identify and assess systemic risks; promote the exchange of information among the financial regulatory authorities and between them and the stabilizing institutions (the Bank of Israel and the Ministry of Finance); improve the coordination and cooperation between the financial regulatory authorities and the stabilizers in analyzing evaluating, developing and operating tools and methods to prevent and reduce systemic risks; issue warnings when a systemic risk could become a material risk; make recommendations of measures to prevent or reduce systemic risks that are identified; and track the actions taken as a result of the warnings and the implementation of the recommendations (slide 15). It is proposed that the staff work for the committee be done by the Financial Stability Division that was recently established in the Bank of Israel Research Department, with the aim of acting to promote financial stability which, according to the new Bank of Israel Law, is one of the Bank’s goals.

A stable financial environment, and a financial system in which the public places its trust, are essential for sustainable growth and a continued increase in the standard of living. I am convinced that completing the steps that are currently being taken, including the establishment of the committee as I have outlined, will contribute to the economy’s ability to withstand shocks which, by nature, will come. We have the privilege of taking these steps during a period of relative calm and stability, and it is therefore important that we complete them soon.

title: Israel  central bank  chief warns of more steps to cool housing prices
text:
JERUSALEM, March 4 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel may take further steps to cool the housing market if fast growth in mortgages continues, Governor Karnit Flug said on Tuesday.

Speaking at a conference, Flug noted home prices rose 8 percent in 2013, which also saw a rapid increase in the number of new mortgages taken out. The central bank has already taken measures such as tightening mortgage rules.

But with interest rates very low and supply rising more slowly than demand, real estate has become a preferred mode of investment in Israel. Home prices have jumped 80 percent in nominal terms since 2007 and the International Monetary Fund recently said Israeli property prices were 25 percent above their equilibrium level.

"The continued rapid growth in the number of mortgages and in their weight in the bank's credit portfolio are a risk factor, and if additional measures are required, we will not hesitate to take them," Flug said.

She said the rise seen in building starts and completions in 2013 was a positive development, adding that if the trend continues and if it includes areas of high demand, "it will act to reduce the pressure and stabilise home prices".

Despite rising home costs, the Bank of Israel unexpectedly lowered its benchmark interest rate to 0.75 percent from 1.0 percent on February 24. It was the first cut since September and reflected concerns about weak global economic growth and the local labour market.

On Tuesday, Flug noted that Israeli economic growth had slowed to below 2.5 percent in the second half of 2013, hit by weak exports that she said were mainly concentrated in the pharmaceuticals, chemicals and electronics sectors.

Flug cited worries that most of the country's job growth has been in non-governmental public services, while private sector work hours have declined and involuntary part-time jobs have risen. "These reflect a certain weakness in the labour market," she said.

Flug also pointed to the fragile recovery in Europe, recent weak data in the United States and some weakness in large emerging market countries. "Growth in Israel moves in line with, and higher than, that of the other advanced economies, and we expect that both the correlation and the gap will continue this year as well," she said.

Inflation has been tame at an annual rate of 1.4 percent in January and expectations for the coming year are well within the government's 1-3 percent range.

"The decline in inflation, together with expectations of moderation in inflation, enabled and even supported the reduction of the interest rate, which is intended to support activity and growth," Flug said.

She added that the Bank of Israel continues to intervene in the foreign exchange market as it battles a strong shekel. It bought $1.73 billion in January to bring foreign currency reserves above $83 billion. Flug said studies show that high reserves reduce the likelihood of a financial crisis. (Reporting by Steven Scheer; Editing by Catherine Evans)

title: UPDATE 2-Israel unexpectedly cuts interest rates to bolster growth
text:
* Cuts main rate by 25 bps to 0.75 pct

* First rate cut since September

* Cites weak consumer confidence, labour mkt (Adds shekel reaction, analysts' comments)

By Steven Scheer

JERUSALEM, Feb 24 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel unexpectedly cut its benchmark interest rate on Monday for the first time since September, citing concerns over slowing economic growth, although analysts do not expect any more easing.

A drop in inflation to 1.4 percent last month and a relatively stable shekel enabled the bank to resume an easing cycle that had been on hold for four months.

It cut its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 0.75 percent, the lowest level since November 2009.

"Various indicators of activity in January pointed to some recovery, but consumer confidence indices continued to signal pessimism, and data continued to indicate a lack of growth in employment and wages in the business sector," the Bank of Israel said in a statement accompanying the rate cut.

A relatively strong economy has helped Israel weather the recent turmoil in emerging markets reasonably well. Growth is projected at 3.3 percent in 2014 for a second straight year.

Still, data this month showed the economy grew by an annualised 2.3 percent in the fourth-quarter, well below expectations. The central bank noted on Monday that excluding the public sector, economic growth was just 1.6 percent in the last three months of 2013.

"This decision (to cut rates) will lead to a weaker shekel, which will help local industry improve its competitiveness and deal more successfully in international markets," said Zvi Oren, president of the Manufacturers' Association, who had lobbied the central bank hard to take action against the currency, which had appreciated by 12 percent since July 2012.

The shekel weakened to 3.5170 per dollar on Monday after the rate cut, from around 3.5060 just before the decision.

The central bank said that even in the fourth quarter, a positive turnaround in exports was based mainly on pharmaceuticals exports which are generally volatile, while exports by labour-intensive industries were still virtually stagnant.

It continued to express concern about house prices though, noting they had risen by 8.1 percent in the past year while the number of transactions continued to rise and the volume of mortgages being granted remained high.

All 11 economists polled by Reuters had predicted no change in rates on Monday, citing the hot property market as a factor. Most believed the easing cycle that began in September 2011, when the key rate was 3.25 percent, was over barring a sharp downturn in growth.

SHEKEL EASES

The central bank - which rarely keeps rates steady for more than four months - said in its statement that inflation expectations for the next year were well below 2 percent and global growth was weak.

"After two quarters of rapid growth, recent U.S. economic data were disappointing, though it is too early to determine if it is a temporary slowdown or a turning point downward. In Europe, slow growth continues, and there are growing concerns of deflation," it said.

At its last policy meeting a month ago, the monetary policy committee (MPC) voted 5-0 to leave the bank's key rate at 1.0 percent, citing a strong shekel as a key factor.

Since then the shekel has been relatively stable with the central bank saying the currency depreciated by 1 percent in terms of the nominal effective rate.

Ofer Klein, head of economics and research at Harel Insurance and Finance, said the central bank's arguments for cutting rates appeared similar to those it had used in recent months in choosing to leave rates unchanged.

"We believe the factors that tipped the balance towards lowering interest rates were weak data recently published in the United States and the possibility that the European Central Bank will also act to counter a continuing decline in inflation in the bloc," he said.

Even if the shekel - which is still near a 2-1/2 year high versus the dollar after a 9 percent gain in 2013 - appreciates further, the Bank of Israel will use foreign exchange market intervention over more rate cuts, he said.

In December and January, the central bank bought more than $2.3 billion of foreign currency to prevent a rapid shekel appreciation.

The MPC will revert to its normal six members starting next month following the cabinet's approval on Sunday of Nadine Baudot-Trajtenberg as deputy to Bank of Israel Governor Karnit Flug. She will start her new post on March 2. (Additional reporting by Tova Cohen; Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: Shekel Weaker Against Dollar Following  Central Bank Intervention  -- Market Talk
text:
xx-DJ The shekel continues to weaken against the dollar Tuesday morning as Israel's central bank again intervened in the market after aggressively buying dollars Monday evening, according to Israeli currency traders. The bank bought between $100 million and $150 million Tuesday after buying about $300 million Monday evening, following its announcement that the February interest rate would remain unchanged at 1%, traders said, although the bank declined to confirm the alleged purchases.

According to traders, the bank has already bought about $1 billion in January, about four times the average amount of its monthly purchases, and about one-fifth of its total foreign currency purchases of $5 billion in 2013.

"Without the bank's intervention, we would not be trading at this level," said Tom Gerszbejn, foreign currency / local market spot trader at Citi Israel in Tel Aviv. At 1001 GMT, USD/ILS was up 0.22% at 3.4966.

But traders said shekel weakness will prove temporary unless the bank continues to intervene aggressively. Market fundamentals - including Israel's relatively high interest rates, steady economic growth and shrinking government deficit - support a shekel that trades at least as low as ILS 3.48 against the dollar, traders said.

Israel's exporters, which make up a large portion of the economy, have called on the bank to lower interest rates and buy more dollars in order to prevent currency strength negatively impacting the competiveness of Israel's goods abroad.

title: Exports not that sensitive to exchange rate -Israel cbank chief
text:
JERUSALEM, Jan 6 (Reuters) - Bank of Israel Governor Karnit Flug suggested the central bank would continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market as long as the shekel's exchange rate was not acting in line with economic fundamentals.

The shekel last week forged a new 2-1/2-year high versus the dollar, leading to calls from exporters for more aggressive action from policymakers.

Exports, which accounted for a third of Israel's economic activity in 2013, are Israel's main economic driver and have struggled in recent years due to a weak global economy.

Flug, though, downplayed the impact of the shekel's strength on exports. She told parliament's finance committee on Monday that total exports were not "highly sensitive" to the exchange rate.

A one percent appreciation leads to a 0.2 percent decline in exports, and vice versa, said Flug, who took over the reins at the central bank in November.

High-tech exports, which account for 44 percent of industrial exports, are least sensitive to the exchange rate. Still, the exchange rate affects the competitive ability of industries that compete with imports, Flug said.

The shekel appreciated some 8 percent versus the dollar in 2013 and its strength stems largely from Israel's economy growing faster than most other countries and the start of natural gas production, which boosted the current account balance.

To prevent a large appreciation of the shekel the Bank of Israel has intervened in the currency market, she said.

"This intervention is intended both to moderate sharp fluctuations in the exchange rate that are not in line with the fundamental economic conditions, and to offset the exchange rate's overshooting due to the effect of natural gas production," Flug said.

It bought $2.1 billion of foreign currency in 2013 to offset the effect of natural gas output and plans to buy $3.5 billion more in 2014. It has also bought forex outside of this programme.

"We are not indifferent to developments in the exchange rate," Flug said. "The Bank of Israel's policy in this area is intended to make the adjustment period easier, and even to prevent excessive harm in the commercial sector as a result of the exchange rate overshooting."

Israel's economy grew an estimated 3.3 percent in 2013 and the Bank of Israel sees a similar pace this year. (Reporting by Steven Scheer; editing by Mike Collett-White)

title: Potential No.2 For Fed: An Activist, More Or Less
text:
(FROM THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 12/13/13) 
   By Jon Hilsenrath and Joshua Mitnick 

As governor of the Bank of Israel from 2005 through this June, Stanley Fischer confronted two potential crises: The risk of a global financial meltdown washing onto Israel's shores, and tensions at home with Palestinian authorities over domestic finances.

Mr. Fischer would face very different challenges if he lands the job of Federal Reserve vice chairman, but would still need a combination of financial know-how and political acumen. He is President Barack Obama's choice for the job, though the pick hasn't been finalized, say people familiar with the matter.

The Fed leadership transition is unfolding as the central bank weighs whether to pull back on its complex easy-money policies. Mr. Fischer will be asked to play a delicate subordinate role to Janet Yellen, who is awaiting Senate confirmation of her nomination to become the Fed's chairwoman in February. His nomination also would be subject to Senate confirmation.

Mr. Fischer, 70 years old, has compiled a four-decade career that provides clues about how he would fill the role as the second-in-command at the world's most powerful economic institution.

Palestinian Monetary Authority Chief Jihad Al Wazir suggested Mr. Fischer was skilled at navigating political sensitivities to focus on economic challenges.

"During Stan's tenure [at the Bank of Israel], the relations remained on a professional level," Mr. Al Wazir said from Ramallah. "It was devoid of politics. There was an understanding of the issues."

Mr. Fischer's record shows he has supported an activist central bank in the past to help the economy, even though he has expressed some skepticism about the Fed's vigorous efforts to spur growth and bring down unemployment in recent months.

In 1977, Mr. Fischer wrote a seminal research paper laying out the case for an activist monetary policy to counter short-run economic downturns. The paper was a counterpunch at University of Chicago economists who saw government intervention as ineffective and became a key part of his world view as a policy maker.

Mr. Fischer taught at Chicago in the early 1970s, but with the 1977 paper he became a leader in the "New Keynesian" academic movement, which accepted some Chicago arguments but still saw a role for government intervention.

In the 1990s, as the deputy director of the International Monetary Fund, Mr. Fischer helped build what came to be known as the "Washington Consensus" on economic policy, which called for flexible exchange rates, free capital flows between countries and balanced budgets.

Critics on the right said the IMF was too quick to intervene in countries jarred by market instability during this period. Critics on the left said the IMF demanded overly harsh policies, such as interest-rate increases and spending cuts in economies in Latin America, Asia and Russia when it did intervene to stabilize them.

In Israel, his interventions won their share of supporters.

Mr. Al Wazir said Mr. Fischer helped ease strain in the Palestinian banking system during recurring liquidity crises because of shortfalls in foreign aid and freezes in Israeli transfers of tax revenue collected on the behalf of Palestinians. He helped to get shipments of cash into the Gaza Strip's blockaded economy.

Mr. Fischer was one of the first central bankers to cut interest rates during the 2008 crisis. He also took the controversial step of intervening in currency markets to help Israeli exporters and build up the country's foreign-currency reserves, bolstering confidence in the economy.

"It was a sign that there was someone in control," said Vered Dar, former chief economist at Psagot investment house.

Mr. Fischer wasn't universally beloved in Israel.

His most consistent detractor, Yaron Zelekha, a former accountant general in the Israeli Finance Ministry, said Mr. Fischer didn't raise interest rates soon enough, thus contributing to a real-estate bubble in Israel.

Last summer, Mr. Fischer was criticized by many in Israel's ultraorthodox Jewish community for pointing to their high birth ates and low labor-force participation as unsustainable for Israel's economy in the long term.

title: Israel should prepare for rate hikes as world economy improves-OECD
text:
JERUSALEM, Dec 5 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel should prepare for interest rate increases once the global economy returns to normal, the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said.

Israel's benchmark interest rate has been lowered in the current easing cycle to 1 percent, with the most recent rate cut in September, from 3.25 percent to support economic growth.

"The authorities should set their sights on returning to more orthodox monetary and exchange-rate policy over the next couple of years if global monetary conditions return to normality," the OECD said in its 2013 report on Israel's economy obtained by Reuters on Thursday.

"While monetary policy became even more accommodative in autumn 2013 ... a tightening phase will have to begin at some point," the report said.

The OECD also recommended the central bank "terminate systematic unannounced intervention in the foreign-currency market".

The Bank of Israel has bought some $50 billion of foreign currency since 2008 to try and prevent the shekel from appreciating rapidly and further harming exports that comprise some 40 percent of economic activity.

It also is buying $2.1 billion of forex in 2013 and $3.5 billion in 2014 as part of a programme intended to offset the effects of natural has production on the exchange rate.

The central bank also needs to take further measures to constrain high-risk mortgage lending amid a sharp rise in housing prices, the OECD said.

It urged the government to prioritise meeting budget deficit targets - unless economic growth falls substantially below expectations - to "avoid further deterioration in fiscal policy credibility."

Israel should be ready to raise tax revenues further, the OECD said, preferably by broadening the tax base and through reducing avoidance and erosion. Raising the value added tax (VAT) was preferable to higher income taxes.

An analyst at Fitch Ratings told Reuters on Thursday he was satisfied with the recent improvement in government finances and said a sovereign credit upgrade is possible within two years if the trend continues.

The OECD projects Israel's economic growth at 3.7 percent this year and 3.4 percent in 2014. It noted that while Israel's growth has been impressive and unemployment is at a 30-year low, Israel must improve living standards and reduce poverty. (Reporting by Steven Scheer; Editing by Mark Heinrich)

title: UPDATE 1-Israel rates to stay low while global policy expansionary -Flug
text:
(Adds comments)

EILAT, Israel, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Israeli interest rates will remain low as long as global rates stay at low levels, incoming Bank of Israel Governor Karnit Flug said on Wednesday.

Flug has been acting central bank chief since Stanley Fischer stepped down at the end of June. Under her leadership, she surprised markets by lowering Israel's benchmark rate by a quarter-point to 1 percent in late September. The bank held rates in its latest decision on Oct. 28.

"As long as monetary policy in developed countries, particularly the United States, is expansionary, our interest rates will also remain low," Flug said at an economic conference.

Flug, whose remarks were broadcast via video link, said very low inflation has made it possible for easy monetary policy but such rate levels encourage taking mortgages in the absence of other investments and lead to higher housing prices.

She said the low rate environment was one of the main short-term challenges for Israel's economy.

Israel's cabinet has already approved Flug for the post of Bank of Israel governor and she only needs the country's president to officially install her. That is expected next week.

Flug hinted that the Bank of Israel would reduce the amount of foreign exchange intervention to prevent the shekel from appreciating rapidly. A strong shekel harms exports, which account for 40 percent of economic activity.

She noted that intervention was just a temporary measure and exporters need to adapt and adjust to the reality.

"Ultimately, exporters will have to deal with the appreciation through productivity and efficiency," Flug said. "Once global economic conditions return to normal, there will be less than a need to intervene."

Since 2008, the Bank of Israel has bought about $50 billion of foreign currency, pushing its forex reserves to a record of near $80 billion.

Part of the dollar's recent strength stems from the start of natural gas production this year - meaning there is little need for gas imports and an improved balance of payments. The central bank is separately buying dollars to offset the impact to the current account, after what Flug called an "over-reaction" by the market to the gas output.

"There are some who think there can be a strong economy and a weak currency but that probably won't happen," she said.

On fiscal policy, Flug said that taxes will have to rise as long as the government wants to spend on providing services similar to other Western countries and Israel continues to have a high defence burden.

She also said Israel could achieve both banking stability along with increased competition in the sector.

title: Change of Guard at Israel's  Central Bank , But Policy Path Intact -- WSJ Blog
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Middle East Real Time blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/middleeast/)

By Joshua Mitnick

Despite the swirling speculation towards the end of Israel's tortured four-month search for a successor to Stanley Fischer, the appointment of Karnit Flug as Bank of Israel Governor -- the first woman to get the job -- failed to stir up much excitement amongst investors and analysts.

That's because Ms. Flug, for the foreseeable future anyway, is seen continuing with the monetary policies of her predecessor. And that means keeping interest rates relaxed enough to spur economic growth and making modest interventions in foreign currency markets to weaken Israel's strong shekel and keep the country's exporters competitive.

"More than anyone else there shouldn't be any surprise," said Jonathan Katz, an economist at HSBC Israel. "We know that her world view is rather similar to Stanley Fischer's."

The central bank appointment certainly had little impact on financial markets. The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange's benchmark TA-25 Index rose just 0.7 percent in the hours after the announcement.

Perhaps Ms. Flug's biggest hurdle will be living up to the outsized reputation of Mr. Fischer's tenure. The former bank of Israel governor won high praise for guiding the country's economy through the fallout from the 2008 financial meltdown with few scratches. Ms. Flug can expect constant comparisons to her predecessor.

Beyond that, her main policy challenge will be balancing the need to keep the shekel weak to help Israel's export dependent economy, while avoiding the creation of bubbles in the local housing and stock markets, say analysts. Of particular concern are surging real estate prices, though that problem is seen as a result of tight supply, say analysts, and the central bank has few tools in its box to reverse the trend.

Perhaps Ms. Flug's first real challenge will come when it's time to raise interest rates.

"With all the noise around the process of the appointment, it isn't a critical factor for the capital markets," said Alex Zabezhinsky, chief economist at Meitav DS Securities. "She will be judged when policy needs to be changed -- whether it is done too soon or too late. That won't happen soon."

title: PREVIEW-Bank of Israel seen holding rates for 4th straight month
text:
* Shekel at more than 2-year peak vs dollar

* Economy grew annualised 4.9 pct in Q2

* Rates decision expected Monday at 1200 GMT

By Steven Scheer

JERUSALEM, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Israel's central bank is expected to leave short-term interest rates unchanged for a fourth straight month due to moderate economic growth and continued gains in home prices.

Along with a tame annual inflation rate of 1.3 percent, the most compelling reason to ease policy again would be a more than two-year peak of the shekel against the dollar at a level of 3.50. But analysts believe the Bank of Israel has other tools - such as market intervention - it is more likely to use to try to prevent a further appreciation of the currency.

That is because the benchmark interest rate is already at 1.25 percent and a quarter-point reduction would likely have minimal impact on the shekel or the economy, they say.

The Bank of Israel's monetary policy committee has been led by deputy governor Karnit Flug since July, after Stanley Fischer stepped down at the end of June. Naming a replacement has hit a number of snags but the government is expected to announce a new governor in the coming weeks.

The Bank of Israel is slated to announce its rates decision for October on Monday at 3 pm (1200 GMT). It last lowered rates in May, by a total of 50 basis points in two reductions.

"The loose monetary stance that has been in place since the third quarter of 2012 remains intact but further easing is becoming unlikely," said Tevfik Aksoy, an emerging markets economist at Morgan Stanley.

"The main issue (for the Bank of Israel) is the appreciation pressure on the currency," he said, adding the shekel should stay strong due to a sound economy and natural gas output boosting Israel's current account surplus.

Much of the shekel's recent gains have also come as U.S. military action in Syria has become unlikely, while the Federal Reserve has delayed tapering off its U.S. bond buying programme - a combination that lifted most global currencies.

Helped by the start of natural gas production at the end of March and robust consumer and state spending, the economy is likely headed for growth of at least 3.4 percent in 2013, according to estimates from the government and analysts. The economy grew an annualised 4.9 percent in the second quarter.

Along with the rates decision, the central bank's research staff on Monday are also expected to publish revisions to their economic growth estimates. The Bank of Israel's economists currently project a 2013 growth rate of 3.8 percent, including a 1 percentage point contribution from natural gas, and a 3.3 percent pace in 2014.

"With growth remaining reasonably resilient and home prices rising, we think the Bank of Israel is reluctant to cut further," said Daniel Hewitt, an emerging markets economist at Barclays Capital. "With the housing market heating up, the Bank of Israel wants to avoid sparking a bubble."

Partly due to low interest rates, home prices have jumped more than 50 percent in recent years, leading the central bank to place restrictions on mortgages. But those steps have not worked since demand has outstripped supply, while real estate has proven to be among the best investments of late.

(Editing by Pravin Char)

title: Shekel gains halted after Bank of Israel buys up to $300 mln of  forex
text:
JERUSALEM, Sept 2 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel bought as much as $300 million of foreign currency on Monday to halt a three-day rally of the shekel, which is being influenced by possible military action on Syria.

Speculation about possible Western military action against neighbouring Syria weakened the shekel to a six-week low of nearly 3.67 against the dollar last week. But after Britain and the United States delayed any strikes, the Israeli currency bounced.

It reached close to 3.59 per dollar and 4.75 per euro early on Monday, prompting the central bank to act.

A dealer at Israel Discount Bank estimated the Bank of Israel bought some $150 million of foreign currency while the head of a trading desk at another large Israeli bank said it was between $200 million and $300 million.

Following the intervention, the shekel has weakened to 3.6150 to the dollar and 4.78 per euro.

"The shekel is back to the same point before Syria," said the head of the trading desk, referring to talk of military action.

When strikes were believed to be imminent, foreign banks bought dollars while Israeli exports enjoyed the higher dollar rate, he said. "They were hoping that if something happened, the dollar would go up," he added.

But now, they were forced to sell the dollar, the dealer noted.

The shekel has been one of the best-performing emerging market currencies this year but last week it shed almost half its 2013 gains on fears of Western military action in Syria that could spark a wider conflict in the Middle East.

A strong shekel is a particular concern for policymakers since a robust currency harms exports, which account for some 40 percent of Israel's economic activity. In addition to intervening from time to time in the market, the Bank of Israel lowered its benchmark interest rate twice in May, citing a strong shekel that neared a two-year peak.

The currency's recent stability was one reason the central bank cited for leaving rates on hold last week.

The central bank has said it would also buy $2.1 billion of foreign currency in 2013 to offset gains made to Israel's current account surplus in the wake of the start to natural gas production at an offshore well. (Reporting by Steven Scheer; editing by Ron Askew)

title: Israeli shekel slides, stocks fall on talk of attack on Syria
text:
JERUSALEM, Aug 27 (Reuters) - Growing speculation about Western military action against neighbouring Syria weakened the shekel and Israeli share prices on Tuesday, sending the local currency to a six-week low against the dollar.

The shekel had been one of the best-performing emerging market currencies this year but it has shed almost half its 2013 gains on fears of Western military action in Syria that could lead to a wider conflict in the Middle East.

The shekel was fixed at 3.657 per dollar, its weakest level since July 8 and a 1.5 percent drop from 3.603 on Monday. In two sessions, the shekel has lost some 2 percent.

"It is purely Syria on how it affects Israel but also how it affects the world," said Rony Gitlin, head of spot trading at Bank Leumi, adding that dollar buying was mainly by foreign banks that were also selling other emerging market currencies.

The United States has called for accountability for those responsible for a gas attack in Syria last week that killed hundreds of civilians, and calls for retribution have come also from some of its allies despite Russian and Chinese opposition.

Talk of Western military action has fuelled a sell-off in other emerging market currencies, with the lira in Turkey - another of Syria's neighbours - hitting a record low , and Russia's rouble at its weakest in four years against a dollar-euro basket

Should there be no attack, Gitlin said the shekel - boosted this year by steady economic growth and the start to natural gas production - would resume its appreciation trend.

A strong shekel had been a particular concern for policymakers since a robust currency harms exports, which account for some 40 percent of Israel's economic activity. In addition to intervening from time to time in the market, the Bank of Israel lowered its benchmark interest rate twice in May, citing a strong shekel that neared a two-year peak.

The currency's stability of late was one reason the central bank cited for leaving rates on hold on Monday.

Daniel Rapoport, head of equities and derivatives trading at Leumi Capital Markets, said the threat of a wider conflict led to across-the-board selling of stocks in Tel Aviv and redemptions by mutual funds.

In late trading, the blue-chip Tel Aviv 25 index was down 2.0 percent at 1161.02 points, while the broader TA-100 index was 1.8 percent lower at 1063.14. Volume of 1.4 billion shekels ($384 million) was above average.

title: DJ  FX  MATH: The Shekel at ILS2.99 to the Dollar Could Be Coming
text:
It's been almost 17 years since the Israeli shekel was quoted with a "2" in front of it against the U.S. dollar, but expect that streak to be broken, possibly soon.

Since July, the shekel has been on a blistering pace, up 14.9% against the greenback. From lows of 4.1 to the dollar on July 26 to today's rate of ILS3.5670.

The reason for the shekel's popularity -- Israel is an easy sell.

If Israel were a new car, the sales pitch might go something like this: the 2013 model sports an International Monetary Fund gross domestic product forecast of 3.6% growth that is expected to improve to 3.9% in 2014. That pairs nicely with the Israeli central bureau of statistics last inflation rate, which is 1.5% as measured by the consumer price index. Couple that with a 10-year bond yield of 3.5%, and an investor is driving off the lot with a comfortable 2% real rate of return.

Fundamentally the economy is sound. Israel is a major exporting nation with the U.S. and euro zone serving as its two biggest trading partners. A steady demand for Israeli goods with an emphasis on technology and pharmaceuticals continues to lift economic growth, while natural gas production beginning off the Mediterranean coastline should further boost prospects. Over time, that production could ease the heavy cost of imported fuel and perhaps one day turn Israel into an energy exporter.

About the only thing standing in the shekel's path to a level not seen since October of 1995 is intervention by the central bank of Israel to stem appreciation. The possibility of intervention remains worrisome for shekel bulls, with the latest such intervention coming just this week.

Traders said the central bank intervened on Tuesday. The central bank itself declined to comment.

But the central bank will need to do much more if it expects to alter the currency rate. Even when Standard & Poor's on Thursday lowered Israel's local-currency rating a notch to A+ from AA-, the currency barely budged.

Israel still maintains an A or better rating from all three major credit rating agencies. Together, the intervention earlier in the week and the credit downgrade have done little to stop the currency's ascent, with the shekel up 10 of the last 11 trading days and falling just 0.1% on the downgrade.

Helping the currency is the shekel's increasing viability as a tradable asset. The currency of Israel has moved from obscurity to the world of black box traders and now appears prominently on radar screens of most hedge funds. Daily trading volume is currently between $4.0 billion to $5.0 billion, according to the Bank of Israel; that is double what it was 10 years ago.

The central bank will likely continue to manage the shekel's appreciation. But with fears of a housing bubble limiting interest rate decreases as a tool, the bank is caught in a bind. The dollar below ILS3.00 is just something exporters are going to have to live with.

title: RPT-Israel's  central bank  to be tested in new battle to tame the shekel
text:
(Repeats story that ran on Wednesday with no changes)

* Bank of Israel bought estimated $100 mln of forex

* First intervention since July 2011

* Natural gas production helping to boost shekel

By Steven Scheer

JERUSALEM, April 10 (Reuters) - After standing by for months, the Bank of Israel has finally run out of patience and could face a lengthy battle to rein in the shekel as Japan's massive stimulus drives funds into emerging markets.

The shekel has gained more than 5 percent over the past four months against the dollar and the euro, posing a risk to Israel's exports which account for 40 percent of economic activity.

Japan's announcement last Thursday that it planned to pump $1.4 trillion into its economy in less than two years is seen as a catalyst that will drive capital flows into higher-yielding emerging market assets, prompting the Bank of Israel to step into the market on Monday for the first time since July 2011.

Japan's move and weak U.S. jobs data on Friday pushed dollar-shekel below what was believed to be a psychologically important 3.6 level for a fresh 17-month low.

Gaelle Blanchard, an emerging markets strategist at Societie Generale, said those events "changed the mood in the market."

"You see the impact in all emerging market currencies. Everything is booming now," she said. "People need to invest money and are trying to find a good place."

The shekel has been one of the best-performing emerging market currencies this year, reflecting Israel's relatively strong economy and high interest rates and expectations that the start of natural gas production last month will improve the government's fiscal position.

After cutting interest rates four times last year, the central bank has kept them steady over the past three months. That suggests it will use intervention as its main tool to weaken the shekel since lowering its benchmark interest rate, now at 1.75 percent, could further inflame Israeli housing prices, which have rallied 50 percent in four years.

"They are in a trap," said Tal Zohar, chief executive of forex broker FXCM Israel. "They don't want to reduce rates so not to increase the housing bubble but they want a weak shekel."

Israel's economy and finances are set to benefit from the start of natural gas production last month at the Tamar field off the Mediterranean coast, which will save the country's electricity utility the expense of having to import expensive fuels.

Natural gas production is expected to add 1 percentage point to economic growth this year, which the Bank of Israel forecasts at 3.8 percent.

Tamar and the larger Leviathan field nearby, which comes online in 2016, will probably export natural gas. The central bank has supported a finance ministry proposal to set up a sovereign wealth fund for income from the two fields to keep the shekel in check in the long run.

TEST OF RESOLVE

Israel's exports of goods, which mostly head to Europe and the United States, grew only 0.1 percent last year and leading exporters have been calling for central bank intervention to tame the shekel for some time.

"The intervention was more of a signal than actual policy," Zohar said of Monday's action.

"What they (the Bank of Israel) are doing is trying to push back the speculators who are weakening the dollar ... They are saying 'we are looking at it very carefully,'" he said.

Since the intervention, the dollar has recovered to 3.64 shekels while the euro has strengthened to 4.76 shekels from 4.66. But dealers say short-term investors have been helping drive the shekel higher and expect them to test the central bank's resolve again.

"It's only a matter of time until they test the bank of Israel again," said a dealer at Israel Discount Bank. "It looks like each side is waiting for the other side to move."

Zohar expects dollar-shekel to move back to 3.70 in the next few months while Blanchard sees it at 3.65 at the end of June.

The central bank said on Monday it "will act in the foreign exchange market in the event of unusual movements in the exchange rate which are inconsistent with the underlying economic conditions or when conditions in the foreign exchange market are disorderly."

During its last interventions between March 2008 and July 2011 the bank bought some $50 billion of foreign currency, mainly dollars, to keep the shekel in check. Analysts doubt the current round will be so large, particularly as current foreign exchange reserve levels of nearly $80 billion are sufficient.

title: Israel's Deficit Widens Sharply in First Quarter
text:
Special to DOW JONES NEWWIRES

JERUSALEM--Israel's government deficit for the first quarter nearly tripled in size compared with the previous year, the finance ministry said Monday, underscoring growing concerns among economists about the country's balance of payments.

The deficit expanded to 4.6 billion shekels ($1.27 billion) from ILS1.6 billion, the finance ministry said. Economists said the deficit was larger than expected.

"The deficit is the biggest risk to the Israeli economy now," said Alex Zabezhinsky, chief economist at DS Investment House in Tel Aviv. On Sunday, the central bank warned that the country's growing deficit was likely to lead to higher borrowing costs.

The government is currently operating without an annual budget after elections were held earlier this year. Each month spending is limited to one-twelfth of last year's total budget until a new one is approved. Such an arrangement usually results in fiscal tightening, but the deficit has been growing due to lower revenue, Mr. Zabezhinksy said.

In 2012, the deficit totaled 4.2% of gross domestic product, well above the country's target of 2% of GDP. Even if the government cuts the proposed 2013 budget by 5%, as currently planned, the deficit for 2013 is likely to reach 3.6% of GDP, again missing the target, the bank said.

title: Israel Industry Leaders Call on  Central Bank  to Weaken Shekel
text:
Special to DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

JERUSALEM--Israeli manufacturers and exporters on Thursday continued to call on the central bank to intervene in the foreign-currency market to stem the shekel's strength, which they say is threatening the whole economy.

Although profit-taking weakened the shekel slightly Thursday morning, it was still trading at levels not seen since 2011, a year when the central bank intervened several times to stabilize the currency.

Currency traders and economists said the start of gas production at a new gas field Sunday was the main reason for the shekel's rise this week, as it reduces the need for local shekel sales to buy dollar-denominated fuel.

In addition, a large interest rate differential with other developed countries and a relatively robust economic performance have been keeping the shekel strong since the beginning of the year.

On Thursday, the Manufacturers Association of Israel and government-backed Israel Export Institute said the Bank of Israel should buy dollars, as it has done in the past, to help weaken the shekel. They said the strong shekel makes Israel's exports more expensive abroad, hurting the whole economy. About 40% of Israel's gross domestic product comes from exports, according to the finance ministry.

"The Bank of Israel understands the importance of manufacturing and exports, and should use all of their tools, including intervention in the foreign currency market, to make sure Israel can succeed in the world market," Ruby Ginel, the Manufacturers Association's deputy director of regulation and economy, told Dow Jones.

He said the shekel's ideal level would be about ILS4 per dollar. "At that level customers abroad will buy our products and it's also strong enough for the local economy in Israel," Mr. Ginel said.

At 1036 GMT, the dollar was trading at ILS3.6280.

Ramzi Gabay, chairman of the Israel Export Institute also called on the bank to buy dollars.

Additionally, he added in a statement that the government needs to work on setting up the sovereign wealth fund it approved last year to invest Israel's gas revenue overseas rather than at home to prevent too strong a shekel, rapid inflation and other economic instability.

The central bank said it wasn't commenting on calls to intervene in the market.

Expectations of central bank intervention in the foreign-exchange market have been running high since Israel's Tamar gas field, which contains about 9 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, started production at the weekend.

The field is expected to add one percentage point to the growth of Israel's GDP this year. The economy is expected to grow 3.8% in 2013, taking into account the gas, most of which is earmarked for domestic consumption.

The shekel is also expected to become stronger because large companies, including the state-owned electric company, will no longer need foreign currency to purchase energy abroad.

title: Israel  Shekel Drops As Traders Brace for  Intervention  Risk

The Israeli shekel fell Wednesday as traders grew nervous that the country's central bank might intervene to weaken the currency from its highest levels in a year and a half.

The dollar pushed 0.5% higher against the falling shekel through the day, reaching a high of ILS3.63. This chipped away at the recent smooth upward path of the Israeli currency, which has been rallying faster since a new gas field started production this week, reducing the need for local shekel sales to buy dollar-denominated fuel.

The shekel's current levels now match the points where the central bank has intervened in the past, making market-watchers jumpy.

"We are closer than ever to another intervention," said Rony Gitlin, head of spot trading at Bank Leumi Le Israel, one of the country's largest banks.

While the central bank doesn't set a target for the shekel's exchange rate, it maintains a policy of intervening in the currencies market in reaction to sudden rises in the shekel that could compromise the country's exports. The central bank couldn't immediately be reached for comment Wednesday.

Expectations for an intervention have been running high since the Tamar field, which contains about 9 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, started production Sunday.

The gas field is expected to add one percentage point to the growth of Israel's gross domestic product this year. Taking the gas production into consideration, the central bank expects the economy to grow 3.8%; without the gas it would grow 2.8%.

The natural gas from Tamar will drastically reduce the amount of money the state-owned electric company and other large companies spend on importing fuel. The reduced need to buy foreign energy also contributes to a stronger shekel, analysts said.

Before the shekel's surge this week, it had already been trading at its strongest points since late 2011, mainly because of Israel's comparatively high benchmark interest rate of 1.75%. Israel has also weathered the global economic slowdown well, with GDP growing about 3% in 2012, as compared with the near-recession levels in Europe.

Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer said Tuesday that the government needs to invest some of its natural gas revenues abroad through a sovereign wealth fund to prevent the shekel from getting too strong. Speaking at a press conference, Mr. Fischer said such a fund, approved last year but not yet set up, should be established immediately.

Although the government approved the fund, it isn't clear what office would govern it, and whether or not it would be for the revenue from the Tamar field, or for the larger Leviathan field, scheduled to begin production later this decade.

title: RPT-POLL-Bank of Israel still seen holding rates steady, but may be close call

 JERUSALEM, Feb 21 (Reuters) - Gains in the shekel  have increased the chances of a Bank of Israel rate cut but most analysts still expect the central bank to hold off for at least another month, a Reuters poll showed.

 Seven of the 11 economists surveyed by Reuters expect the monetary policy committee (MPC) will keep the benchmark rate at 1.75 percent for a second straight month. The others foresee a quarter-point reduction to 1.5 percent.

 The central bank will announce its decision on Monday at 5.30 pm (1530 GMT).

 Minutes from the Jan. 28 decision showed the MPC was in no rush to lower rates further amid signs of economic and price stability and concerns over rising home prices. Policymakers noted that the level of pessimism in the economy had declined and no longer indicated a continued slowdown in activity.

 Rafael Gozlan, chief economist at the IBI Investment House, said that while he expects at least one more rate cut in the next couple of months, the MPC would prefer to wait until Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu completes the building of a ruling coalition before adjusting rates again.

 "It will be a close call," Gozlan said. "I wouldn't be surprised if they do or don't go but I would be surprised if they don't cut in one of the next two meetings."

 Much depends on how concerned central bank officials are over the shekel's appreciation to 3.67 per dollar, its strongest level since November 2011. 

 Analysts noted that more importantly, the shekel has also risen more than 2 percent on a trade weighted basis since the last rate decision. With exports - which account for more than 40 percent of Israel's economic activity, slowing - exporters want action by the central bank, which has also raised speculation of a resumption of currency intervention.

Israel posted a budget deficit of 39 billion shekels in 2012, a much higher than planned 4.2 percent of gross domestic product. To meet a 3 percent target in 2013, the government will need to make steep spending cuts and hike taxes, according to the Bank of Israel.

 Those who expect a rate cut next week point to a series of weak economic numbers in the past week. The annual inflation rate edged down to 1.5 percent in January as local demand remained weak; fourth-quarter GDP grew at an annualised rate of 2.5 percent for its slowest pace in 3-1/2 years and industrial production slid in December.

 The economy grew 3.2 percent in 2012 and should grow 2.8 percent in 2013 excluding the start to natural gas production.

 Analysts also believe the central bank has largely given up in its fight against rising home prices. It tightened mortgage regulations this week in a move analysts believe could pave the way for further rate cuts without worrying about home costs.

title: UPDATE 2-Israel faces major budget challenge, says cbank

* Cbank head Fischer says budget a priority for new government

* Suggests bank may intervene if strong shekel keeps rising

(Recasts with central bank chief Fischer's comments)

By Ari Rabinovitch

JERUSALEM, Feb 13 (Reuters) - Israel's incoming government faces a major task to keep public finances in order, the head of its central bank said on Wednesday, while dropping hints the bank may intervene to weaken a strong shekel.

"It must be the hope of the government, of the prime minister, to get the budget in shape immediately. And that's something which would certainly benefit the country," Stanley Fischer told reporters.

"Whether it will be politically possible is something we'll have to wait and see," he said, as the Bank of Israel forecast a higher-than-target 2013 deficit of at least 3.6 percent of gross domestic product.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who was narrowly reelected in a Jan. 22 vote that had been brought forward because his previous government was unable to pass a 2013 budget, is still negotiating with potential coalition partners.

His party won 31 seats in the 120-member parliament and he has until mid-March to cobble together a new coalition.

Once formed, it will have to fill a budget hole that in 2012 ballooned to nearly 40 billion shekels ($11 billion), mostly due to lower than expected tax income. In GDP terms, that translates to 4.2 percent, more than double an initial aim.

"There are no easy solutions to this problem. In such cases there is frequently a temptation to kick the can down the road. We've seen that in other countries," Fischer said.

The budget deficit could jump to as high as 4.9 percent of GDP if the state does not cut spending or raise taxes, or 3.6 percent without tax hikes, the Bank of Israel said in a statement. The finance ministry's forecast is 3 percent.

The bank based its deficit prediction on 3.8 percent growth rate, and Fischer said Israel's economy remained strong in comparison to the rest of the world.

That rate includes natural gas production set to begin in a few months at a newly discovered off-shore field.

SHEKEL INTERVENTION?

Tapping into an increasingly fraught global debate about competitive devaluations, Fischer said the Bank of Israel might intervene in the currency market to weaken the shekel if it strengthened further.

Noting the shekel has been rising as other countries keep their interest rates low in comparison to Israel's 1.75 percent benchmark, he told reporters: "More money started coming into Israel to take advantage of the small differential...

"That's something we're going to have to watch."

The Bank of Israel has intervened to weaken the shekel in the past to protect the economy, and the currency is now at a 15-month high against the dollar.

Fischer's comment on Wednesday offered the clearest indication since last month - when he made similar remarks to Reuters Television at Davos - that it may do so again.

The strength of the currency has weighed on exporters, who account for 40 percent of Israel's economic activity and have urged intervention.
