title: UPDATE 1-Israel cbank sees  FX  buying as "essential" -minutes
text:
* Jan. 24 rate hike supported by all 4 cenbank officials

* Forex intervention "essential, should continue"

* Housing prices likely to gain further in 2011

* Global economy improving

(Adds details, comments)

By Steven Scheer

JERUSALEM, Feb 7 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel has decided that it would continue a nearly three-year policy of buying foreign currency to keep the shekel <ILS=> from appreciating rapidly, minutes of a Jan. 24 rates decision showed on Monday.

In the meeting that ended with a quarter-point increase in the benchmark rate <ILINR=ECI> to 2.25 percent, the question came up whether there was a need for intervention in the foreign exchange market, and if so, what degree was required.

"Discussion focused particularly on how much flexibility the exchange rate should be allowed, and the implications of various scenarios on the trade balance and on capital flows. It was agreed that in light of the developments on the real side during 2010, the Bank of Israel's policy ... was still essential and should continue," the minutes said.

The central bank started intervening in the market in March 2008 with $25 million a day, a level that rose to $100 million four months later. Since August 2009, intervention has been on days the Bank of Israel deems necessary.

It bought $2.085 billion of foreign currency in January after buying $1.815 billion in December.

The Bank of Israel, which has made slowing the shekel's rise central to its monetary policy, has bought tens of billions of dollars over the past three years but the Israeli currency has stayed strong, partly due to a wide interest rates gap with the United States and Europe -- Israel's main trading partners.

Some officials expressed fears of a further appreciation of the shekel should the central bank raise rates. But new central bank directives [ID:nLDE70J1KN] aimed at moderating the effects of wider interest rate differentials on the shekel allowed the rate hike to proceed, the minutes said.

Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer's decision to raise the key rate was supported by all four central bank officials. The increase was the first such move in four months and the seventh time since August 2009. The current interest rate is deemed expansionary, the bank said.

INFLATION

Inflation, according to the bond market and economists, is expected to remain at 3 percent or above for most of 2011, higher than an annual target of 1-3 percent. That, the minutes said, "indicate the need for an increase in the interest rate."

Israel had inflation 2.7 percent in 2010, much of that stemming from gains in housing costs, an issue that was a major challenge for the central bank last year.

House prices rose 17 percent in 2010 as low interest rates led to a rapid expansion of housing credit, while housing demand outpaced supply. Central bank officials agreed "there was a significant probability that housing prices would continue their rapid rate of increase in the coming year".

In addition to interest rate hikes, the Bank of Israel has already taken a number of steps aimed at raising banks' mortgage loan rates. Policymakers said they would introduce further measures "if there was no change in the path of prices and in the degree of leverage".

Also supporting a rate increase last month was Israel's "substantial expansion" of the economy and employment levels. After growing 4.5 percent in 2010, the central bank sees strong growth continuing in the first quarter of 2011, which would boost inflation, the minutes said.

"It was also noted that the most recent data indicate more positive assessments of the recovery of the global economy from the economic crisis," the central bank said.

(Editing by Ron Askew)

title: WSJ BLOG/Real Time Economics: Israel Minister Crows About Growth
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Real Time Economics blog at blogs.wsj.com/economics)


 
   Posted By Brenda Cronin 
 

Yuval Steinitz, the philosophy scholar-turned-finance minister of Israel, took a victory lap in the U.S. this week, noting that 2010 was "one of the best economic years ever for Israel."

In a conversation with The Wall Street Journal in New York, Steinitz said it was too early to predict the long-term effect of the upheaval in Egypt on Israel and the surrounding region. "If the result is more democracy, that's good," he said.

The economic ties between Israel and Egypt are "very low profile," he said, noting that, for the moment, there seemed to be "no direct substantial impact" from the instability.

Israel's export-oriented economy, after getting off to a strong start early last year, slowed its pace, notching an estimated annual growth rate of 4.2% in 2010. The growth is thanks in part to booming high-technology and tourism industries. Israel also has steadily trimmed its debt to 75% of gross domestic product from 80% in 2009 and is aiming for annual growth between 5% and 6%.

The country saw a record year for tourism, notching more than three million visitors in 2010. Among those tourists, 21% came from the U.S. and 15% from Russia. Israel added 120,000 jobs during the year--many in the tourism sector--and hopes to add 50,000 new jobs annually in coming years, Steinitz said.

The finance minister credited the recovery in part to a "very resilient" private sector, which held up despite the country's decision to raise taxes during the crisis. A new challenge, he indicated, is navigating "between a rock and hard place" of rising inflation and an appreciating currency. In the past three years, the shekel has risen 15% against the dollar. The central bank has intervened to keep the shekel from rising. Israel also has enlisted capital controls to contain inflows of capital drawn by the country's 4.5% rate.

Steinitz also echoed a refrain currently popular among leaders, noting that Israel is focusing on being a "competitor" on the world stage. However, he said that increased global competition doesn't mean a return of trade barriers and protectionism.

Recently, Stanley Fischer, governor of the Bank of Israel noted that, amid an uneven rise in commodity prices around the world, the international cooperation that flowered as nations sought to dig out together from the financial crisis has dwindled.

"I don't think there's much hope of international coordination on the issue of how to deal with rises in commodity prices," Fischer said. "Each country is going to do what it thinks best for itself."

However, Steinitz said international coordination is a prerequisite for competition. As long as there is "regulated competition," where everyone knows the rules, "then nobody will block it," he said.

title: FX  COLUMN-Israeli shekel might be worth a cautious look
text:
-- Neal Kimberley is an FX market analyst for Reuters. The opinions expressed are his own --

By Neal Kimberley

LONDON, Feb 2 (Reuters) - With protesters still thronging the streets of Cairo and deep political uncertainty over the future of Egypt, this might not seem the best moment to buy the Israeli shekel <ILS=>.

But adventurous traders might conclude that the fall in the Jewish state's currency against the dollar from 3.5130 on Jan. 18 to Wednesday's 3.6700 is overdone.

After all the abrupt slide in the shekel has rapidly taken it back to levels last seen in September with barely a pause.

The acceleration in shekel weakness since Thursday drove it to 3.75 per dollar on Monday and has mirrored the surge in popular unrest in neighbouring Egypt.

The 1979 peace treaty between the two countries has been a cornerstone of Israeli security for more than 30 years.

Yet there seems no indication so far that the popular calls for political change in Egypt include demands for a wholesale reassessment of the relationship with Israel.

So, although the political situation in Egypt and other Middle East and North African (MENA) countries is very fluid, a weakening of the shekel on geopolitical factors alone may have overshot.

Of course, traders will be aware that Israel's central bank has pushed against the strength of the shekel in recent months, intervening repeatedly to stem its rise.

The Bank of Israel bought $2.3 billion of foreign currency in December and on Jan. 20 imposed a reserve requirement on some foreign exchange derivative deals. [ID:nLDE70J1KN]

On Thursday, the finance ministry announced a proposal to tax profits on foreigners' investments in short-term debt -- another step to curb speculative inflows. [ID:nLDE70Q1HO] [ID:nLDE70J1KN]

Yet the central bank raised interest rates on Jan. 24, saying inflation expectations for the coming 12 months had increased to 3 percent, the upper limit of its target range. [ID:nLDE70N1Y5]

The central bank, noting imports into Israel rose 5 percent in December, said: "Inflationary pressures continue to mount in the emerging market economies, deriving from the steep increases in commodity prices in general, and food prices in particular."

Some might feel that continuing to seek a weakening of the shekel, especially in the face of the unrest-related sell-off, sits uncomfortably with an anti-inflationary strategy that recognises the threat of imported price pressures.

The central bank acknowledged in minutes of its Dec. 27 meeting that the "appreciation of the shekel in the last few months had helped to moderate inflation". [ID:nLDE7090V3]

And while bank governor Stanley Fischer, speaking in Davos on Jan. 26, still thought the shekel was slightly too firm (USD/ILS was then around 3.62), the International Monetary Fund on Jan. 24 took a different tack on the value of continued intervention against shekel strength. [ID:nLDE70P29I] [ID:nSLAOCE7NE]

"Given that reserves and central bank sterilisation losses are already considerable, and that persistent one-sided use of this instrument undermines the credibility of the floating exchange rate regime, it is ill-suited as the main means of reconciling inflation and competitiveness objectives."

After the sharp weakening of the shekel on Monday, and despite a subsequent rally to Wednesday's 3.67 level, traders could feel the Bank of Israel might be less inclined to lean against shekel strength at this level.

After all, the IMF said Israel needs to tighten monetary policy further and curb an overheating housing market.

LEVIATHAN

Another factor could contribute to a stronger shekel.

The discovery of the Leviathan offshore natural gas field could transform Israel's long-term energy security. [ID:nLDE6BT0FS]

Leviathan is estimated to have 16 trillion cubic feet (450 billion cubic metres) of gas. Nearby Tamar was the largest gas find in the world in 2009, at 8.4 trillion cubic feet.

While it will take some years before both projects come onstream, the combination of natural resources and Israel's high-tech industries could be attractive to international investors and ultimately boost the currency.

Taking a punt on the shekel is undoubtedly high-risk but it may be worth a tentative second look.

title: Israel FinMin Steinitz: Egypt Crisis A 'Surprise,' No Plans To Roll Back Capital Controls
text:
- Egypt Crisis A 'Surprise,' No Plans To Roll Back Capital Controls

- Impact Of Egypt Crisis On Local Economy Minimal For Now

- Strong Shekel Problem For Israel Exporters

- Future Hikes In Euro, US Rates Will Eventually Ease Shekel Pressure

- No Plan To Roll Back Capital Controls

- Stands By New Tax Regime For Energy Companies


 
   By Bradley Davis 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The turmoil in Egypt caught Israel by "surprise," the country's finance minister said Tuesday, but despite the conflict, the government will not roll back recently implemented capital controls designed to curtail appreciation in the Israeli shekel.

Israel Finance Minister Yuval Steinitz said it was too early to determine the outcome of the Egypt crisis, but that for now its impact on Israel's economy had been minimal. Israel has a miniscule trading relationship with Egypt and its other Middle East neighbors, he said.

If the crisis were to worsen, triggering the need for increased security measures in Israel, "that might put a burden on our budget," Steinitz said in an exclusive interview with Dow Jones Newswires and The Wall Street Journal.

The shekel weakened in the wake of the initial protests against the regime of Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak, but had already been on a weakening path in response to the government's recent implementation of capital controls. Those measures, which involved removing an exemption that foreign investors had for investing in Israeli government bonds, were implemented in response to a stream of so-called hot money making its way to Israel in a chase for returns on its relatively higher interest rates.

The capital controls are "around to stay," Steinitz said, as is the recently hammered-out tax regime for energy companies that will develop two giant gas finds off the coast of Israel, he said.

The central bank of Israel has intervened in currency markets to stem shekel strength; the finance minister said he supported such intervention, because Israel is heavily reliant on exports.

The bank had to act against the strong shekel because the loss of competitiveness could have been "disastrous" for a country whose exports account for 50% of gross domestic product, Steinitz said. The country found itself in a "very unique situation" as its economy marches to recovery, while many of its biggest trading partners among developed countries are seeing sluggish growth.

So far the capital controls have been effective. Although the safe-harbor dollar weakened by about 0.7% against the shekel Tuesday, over the past month the U.S. currency has appreciated by nearly 4.5%. This went some way to reverse the strong gains of recent years. From early 2007 to the end of 2010, the shekel rose 15% against the dollar.

With interest rates low in the U.S. and euro zone, investors have turned to fast-growing emerging markets for returns; many emerging markets, including Israel, have weathered the financial crisis in better shape than more-established economies, and are already on the path to normalizing monetary policy.

Israel's 4.5% growth for 2010 makes it an attractive destination for investors chasing yield, Steinitz said, as do its 2.25% key government rates.

But those key rates put Israel between a "rock and a hard place," Steinitz said, because as Israel's economy has recovered, it has needed to increase key rates even more to strangle possible inflation pressures--increasing those rates only increases the appeal of the shekel.

As the U.S. and euro zone increase their key rates, likely over the next year, he said, pressure on the shekel will ease.

Meanwhile, energy companies drilling for gas in the latest large find off the coast of Israel will "of course" pay higher tax in their exploitation of Israel's natural resources, he said, citing the reforms that his Ministry recently introduced to increase the "government's take" from resource exploitation. Previously, he said, Israel received no net royalty revenue from its natural resources.

title: UPDATE 1-Bank of Israel buys $100 mln after rate hike
text:
(Adds quotes, background)

TEL AVIV, Jan 25 (Reuters) - Israel's central bank intervened in the currency market on Tuesday to contain the shekel's appreciation a day after it raised its key lending rate by a quarter point to 2.25 percent.

The shekel weakened to 3.6010 per dollar after the bank stepped in and dollar buying by locals weakened the currency further to 3.6140. That compared with Monday's official rate of 3.6250, which was set before the interest rate announcement.

"They came in at 3.59 (shekels per dollar) and bought $100 million," a dealer at a large Israeli bank said.

The central bank has intervened repeatedly to contain a rally in the shekel, which hit a 27-month high of 3.528 shekels per dollar earlier this month. Last week the bank also imposed a reserve requirement on some foreign exchange derivative deals. [ID:nLDE70J1KN]

Local media has speculated more controls might be in the works, including possibly imposing a tax on capital movements. [ID:nLDE70J1KN] The Finance Ministry has declined comment on the reports.

The introduction of a reserve requirement briefly took some pressure off the shekel, giving the Bank of Israel more room to raise interest rates.

It raised its key lending rate <ILINR=ECI> by a quarter point on Monday to try and bring inflation back within target and analysts see further tightening in coming months. [ID:nLDE70N1XW]

"The interest rate hike was expected by the market," said Rony Gitlin, head of spot trading at Bank Leumi.

INFLATION PRESSURE

Ron Eichel, chief economist at Meitav Investment House, expects another quarter point rate increase in late April and sees the key rate reaching 3 percent by the end of 2011.

The rate hike was the first since September and came as rising housing prices and strong economic growth add to inflation pressure.

The central bank, in a statement on Monday, said inflation measured over the previous 12 months was likely to be above the upper limit of the 1-3 percent target inflation range for most of 2011 but return to within the range towards the end of the year.

Gitlin said the outlook for the shekel would depend on what further measures the central bank takes to contain the currency's rally, which threatens Israeli exports.

"The expectations are for more measures but it depends on what happens with the exchange rate," Gitlin said. "If the rate stays at about this level then maybe there won't be more measures."

After the bank imposed the reserve requirement the shekel weakened to 3.62 to the dollar from 3.56. The central bank said the reserve requirement was "expected to moderate the effect of the increase in the interest rate differentials on the strengthening of the shekel".

The imposition of a reserve requirement came after the central bank stipulated that Israelis and foreigners must report on transactions in foreign exchange swaps and forwards of more than $10 million in one day.

title: UPDATE 1-Israel fights shekel strength with reserves move
text:
* 10 pct reserve required on non-resident derivative deals

* Shekel sheds 1.7 pct but rally seen continuing in long run

* Move seen helping central bank raise interest rates

(Adds analysts' quotes, background)

By Tova Cohen

TEL AVIV, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Israel on Wednesday became the latest country to combat speculative money flows which have strengthened its currency when it imposed a reserve requirement on some foreign exchange derivative deals.

From Jan. 27, banks in Israel will have to meet a 10 percent reserve requirement on the value of foreign exchange swaps and forwards transactions by non-residents, the Bank of Israel said, as it seeks to protect exports and contain inflation.

"In the last few months the volume of foreign exchange derivative transactions by non-residents has increased markedly," the Bank of Israel said.

"A significant part of the increase in non-residents' transactions is in short-term instruments. This measure will strengthen the Bank of Israel's ability to achieve the objectives of its monetary, foreign exchange and financial stability policies."

In December foreigners made swaps worth $76 billion compared with $19 billion by Israelis and up from $59 billion in November.

The shekel weakened to 3.62 shekels per dollar from 3.56 prior to the announcement. The Bank of Israel is trying the reduce the amount of speculative capital flows by imposing a liquidity requirement of 10 percent of the value of the transaction, Ron Eichel, chief economist at Meitav Investment House, said.

"This can change short-term trends and reduce noise in the market but if the economic fundamentals are strong, in the end the currency will strengthen," Eichel told Reuters.

"Israel is like Brazil and other countries, it is trying to help exports and growth."

Brazil, Chile, Peru, Taiwan, South Korea, Turkey, South Africa and others have taken measures to keep their currencies from strengthening or control the flow of money into their economies as investors pour money into higher-yielding markets.

SHEKEL WILL CONTINUE TO GAIN

The shekel reached a 27-month high of 3.528 shekels per dollar earlier this month and the Bank of Israel has intervened repeatedly to contain the currency's rally. It bought $2.3 billion of foreign currency in December, bringing its forex reserves to a record $70.9 billion.

Eichel said the shekel will continue to strengthen in the long term even without speculators because economic growth is strong, interest rates are expected to rise and there is a surplus in the country's balance of payments. Israel's economy grew a provisional 4.5 percent in 2010.

"I don't think anyone in the Bank of Israel is innocent enough to believe this will change the trend," Eichel said.

Fourteen of 15 economists polled by Reuters expect the central bank to raise its short-term lending rate by 0.25 percentage point to 2.25 percent on Monday. The rate is expected to reach 3.0-3.5 percent by the end of 2011.

Michael Sarel, head of economic research at Harel Finance, said even a short-term depreciation of the shekel will enable the central bank to raise rates more rapidly.

"We estimate that in the wake of the Bank of Israel's measure, the chances for a rate hike on Monday have increased considerably and the rate of increases in the interest rate in the coming year is expected to be more rapid," Sarel said.

A Bank of Israel source said the reserves measure will make this type of transaction less attractive for foreign players.

"It makes the transaction more expensive for local banks," the source said, as the banks will not get interest on the 10 percent reserves and this will carry over to foreign banks.

The Bank of Israel's order follows its announcement on Wednesday that it will require Israelis and foreigners to report on transactions in foreign exchange swaps and forwards of more than $10 million in one day.

Additionally, non-residents who perform transactions in short-term Bank of Israel bills known as makams and short-term government bonds of more than 10 million shekels in one day will be required to report details of the transactions and their balance of holdings of such assets.

title: UPDATE 1-Shekel slides on aggressive Israel cbank buying
text:
* Bank of Israel buys $450 million of forex -dealers

* Intervention this week estimated at $1 billion

* Euro-shekel moves off 8-1/2 year low

* December inflation data due on Friday

By Steven Scheer

JERUSALEM, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Israel's shekel slid against the euro <EURILS=> and dollar <ILS=> on Thursday, as the European currency spiked globally and on another day of aggressive Bank of Israel intervention.

The combination of the two sent the shekel sliding more than 3 percent against the euro, a day after the single currency hit an 8-1/2 year low against the Israeli currency.

Dealers estimated the central bank bought some $450 million of foreign currency in three rounds during the day as it continues to fight powerful market forces in trying to prevent a rapid appreciation of the shekel, which risks hurting Israeli exports.

One dealer at a large Israeli bank said the Bank of Israel had bought around $1 billion of foreign currency this week. That compared with purchases of $1.82 billion for all of December.

On most days, intervention has marginal, if any, impact on daily trading but dealers said the central bank caught the market off-guard on Thursday.

"The Bank of Israel understood the market was short dollars and it really had an impact," said the dealer, who asked not to be named. "When the market is short, you don't need a lot of dollar buying ... It was a very crazy day."

Last week, the shekel had reached 3.5280 per dollar, its strongest level since October 2007. On Wednesday, it hit 4.5855 per euro, its highest point since August 2002.

"The Bank of Israel is defending the 3.50 per dollar and 4.60 per euro levels strongly," the dealer said.

At 1330 GMT, the central bank fixed the shekel at 3.5660 to the dollar and 4.7052 per euro, up 0.8 and 2.6 percent, respectively.

Dealers said that buying by hedge funds and foreign banks of a few hundred million dollars helped to push the dollar up to near 3.59 shekels and the euro to 4.76 after the fixing, before profit taking set in and pared those gains late in the session.

Also boosting euro-shekel was another strong rally in euro-dollar to above $1.33.

Another dealer at an Israeli bank said there was talk of the Finance Ministry buying foreign currency but the ministry said it was just a regular operation of swapping dollar-denominated debt into shekels.

Last week, a ministry official said the ministry planned to swap a few billion dollars of its debt in 2011 to take advantage of the shekel's strength. [ID:nLDE7040X3]

Analysts say the trend is for the shekel to further appreciate due to a strong economy and expectations of a few more interest rate increases this year that will further widen the gap with the United States and Europe and encourage more capital inflows.

The Bank of Israel has raised its benchmark rate by 1.5 percentage points to 2 percent since August 2009 but it left the rate unchanged at its past three meetings. Still, the market believes the rate will rise to 3 percent or more this year.

The timing depends on the inflation outlook. Inflation data from December is due on Friday, with the consumer price index forecast to have risen 0.3 percent from November and 2.6 percent over the past 12 months. [ID:nLDE7090NX] (Editing by Susan Fenton)

TEL AVIV, Dec 13 (Reuters) - Israel's central bank will continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market to ensure Israeli exports remain competitive, Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer said on Monday.

Some analysts have questioned whether Fischer can continue contradictory policies of buying foreign currency while also raising interest rates, especially with the country's forex reserves nearing $70 billion.

The rate hikes have helped strengthen the shekel, which in turn has led the central bank to buy tens of billions of dollars to curb its own currency's gains.

Fischer also said that the central bank would not allow surging housing prices to turn into a real estate bubble and that the Bank of Israel would continue to take steps if prices did not fall.

He said inflation will likely end 2010 within an annual government target of 1-3 percent. The rate was 2.5 percent in October.

Fischer said Israel's economy, which is on track to grow 4 percent in 2010, is in a good situation. He downplayed a rise in the unemployment rate to 6.6 percent in the third quarter from 6.4 percent in the previous three months -- near an all-time low of 5.9 percent -- saying the gain was due to a jump in the labour participation rate.

Also at the conference, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel must stick to responsible fiscal policies.

"Keeping responsible fiscal policies is critical," he said, adding he intended for Israel to become one of the world's top 15 economic powers in the next 15 years.

"We have to lower, restrain or reduce spending. We have to lower taxes. We have to invest in education. We have to expand infrastructure and we have to encourage entrepreneurship and cut bureaucracy," he said.

title: FACTBOX-OECD ups most 2010 GDP fcasts for E.Europe, Israel
text:
PRAGUE, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The OECD raised its 2010 growth forecasts for most its members in emerging Europe on Thursday, although it reduced that of Hungary and tempered its 2011 outlook for Israel, the Czech Republic and non-member Estonia.

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said Polish inflation indicated monetary tightening ahead and Israel's central bank should continue raising rates, although currency interventions there were increasingly unwarranted.

Following are the main points from the OECD Economic Outlook report on OECD members including Israel and ex-communist European Union states.

POLAND Poland is seen growing 3.5 percent this year and 4 percent in 2011, helped by booming exports, a surge in domestic demand, infrastructure investments partly funded by the EU, and preparations for the 2012 Euro football Championship.

The OECD said inflation was expected to rise, "pointing to the need for an early start to monetary tightening". Many analysts believe Poland's central bank may raise its 3.5 percent base rate at a meeting next week.

Poland's fiscal deficit is seen rising to 8 percent of economic output this year, well above the 6.9 percent originally planned, and should decline to 6.7 percent of GDP next year.

The OECD said plans to cap public spending and hike taxes, twinned with strong growth, should put public finances on a more sustainable path in 2012, but it said Poland's request that it and other new EU members be allowed to exclude spending tied to pension reform would jeopardise fiscal consolidation if granted.

CZECH REPUBLIC The OECD expects the Czech economy to grow by 2.4 percent in 2010 and 2.8 percent in 2011, driven by exports to its main trading partner Germany as a weak labour market and austerity steps by the right-of-centre government curb domestic demand.

It said growth should accelerate to 3.2 percent in 2012, with the main risks being developments in major export markets, while consumers could also reduce activity due to austerity and an expected increase in electricity prices next year.

It said Czech monetary policy can remain accomodative for some time because, even though headline inflation has picked up to near the centre of the central bank's target range, fiscal consolidation would tame price pressure.

HUNGARY The OECD trimmed its 2010 growth forecast to 1.1 percent, from 1.2 percent previously. It saw Hungary's expansion quickening to 3.1 percent in 2012 on the back of a strong German recovery, while inflation should stabilise at around the central bank's 3 percent target, the OECD said.

It said that after the government passed temporary measures to stabilise finances, including ad-hoc taxes on banks and mostly foreign-owned utilities and retailers and a decision to roll back pension reform, it needed to spell out a credible, long-term fiscal plan to avoid losing investor confidence.

The OECD said downside risks could be compounded if Budapset does not reach a precautionary safety net agreement with international lenders following the expiration of a 20 billion euro International Monetary Fund-led deal that ended last month.

ISRAEL

Israel's economy is expected to slow slightly in the second half of this year for full-year growth growth of 3.9 percent, inching up 4 percent or more in 2011 and 2012.

The OECD said inflation was likely to trend towards the upper limit of the central bank's 1 to 3 percent target band and therefore policymakers needed to continue raising interest rates. It also said foreign currency purchases meant to shield the export sector were "increasingly unwarranted".

ESTONIA

The OECD said a return to robust consumer spending would drive growth to 3.4 percent next year and about 4 percent in 2012. It said headline inflation was "worrying", although persistent double-digit unemployment and general economic weakness meant core price growth would pick up more slowly.

It said fiscal policy was under control and the fiscal gap was not expected to exceed the EU's prescribed ceiling of 3 percent of gross domestic product.

(Reporting by Michael Winfrey; Editing by John Stonestreet)

title: WSJ(10/20)  Israel 's Bank Chief Stands By  Interventions
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL) 
   By Charles Levinson 

JERUSALEM -- Israel's influential central bank chief Stanley Fischer defended his aggressive attempts to keep a lid on the shekel, saying his long-running currency intervention has successfully protected Israel from the worst of the global economic and financial crisis.

His defense, in an interview at the Bank of Israel here, comes as other countries, including Japan and Brazil, have more recently moved to keep their own currencies in check to stimulate exports and, by extension, broader economic growth.

That has roiled currency markets in recent weeks, triggering a debate on the need for new global accords to better regulate exchange-rate policy. Mr. Fischer's weak-shekel policy predates the current turmoil, and hasn't generated much fuss because of the relatively small size of Israel's economy.

But Mr. Fischer commands an outsized voice in global financial markets, in part because of his role tamping down the Asian crisis in the late 1990s, when he was the International Monetary Fund's second-in-command.

"The prime reason we're continuing to intervene is we want to protect, we want to not penalize the export sector excessively" from exaggerated currency fluctuations, he said.

Mr. Fischer, meanwhile, has steadily raised interest rates amid a real-estate boom -- adding upward pressure on the shekel by luring investors.

He shrugged off the competing challenges. "It's rare in central banking that you're not engaged in an act of trying to balance various conflicting factors," he said.

Israel's challenge is similar to that of many other export-dependent economies that have struggled to keep their currencies relatively weak and their exports competitive as global investors -- in search of higher yields -- pour money into their markets.

Mr. Fischer began buying up dollars in March 2008, the first intervention by the Israeli central bank in currency markets in over a decade. The global financial crisis was starting to snowball, and the buying was aimed at bolstering Israel's foreign reserves for tough times ahead, as well as depressing the shekel to help ailing exporters, who account for between 40% and 45% of Israel's economic output.

From mid-2008 to mid-2009, the bank snatched up $100 million a day. It has continued at a furious pace, adding over $7 billion to its reserves so far this year. In mid-2008, the dollar was fetching about three shekels; through most of 2010, it was buying just under four shekels. It has fallen back again to around 3.6 shekels in recent weeks.

The dollar buying equals roughly 3% of gross domestic product. Foreign reserves stand at nearly $70 billion, up from $29 billion before Mr. Fischer began his dollar binge.

Mr. Fischer has faced criticism for his policy. The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development has urged a halt. Mr. Fischer's two predecessors and Finance Minister Yuval Steinitz have publicly questioned the policy.

Carrying large dollar reserves when U.S. interest rates are at or near zero is also expensive. Mr. Fischer said broader economic concerns outweigh any losses from interest-rate gaps.

His policy, meanwhile, appears to have helped Israeli exports, which bottomed out in the first quarter of 2009, but have steadily rebounded.

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: ANALYSIS-Strong growth, shekel create dilemma for Israel cbank
text:
* Israeli currency at 2-year high, hurting exports

* House prices driving surge in inflation

* Central bank hiking rates while buying dollars

* Analysts see unorthodox twin-track policy continuing

By Steven Scheer

JERUSALEM, Oct 18 (Reuters) - Concerns about price pressures at home and a shaky economic outlook abroad mean the Bank of Israel looks set to continue raising interest rates while buying dollars as the price of keeping an export-driven recovery on track.

Inflation worries prompted mainly by the surging cost of housing together with a rampant stock market -- Tel Aviv share indices are at all-time highs -- have led to a series of rate hikes over the past year.

Those moves, along with expectations of more tightening that would further widen the rate differential between Israel and the United States, have helped propel the local shekel currency <ILS=> to a two-year high against the dollar.

That in turn has eroded the competitiveness of the country's exports, which account for more than 40 percent of economic activity, so the central bank has bought tens of billions of dollars to try to slow the Israeli currency's appreciation.

At a time of marked dollar weakness, Israel's foreign currency reserves are rising steadily and topped $66 billion in September, more than double the level of two years ago.

Central banks typically do not raise rates -- putting upward pressure on the domestic currency -- and intervene in the foreign exchange market at the same time.

But many analysts believe Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer has little choice but to carry on doing just that.

"By stopping interventions he would infuriate exporters and if he stopped raising rates, it could create a housing bubble and risk higher inflation especially with (global) oil prices going up," said Elisabeth Gruie, a strategist at BNP Paribas.

BITING THE BULLET

Rafi Gozlan, an economist at Leader Capital Markets, said Fischer will continue to do both for as long as it takes to help the Israeli economy, which could face slower growth in 2011 due weakness abroad, notably in the United States and Europe.

In a possible foretaste, the statistics bureau trimmed its 2010 growth estimate on Sunday to 4 pct of GDP from 4.1 pct, saying it now expected exports to expand by 9.1 pct rather than the 13.1 percent it forecast just a month ago. [ID:nLDE69G069]

The Bank of Israel started intervening in the currency market in March 2008 with purchases of $25 million a day. Now it intervenes whenever it deems necessary and has bought more than $1 billion in the past month.

"Intervention is the main reason that enabled Israeli exports to survive," said Ori Yehudai, chairman of the economics committee at Israel's manufacturers' Association. "We are competing in a very competitive world."

But the Finance Ministry has criticised both the rate hikes and intervention, saying the rates gap with the United States was leading to speculation and that central bank was losing money by holding such high foreign currency reserves.

"The Bank of Israel is not a bank of profits," Fischer said on Oct. 3 in response, while holding out against government proposals to tax speculators.

BALANCING ACT

Israel, a high-tech powerhouse, experienced only a minor hit from the global crisis. The economy is forecast to grow at least 4 percent this year and at a slightly slower pace in 2011, well above estimates for the United States and Europe.

Annual inflation, at 1.8 percent in August, is meanwhile expected to reach 3 percent in the coming year -- the top end of a target of 1-3 percent. House prices in particular have jumped.

"(Fischer) needs to perform a balancing act," said UBS economist Reinhard Cluse. "He needs to ensure against all kinds of risks like a global double dip (recession), which would hit the Israeli economy. On the other hand there is a risk to inflation, with the real estate market turning into a bubble."

Since August 2009, Israel has raised its benchmark rate by 1.5 percentage points to 2 percent and most analysts see one more hike by year-end, with the rate above 3 percent in 2011.

Cluse views Fischer's rate hikes as measured to limit further shekel gains while avoiding stifling economic growth.

"At 2 percent, rates are above the United States and the European Central Bank but still... quite accommodative," he said.

The shekel stands at around 3.58 per dollar, rising nearly 7 percent since rate hikes resumed in late July. Fischer contends the currency, which has also been bolstered by a current account surplus, would be stronger still but for the interventions.

Analysts remain bullish on the shekel, given expectations of further easing measures by the U.S. Federal Reserve and scope for more Israel rate hikes. Goldman Sachs on Thursday forecast a rate of 3.30 per dollar within six months.

"If you have a strong economy, you have a strong currency," added Psagot brokerage chief economist Vered Dar, who questions the wisdom of the central bank's approach.

"The interest rate tool isn't sharp enough to help with housing prices," she said, noting it took 400 basis points of hikes over two years last decade to cool the U.S. property market.

(Additional reporting by Tova Cohen; Editing by John Stonestreet)

title: Israel FinMin urges c. bank not to raise s-term rates
text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Israeli Finance Minister Yuval Steinitz on Tuesday again urged Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer not to raise short-term interest rates, saying a widening rate gap with Western countries was pushing the dollar down against the shekel.

Both Steinitz and Fischer have warned repeatedly over the past two years that a strong shekel is hurting Israel's exports.

"We need to keep reasonable gaps between us and the world because when the interest rate gap with the United States widens, dollars search for a place to go, and go to the place where rates are the highest," Steinitz told a conference.

"We need to be careful not to raise rates too much in comparison with Western countries," he added.

Steinitz, in a meeting with ministry officials, had also requested the central bank leave rates unchanged last month.

But the Bank of Israel on Sept. 27 raised its benchmark rate by a quarter-point to 2 percent, compared with zero for the United States and 1 percent for the euro zone. It was the sixth move since August 2009 and comes as surging housing prices threaten higher inflation.

The higher rates, coupled with a stronger euro-dollar, have led to a sharp appreciation of the shekel <ILS=> against the U.S. currency to a two-year high, hurting the export sector which accounts for more than 40 percent of Israel's economic activity.

To stem the dollar's slide, the Bank of Israel has intervened in the market by buying hundreds of millions of dollars in recent weeks as the shekel rose from 3.85 per dollar in late July to 3.60.

Steinitz, who believes exporters should diversify more to rapidly-expanding markets in Asia, said he supported the central bank's intervention. He said his relationship with Fischer was good, even though the two do not always agree on policy.

Steinitz also said the problem of Israel's high housing prices could not be solved by raising interest rates or taxes, but instead with more supply of homes. The problem would not be resolved for "a year or two", he said.

On the economy, Steinitz said that despite growth expected to top 4 percent this year, "we have not returned to normal" since weakeness in the United States and Europe would affect Israel. (Reporting by Steven Scheer; Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: Israel shekel at 2-year peak vs dollar, rate rise seen
text:
JERUSALEM, Sept 29 (Reuters) - The Israeli shekel <ILS=> rose 0.3 percent to a nearly two-year high against the dollar in light holiday trading on Wednesday on expectations of further Israeli rate rises and global dollar weakness.

The shekel was fixed at 3.6650 per dollar -- its strongest level since Oct. 15, 2008 -- from Tuesday's rate of 3.6770, which had been an 8-1/2-month peak.

The fix took place three hours earlier than usual because of the Jewish festival of Sukkoth, which ends on Thursday evening. Trading volumes were very low and volatile. Financial markets will be closed on Thursday.

BNP Paribas said in a client note that it expects the shekel to strengthen further to 3.60 now that it has broken above 3.67.

The shekel's advance from a low of 3.85 began after the Bank of Israel surprised the market with a rate rise in late July. The benchmark rate was held in August, but the shekel rose further in September on expectations of a rate hike this week.

As expected, the central bank raised its key rate by a quarter-point to 2 percent on Monday, its sixth such move since August 2009, in a bid to damp down surging real estate prices and rising inflation.

Analysts expect one more hike by the end of the year, and further rises in the key rate to as much as 3.5 percent in 2011.

The dollar's recent global weakness has been exacerbated by expectations of further easing measures by the Federal Reserve.

The Bank of Israel has intervened frequently in the past month to prevent a rapid appreciation of the shekel, which would hurt exports. It bought an estimated $250 million of foreign currency in the open market on Tuesday, but dealers did not report any intervention on Wednesday. (Editing by Tim Pearce)

title: UPDATE 2- Israel  shekel strong after rate hike,  intervention
text:
* Near 8-1/2 month highs after Monday's 25 bp hike

* Central Bank buys dollars to stem shekel appreciation

* House prices seen rising further, adding to inflation

* C.Bank focused on shorter-term econ factors - analyst

(Adds c.bank intervention, closing prices)

By Tova Cohen

TEL AVIV, Sept 28 (Reuters) - The Israeli shekel <ILS=> ended close to multi-month highs on Tuesday in the face of central bank intervention to stem its rise, a day after the bank raised interest rates as part of efforts to keep inflation in check.

The shekel's official rate was set at 3.6770 per dollar, setting a new 8-1/2 month high for the daily fixing and compared with a traded rate of 3.6650 after the rate rise was announced on Monday.

The currency weakened to 3.682 after the fixing as the Bank of Israel bought $250 million to counter its appreciation, which is hurting exports.

The rate increase, by 25 basis points to 2 percent, was largely expected by the market, though Finance Minister Yuval Steinitz had urged the central bank on Sunday not to raise rates to avoid stifling the economic recovery.

An analyst said the tightening showed the central bank was focused on the economy's near-term prospects. The bank on Tuesday lowered its 2011 GDP growth estimate, after raising its forecast for 2010 on Monday. [ID:nLDE68R114]

Higher vegetable prices are likely to push up the consumer price index in September, but the central bank will look primarily at currently soaring house prices to determine the next interest rate move, said Amir Kahanovich, chief economist at the Clal Finance brokerage.

"If the situation continues like it was in August and September, when housing prices kept rising, inflationary expectations are up and stocks are gaining, the central bank will have to raise rates again," Kahanovich said.

There is a more than 50 percent chance of a rate rise at the end of November, he said, but an October increase is less likely.

"The central bank is looking more at the short term. They raised their forecast for 2010 and this is more important to them right now. The growth in 2011 of 3.8 percent will still be rapid.

"Growth is still strong and negative real interest rates aren't appropriate for this growth," he said, adding that the long-term forecasts were problematic as it was difficult to forecast long-term global trade trends.

An Israel Discount Bank dealer said the shekel dip "looks like a normal correction, but a lot will depend on the Bank of Israel."

BONDS, SHARES FLAT

Government bond prices <0#ILGOI=TA> edged down 0.1 percent.

The blue chip Tel Aviv 25 index <.TA25> was flat. "The rate hike was expected and in days leading up to the move the market rose strongly," said a Tel Aviv equities trader.

Kahanovich said bonds linked to the consumer price index were falling across the board as the Bank of Israel's move will likely lead to a decline in inflation expectations.

Some market players thought the central bank would not raise rates this month in light of the shekel's recent rise. The Bank of Israel has bought dollars several times this month to try to stem the shekel's gain.

The bank said on Monday that inflation, an annual 1.8 percent in August, was expected to reach 2.5 percent in the next year -- near the top of an official 1-3 percent target -- with the interest rate likely to gradually rise to 2.7 percent, according to a consensus of the bank's economists.

"This will be a game of cat and mouse," the dealer said. "The market will wait for another rate hike. If the central bank raises the rate two months in a row that would be a lot."

title: The Bank of Israel - Letter of the Governor accompanying the Inflation Report for April-June 2010
text:
Release date - 03082010

This Inflation Report, covering the second quarter of 2010, is submitted to the government, the Knesset and the public as part of the process of assessing the inflation rate in relation to the inflation target set by the government.

The Report was prepared in the Senior Monetary Forum of the Bank of Israel, headed by the Governor, the forum in which the Governor makes decisions on the interest rate[1].

The CPI rose by 1.6 percent in the second quarter of 2010, mainly due to seasonal factors. The CPI excluding the seasonal components-fruit and vegetables and clothing and footwear-rose by 0.7 percent. The housing component, which reflects the price of housing services by means of apartment rentals, increased by 2.3 percent in the second quarter, faster than the other components. The rate of inflation over the previous twelve months moderated in the second quarter to 2.4 percent, after a lengthy period in which it was close to or even above the upper limit of the target inflation range.

In the first quarter, the recovery in real global activity and world trade continued, led by the U.S. and the emerging market economies, while growth in Europe was slower. Against the background of the lower than potential level of activity and relatively high unemployment rates, the global inflation environment remained low.

The fiscal debt crisis in several countries, mainly in South Europe, became more severe in the second quarter, leading to a significant rise in the level of uncertainty in the financial markets around the world, including Israel’s. This was most notable at the beginning of the second quarter, until the EU and the IMF announced the availability of funds to assist countries in financial difficulties in the euro zone, and until these countries started to tighten fiscal policies to deal with the crisis. These halted the decline in the financial markets, but the level of uncertainty remained high.

Economic activity in Israel continued to expand in the second quarter, although some of the indicators relating to that quarter point to a slowdown in the rate of expansion. Available data indicates that although domestic demand continued to grow, the increase in exports, which are affected directly by developments around the world, slowed. The recovery trend was also evident in the labor market, with a decline in the rate of unemployment and an increase in the real wage.

The fiscal crisis in some European countries is likely to have an impact on Israel’s economy due to its potential effect on the demand for Israel’s exports and the effect on Israel’s capital markets due to its close links with financial markets around the world.

The shekel appreciated in both nominal and real terms during most of the second quarter; however, in mid- June the trend reversed, and the shekel depreciated until the end of the quarter and in July. Purchases of foreign currency by the Bank of Israel in April and May served to moderate the appreciation of the shekel in those months. In June the Bank of Israel did not intervene in the foreign currency market.

The Bank of Israel’s monetary policy in the second quarter was set in the framework of the process of returning the interest rate to a normal level appropriate to the economic conditions and the inflation environment. At the same time the heightened uncertainty regarding the global economic situation and its effect on Israel’s economy was reflected in a slowing of the pace of increases in the interest rate in the second quarter. The Bank of Israel interest rate was increased by 25 basis points in April 2010 to 1.5 percent, and was left unchanged until July. For August the interest rate was increased by 25 basis points to 1.75 percent. The downward trend in inflation, measured over the previous twelve months, towards the midpoint of the inflation target range, the increased uncertainty about the rate of Israel’s economic recovery later in the year, and the expectation that the major central banks around the world would leave their interest rates at low levels for a considerable time, all lent support to the decision to leave the interest rate unchanged in the second quarter.

To moderate the continued steep increase in housing prices at the beginning of 2010 and the rapid growth of housing credit, affected among other things by the low rate of interest, and to support financial stability, the Supervisor of Banks issued a directive which went into effect on July 1, instructing banks to investigate their housing credit closely, and requiring an additional provision for housing loans with a high loan-to-value ratio. This step is in accord with the approach that in order to implement the central bank’s policy, macro prudential tools should be employed in addition to the usual monetary instruments, to deal with issues related to financial stability. The use of such tools enables a more focused effect than can be achieved by changes in the interest rate, which have broader implications for the economy as a whole.

The inflation rate in the next twelve months is expected to be in the upper part of the inflation target range, and growth is expected to be slightly below 4 percent, so that the negative output gap will contract a little. Nevertheless, due to uncertainty about the development of the crisis in Europe and its effect on the global economy and on Israel’s economy, economic activity and inflation may deviate significantly from the forecasts. The development of housing prices in the near future is also expected to affect the inflation rate.

The Bank of Israel will continue to monitor developments in Israel and world wide and will act to maintain inflation within the target, while supporting real economic activity and the maintenance of financial stability. The path of the interest rate will continue to be determined in accordance with the inflation environment, the situation in Israel’s economy, global developments, including the path of global interest rates, and developments in the exchange rate of the shekel.

The Knesset passed the new Bank of Israel Law in March 2010, and it became effective in June. The new law provides the legal basis for the independence of the Bank of Israel, by clearly defining the Bank’s objectives, its functions, its decision-making methods, and the tools the Bank can use for achieving its objectives and how they can be operated. The Law sets the maintenance of price stability as the main goal of the central bank, together with the support of other objectives of the Government’s economic policy and the support of the stability of the financial system When the Monetary Committee is appointed in accordance with the Law, monetary policy decisions, including decisions on the interest rate, will be made by the Committee.

[1] When the Monetary Committee is appointed, in accordance with the new Bank of Israel Law, interest rate decisions will be made by the Committee.

title: INTERVIEW-UPDATE 1-Low global rates bar 'normal' Israel rates
text:
(Adds Stanley Fischer comments)

JERUSALEM, July 12 (Reuters) - Israeli interest rates cannot revert to "normal" levels as long as U.S. and European rates remain low, Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer said on Monday.

The central bank raised its key lending rate by 1 percentage point between August and March as Israel's economy rebounded from a downturn and as annual inflation remained above an official target of 1-3 percent.

Policymakers seek to return the key rate, currently at 1.5 percent, to a more "normal" level that reflects the economic environment. Yet rates have been on hold for the past three months as inflation has eased and the European debt crisis has increased uncertainty over the global economic recovery.

While Fischer did not define "normal", Israel's benchmark rate stood at 4.25 percent in September 2008 before the global financial crisis deepened.

"We can't go back to 'normal' if the Federal Reserve is at 0-25 basis points and the ECB is at 1 percent," Fischer told Reuters in an interview.

He noted that further interest rate increases while global rates were still low would mean Israel would have to "absorb large amounts of foreign currency and that would make policy more complicated".

More foreign inflows would lead to a stronger shekel <ILS=> <EURILS=>, which the central back opposes since it would hurt exports and the economic recovery.

"We don't have to go back to normal if the rest of the world doesn't go back to normal," Fischer said.

U.S. and European rates had been expected to rise by now.

"But it seems pretty clear that they will be delayed," Fischer said, adding that the expectation was that Fed and ECB rates would start going up about now. The central bank believes global rates will stay on hold for the rest of 2010.

"We require a careful balance in continuing to keep the economy going and ... keeping inflation in the target range," Fischer added. "We can't let inflation get out of control -- which is above 3 percent."

Inflation -- at an annual rate of 3 percent in May -- is expected to ease to 2 percent in a few months before returning to near 3 percent the next 12 months.

Analysts have scaled back expectations of interest rate hikes. In minutes of the June 28 rates decision, the Bank of Israel said forecasters expect rate hikes of 1 to 1.5 points in the next 12 months.

HIGH HOUSING COSTS

Fischer said the main inflation concerns are high housing prices and indirect tax increases. House prices, which are some 21 percent of the CPI, rose 4.8 percent in May year-on-year.

The central bank recently imposed fees on banks to try and cool morgage lending. Fischer said the central bank would wait and see if that helped to lower housing prices before enacting additional steps.

Fischer in May started a second term as central bank chief. When asked whether he planned to stay the entire five years, Fischer said much depended "on how the second term goes" and how much he achieves. "I am happy with what I am doing," he said.

One key goal is to implement a new Bank of Israel law that includes a monetary board to set interest rates. At present, the governor decides on rates after discussions with bank officials. The government still needs to nominate candidates to the board.

"I hope to see the board soon," said Fischer, saying another goal for his second term was integrating Israeli Arabs and ultra-Orthodox Jews into the workforce, which would boost Israel's economy.

Fischer said Israel's economy is showing a host of mixed signals -- a 3.6 percent annualised rise in first quarter economic growth and a central bank companies report indicating continued expansion in the second quarter but expectations for weaker exports later in the third quarter, and a drop in the May purchasing managers' index.

He said there was no reason for the Bank of Israel to change growth forecasts of 3.7 percent in 2010 and 4 percent in 2011.

Still, a stronger shekel versus the euro should weigh on exports to Europe, he said, although the shekel has dipped against the euro recently.

"A lot of the pessimism a month ago for the second half of the year has moderated of late," Fischer said, citing the IMF raising global growth estimates.

"For (Israeli) exporters, it doesn't as bad as it did 10 days ago" when the euro was very weak, he said.

On fiscal policy, Fischer said he supported a rise in annual budgetary spending to 2.66 percent the next two years from a 1.7 percent ceiling in place the prior few years.

Such spending levels continue to ensure funding for education and vital programmes while also pushing the debt-GDP ratio lower, as long as the economy continues to grow.

The ratio is about 80 percent and Fischer expects a 1-2 percent a year decline in the next few years.

Fischer also said that while the central bank will not issue a formal announcement that it will stop buying foreign currency, he hopes it will not be necessary. The bank has not bought foreigh exchange since May.

"If the market goes back to some normality, the Bank of Israel ... will intervene less," he said.

(Editing by Ron Askew)

title: PREVIEW-Bank of Israel seen holding rates
text:
* WHAT: Israel monetary policy decision

* WHEN: Monday, May 24, 5:30 pm (1430 GMT) * REUTERS FORECAST: 10 of 15 analysts polled expect short-term borrowing rate to stay on hold at 1.5 percent. Five analysts see a quarter-point rate increase to 1.75 percent.

FACTORS TO WATCH

The Bank of Israel is committed to a gradual tightening of monetary policy as the economy continues to rebound and inflation expectations remain high.

Governor Stanley Fischer surprised some analysts by leaving the key rate unchanged on April 26 after a quarter-point hike in March. Fischer has raised the key rate four times since August, by one percentage point in total.

The consumer price index rose by a higher-than-expected 0.9 percent in April from March, but the annual inflation rate slipped to 3 percent from 3.2 percent, at the top of an official 1 to 3 percent target range.

Analysts predict inflation will slip below 2 percent for 2010 but see annual inflation of about 2.5 to 3 percent over the next 12 months.

At the same time, the economy continues to rebound although growth slowed in the first quarter to an annualised 3.3 percent, from a 4.8 percent expansion in the final three months of 2009 and a 3.6 percent rise in the third quarter.

MARKET REACTION

In keeping rates unchanged a month ago, the central bank cautioned that rapid rate increases could put too much appreciation pressure on the shekel, potentially damaging exports. [ID:nLDE64916Y]

However, the shekel is now moving in the opposite direction. It has weakened significantly against the dollar <ILS=> in recent sessions, hitting a five-month low of 3.82 on Thursday as the dollar has appreciated sharply versus the euro.

The euro <EURILS=>, however, has fallen by some 8 percent against the shekel in the past month and was quoted at 4.7 on Thursday, close to an 18-month low of 4.65 reached last week.

To keep the shekel from appreciating too much, the Bank of Israel has continued to intervene in the open market. It bought $2.5 billion of foreign currency in April and a yet to be disclosed amount so far in May. (Reporting by Steven Scheer; Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: Israel c.bank has "green light" to buy  forex  -finmin

JERUSALEM, April 8 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel's policy of intervening in the foreign exchange market has the full backing of the government, Finance Minister Yuval Steinitz said in an interview published on Thursday.

Israel's central bank has been buying foreign currency for two years in a bid to prevent the shekel from appreciating too much against the dollar <ILS=> and euro <EURILS=> and hurting exports, which are some 40 percent of economic activity.

"The Bank of Israel has a green light from my point of view to continue to buy foreign currency if it needs to," Steinitz told the Maariv newspaper.

"I don't want to tell the governor (Stanley Fischer) when and where to stop."

The Bank of Israel last August halted a more than one-year programme of buying $100 million a day of forex and instead decided it would intervene on days of "unusual developments" in the market.

The central bank had initially set a target of reaching as much as $44 billion in foreign currency reserves but they rose to $62 billion in March.

"The current level of $62 billion in reserves is not high given Israel's geopolitical situation and the global economic storm which in my estimate is not yet over."

Buoyed by a rapidly recovering economy and the Bank of Israel's fourth short-term interest rate increase since last August on March 28, the shekel gained 0.2 percent to 3.6990 on Thursday versus the dollar and 0.7 percent against the euro to 4.9247, a fresh 17-month high.

Since then, the central bank has bought $50-$200 million of forex on a number of days to keep the shekel from appreciating.

Steinitz rejected calls for Israel to impose taxes on capital flows as a means of limiting speculators selling dollars.

"I do not support going back 10-20 years and impose barriers on foreign trade and raw materials," he said.

title: UPDATE 1-Bank of Israel raises key rate 25 bps to 1.5 pct
text:
* First increase since December

* 6 of 14 economists in poll had forecast correctly

* Bk of Israel says monetary policy still expansionary

(Adds comments from central bank statement, analysts)

By Steven Scheer

JERUSALEM, March 28 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel raised its key short-term borrowing rate <ILINR=ECI> by a quarter point to 1.5 percent on Sunday, its first increase since December, to combat inflationary pressures as the economy recovers.

Six of 14 economists polled by Reuters had predicted a quarter-point increase, with eight expecting no change.

"The current increase is made against the background of growth that continues to become more firmly based, inflation expectations that are close to the upper limit of the (1-3 percent) target inflation range, and the rise in asset prices," the Bank of Israel said in a statement.

"However, monetary policy continues to be expansionary, even after this increase," the central bank added.

The decision was made a day earlier than usual due to the seven-day Jewish festival of Passover, which begins on Monday at sundown. Israeli financial markets will not be able to react until Wednesday, when markets reopen for a shortened session.

Markets were already closed on Sunday at the time of the rates decision, which was the central bank's fourth quarter-point move since August.

Analysts had been largely split over the prospects of a rate hike, especially since an increase would tend to support a stronger shekel <ILS=> <EURILS=>, something the Bank of Israel has been trying to fight by intervening in the currency market.

"It was a correct decision," said Rafi Gozlan, economist at Leader Capital Markets. "A rate hike at this time sends a determined message against the latest rise in inflation expectations, thus preventing unnecessary future rate hikes."

Consumer prices fell by 0.3 percent in February from January to push annual inflation down to a rate of 3.6 percent, still above an official 1-3 percent target. The CPI had fallen a bigger-than-expected 0.7 percent in January.

INFLATION EXPECTATIONS

But the central bank noted inflation expectations for the next 12 months were on average at 2.6 percent. It added that annual inflation is expected to move back within the target range in a month.

"It seems as if the governor (Stanley Fischer) gave more weight to the higher inflation expectations than the recent negative CPIs," said Dan Ron, vice president of investment at the Tachlit investment house.

The central bank raised the key lending rate three times in the second half of 2009 on concerns of rising inflation pressures, which started to ease early in 2010.

The Bank of Israel said in its statement that it was in a process of gradually returning the interest rate to a more "normal" level that was intended to return inflation to its target -- and "keep it there" -- while contributing to the further recovery of economic activity.

Israel's economy grew an annualised 4.9 percent in the fourth quarter and 0.7 percent for all of 2009. It is forecast to grow at least 3.5 percent in 2010. The Bank of Israel said uncertainty remained regarding the strength of the expansion.

The central bank reiterated the path of rate increases will be determined by inflation, global and domestic growth and the pace of rate increases globally.

"Despite today's rate increase, real rates are still negative and too low in comparison to the pace of the economic recovery," Ron said.

"The process of rate hikes is not over," he said, adding much depended on upcoming CPIs and the U.S. Federal Reserve. (Additional reporting by Tova Cohen, Ari Rabinovitch, editing by Will Waterman)

title: Israel FX intervention  depends on recovery -Fischer
text:
TEL AVIV, March 11 (Reuters) - Israel's central bank will cut back intervention in the foreign exchange market as local and global economic conditions stabilise, Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer said on Thursday.

"A central bank in a small and open country cannot be indifferent to the exchange rate," Fischer said at a conference. "Gradually we will reduce our need to intervene in the foreign exchange market. That is our hope but it very much depends on what happens in Israel and the world."

The Bank of Israel last August halted a more than one-year programme of buying $100 million a day of foreign currency, shifting to a policy of intervening when it saw unusual movements in the market.

It bought just $209 million of forex in February after buying $1.56 billion in January, when the shekel <ILS=> gained to a 15-month peak of 3.66 versus the dollar.

Fischer reiterated that the central bank was in the process of returning short-term interest rates to a more normal level. He noted the pace of rate hikes depended on growth in Israel and the world, inflation and global interest rates.

Israel's economy, Fischer said, was starting to return to growth rates seen before the global crisis. The economy grew at least 5 percent a year between 2003 and 2007, and 4 percent in 2008.

After a weak first half of 2009, the economy grew an annualised 3.6 percent in the third quarter and 4.9 percent in the fourth quarter of 2009.

The economy is forecast to grow around 3.5 percent in 2010.

Fischer said global growth was still slow, although Asia with the exception of Japan, was doing well.

"In the United States, there are points of weakness but the likely scenario is a continuation of growth at a slower pace than it had been before," he said.

The major worry for the global economy remains Europe, Fischer said. He pointed to Greece's debt problems and failed attempts so far to bail out the country.

Fischer's five-year term as governor ends next month and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has decided to ask him to stay on for another term though a formal offer has yet to be made.

Fischer is hinging his decision on final approval of a new law that would reform the central bank's policymaking, such as setting up a board of governors.

The plan on Wednesday was approved by parliament's finance committee [ID:nLDE6291N6] but still needs approval from the plenum.

"We hope in the next week it will pass," Fischer said. "The new law will make the central bank more modern with targets more appropriate for the 21st century."

title: DAVOS-UPDATE 1-Israel's Fischer hopes to phase out  FX  action
text:
* Fischer hopes to phase out foreign exchange intervention

 * 2010 inflation likely to be below 2.3-2.7 pct estimates

 * Israel rates to be normal when global interest rates rise

 By Krista Hughes and Natsuko Waki

 DAVOS, Switzerland, Jan 28 (Reuters) - Israel's central bank hopes to phase out foreign exchange intervention in the shekel market as the world economy returns to normal, Governor Stanley Fischer said on Thursday.

 Speaking to Reuters Insider television at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Fischer also said the central bank was not defending any particular level of the shekel <ILS=>.

 "We hope this is part of (the) transition out of extraordinary measures we took during the global meltdown during which we bought dollars daily. We've intervened since then if the market moved rapidly from what we regard (as) its fundamentals," Fischer said.

 "We hope this will phase out as the situation returns to normal."

 The Bank of Israel last August halted a more than one-year programme of buying $100 million a day of foreign currency and instead said it would buy only on days of "unusual movements".

 After no intervention in November and buying a minimal amount in December, the central bank has intervened some seven times so far in January -- the last coming a week ago -- as the shekel <ILS=> has appreciated against the dollar and euro.

 The intervention has helped weaken the shekel to a rate of 3.73 per dollar from a 15-month peak of 3.66 earlier this month.

 "We are not going to defend any particular value of the shekel. You can't forever stand against the market," Fischer said. "We go with our judgment of whether the market is right. We are a long way from where we were a few months ago."

 INFLATION

 Fischer said buying foreign currency was not inflationary. "We sterilise it so it doesn't affect money supply," he said.

 Inflation reached a rate of 3.9 percent in 2009. Forecasts for 2010 range from 2.3 to 2.7 percent but Fischer said it would "probably be on the lower side" although it is volatile since it is influenced by external factors such as oil prices.

 The Bank of Israel on Monday held its key short-term borrowing rate at 1.25 percent after raising it by a quarter-point in August, November and December. The central bank said rates would gradually return to "normal".

 "I think we will start returning to normal when other central banks start raising interest rates," Fischer said. "We're all waiting for central banks of leading countries to raise interest rates."

 He said central bankers were gradually withdrawing the large amount of monetary stimulus. "The last thing they will do is to raise interest rates, probably," Fischer said.

 He also said while Israel lowered its public debt burden to about 77 percent of gross domestic product from above 100 percent in five years, a similar move over the next five years was doubtful. 

 "We can probably do it by the end of the decade for sure if (the economy) continues to grow," he said. "We would like to go to something like 60 percent."  (Writing by Steven Scheer, editing by Mike Peacock)

title: DJ OECD:  Israel  Must Cut Public Debt, Stop  Forex Intervention
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--Israel's economy has weathered the recent economic downturn better than most, but faces major challenges in reducing its public sector debt and dealing with high poverty rates among its minority populations, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development said in its first-ever review of Israel's economy.

The report called on the Bank of Israel to stop intervening in foreign currency market by purchasing dollars, and said the central bank's foreign currency reserves are more than adequate.

In recent months, the bank has been purchasing dollars to prevent the shekel from gaining too much strength against the U.S dollar, and in turn, making Israel's exports more expensive. Such a policy is not sustainable for the long term, OECD secretary general Angel Gurria said.

Israel is near the end of a three-year long accession process to become a member of the OECD, and OECD officials are in Jerusalem this week presenting the review and meeting with Israeli officials.

Gurria said Israel is "in the home stretch" of being accepted to the OECD, and is expected to have membership by May. Membership of the group would cement Israel's status as a developed economy. Earlier this month Chile joined the organization, becoming its thirty-first member.

Although the OECD report highlights problematic issues in Israel's society and economy, Israel's admission to the OECD is not contingent on solving these problems or implementing OECD recommendations.

The review focused much attention on the low employment and high poverty rates among Israeli Arabs and ultra-Orthodox Jews, which together make up 28% of the population.

About 20% of Israeli households live below the relative poverty line, compared to an average of 11% for the OECD countries, the report said. This is mainly due to high rates of poverty and low rates of labor-force participation among Israeli Arabs, which make up 20% of the population, and among ultra-Orthodox Jews, which make up 8% of the population.

The report encouraged Israel to invest in increasing educational and employment options for those groups.

Avishay Braverman, Israel's minister of minority affairs, said belonging to the OECD will make Israel more accountable in how it treats its minorities and will help spur efforts to create more equal opportunities for Arab and ultra-Orthodox Jewish Israelis.

"The importance is, when you join a prestigious club, you have to act according to the club," Braverman said.

"The message we get from the report is that there are solutions to our problems," said Stanley Fischer, governor of the Bank of Israel, at a symposium in Jerusalem Wednesday, which was attended by OECD officials and Israeli government officials.

Israel's economy grew by 0.5% in 2009, while many other developed economies around the world contracted. Gurria said the OECD expects Israel's GDP to increase at least 3% in 2010, and 4% in 2011.

Gurria said Israel has much to gain from joining the OECD, including increased foreign investment. But perhaps more importantly, belonging to the OECD will allow Israelis to mix with social and economic experts from other member states, and will give Israel access to policy recommendations and reviews from the OECD.

Israel, with its booming high-tech industry and high number of startup companies can also contribute knowledge to other member states, he said.

"We are going to learn from Israel and Israel is going to learn from the member states," Gurria said.

In many categories, Israel lags behind OECD countries. Israel's public sector debt is likely to be 82% of gross domestic product in 2010, much above the 60% that is the target for OECD member countries.

The high level of debt is due in part to high spending on defense. The report said that Israel's spending on defense was equal to about 8% of annual GDP, whereas the OECD average for defense spending is around 2% of GDP.

The report called for increasing the sales tax to help limit the debt, and urged Israel to rethink the exemption from sales tax for fruits and vegetable and on all products and services in its southern tourist city of Eilat.

By Sara Toth Stub, contributing to Dow Jones Newswires; saratoth@gmail.com

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

January 20, 2010 06:09 ET (11:09 GMT)
