title: UPDATE 1-OECD calls for  Israel  to end  forex intervention
text:
(Adds comments from OECD, Bank of Israel)

JERUSALEM, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Israel's central bank should stop buying foreign currency "as soon as possible", saying such intervention could counter interest rate increases that aim to combat inflation, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said on Wednesday.

In a report coinciding with the run in to Israel's expected entry to the OECD this year, the Paris-based group also called on Israel to work on significantly reducing its public debt burden and combat poverty.

OECD chief Angel Gurria said the report, the group's first ever on Israel, "had nothing to do with the accession process."

On Tuesday, he told Reuters that Israel should become the 32nd member of the OECD by the middle of 2010. [ID:nLDE60I1PH]

The report said the economy has weathered the global downturn well and policy responses have been "generally appropriate", with the Bank of Israel's intervention in the foreign exchange market helping build international reserves while tempering gains in the shekel.

"Nevertheless, a 'clean-float' should be re-adopted as soon as possible," the OECD said. "With the pickup in economic activity, continued discretionary interventions could bring undesirable inflation pressures that work in opposition to any monetary tightening, a process that has begun in recent months."

The Bank of Israel in August halted a more than one-year programme of buying $100 million a day of foreign currency and instead said it would intervene on days of "unusual movements".

Such purchases have fallen sharply, with no intervention in November and just $132 million in December. But the Bank of Israel has intervened numerous times so far in 2010 as the shekel <ILS=> gained some 3 percent against the dollar to a 15-month peak of 3.68.

The OECD noted that intervention damages transparency and credibility in monetary policy while also bring expensive.

And, "if the intervention aims to provide a floor or ceiling to the currency, this can easily be thwarted by global markets," it said.

Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer told reporters after an OECD forum that intervention is temporary.

"We describe intervention as a step we hope to stop when we get out of the crisis," Fischer said. "I hope we get to a situation like that. As long as there are differences in interest rates in the world this is an abnormal situation."

The OECD praised Israel's government for responsible budget policies and lowering the tax burden to close to the OECD average of 37 percent of gross domestic product. But it cautioned against further tax reductions and said Israel needs to significantly lower its deficits and debt-to-GDP ratio.

Its public debt is expected to reach 82 percent of GDP and a goal of falling to 60 percent isn't expected until 2019 assuming real economic growth of 3.5 percent starting in 2011.

The report also called for a host of education reforms, such as leveling the educational playing field for Israeli-Arabs and boosting secular training for Israel's ultra-Orthodox population. Both sectors have low labour participation.

Gurria estimated the Israeli economy would grow 3-3.5 percent in 2010 and some 4 percent next year after growth of 0.5 percent in 2009.

"Growth of 0.5 percent might be small but it's like tying Barcelona -- you go home feeling like it was a victory," he said.

title: UPDATE 1-Israel shekel up 0.9 pct vs dollar to 15-month peak

JERUSALEM, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Israel's shekel <ILS=> gained 0.9 percent to its highest official rate since October of 2008 on Monday, as foreign banks continued to dump dollars.

The shekel was fixed at 3.6830 to the dollar -- its strongest level since Oct. 15, 2008 -- from 3.7180 on Friday.

So far in 2010, the shekel has gained some 2.5 percent versus the U.S. currency.

"It's mostly foreign banks selling dollars," said a dealer at Israel Discount Bank.

Dealers said the Bank of Israel did not intervene in the market on Monday, after buying dollars in three sessions last week when the exchange rate moved rapidly from 3.7750 at the end of 2009 towards 3.70.

Dealers estimate the central bank bought as much as $500 million of foreign currency last week to try and prop up the ailing dollar versus the shekel. But unlike similar episodes during the summer, the operations did little to halt the dollar's decline.

Since the beginning of the year, foreign banks have dominated the market, taking on short dollar positions against the shekel after sitting on the sidelines during December.

The dollar hit a three-month low versus the euro on Monday, but global dollar weakness only partly explains the weak dollar-shekel.

Israel's economy has emerged far more quickly from a recession than anticipated, growing an estimated 0.5 percent in 2009 on the heels of a strong second half. That had prompted the Bank of Israel earlier on Monday to raise its 2010 economic growth estimate to 3.5 percent from 2.5 percent. [ID:nLDE60A0IV]

The fast rebound, largely due to expected gains in growth of exports and consumer spending, has led to three quarter-point short-term interest rate increases by the Bank of Israel.

Minutes of discussions from the last move on Dec. 28 showed most policymakers supported Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer's decision. [ID:nLDE60A0ZZ].

title: UPDATE 1-Israel cenbank to raise 2010 GDP f'cast soon -Fischer
text:

JERUSALEM, Jan 7 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel will soon raise its economic growth forecast for 2010, currently at 2.5 percent, Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer said on Thursday.

"Our current forecast is for gross domestic product growth of 2.5 percent but soon we will revise it upwards," Fischer said in remarks prepared for delivery at a conference. He did not say what the new estimate would be.

He noted that after growth of an annualised 3 percent in the third quarter, fourth-quarter GDP growth is expected at 4 percent -- resulting in a "V" picture for Israel's economy.

Israel's economy grew an estimated 0.5 percent in 2009, compared with a contraction of 3.5 percent for OECD countries. In 2010, the OECD countries are estimated to grow 1.9 percent.

Bank Leumi, Israel's largest bank, on Thursday raised its GDP growth forecast for 2010 to 3.5 percent from a previous estimate of 2.7 percent.

Fischer also said that with tax revenues higher than expected, Israel's budget deficit looks to be just above 5 percent of GDP in 2009, below a target of 6 percent. For 2010, the deficit should be lower than a target of 5.5 percent of GDP, he said.

As a result of the government's fiscal policies the public debt burden is expected to have grown only slightly, Fischer said. The central bank estimates Israel's debt to GDP ratio at 78.7 percent in 2009 and 78.8 percent in 2010, above 2008's level of 77 percent.

The growth of 2 percent since the start of the global crisis is far below the OECD average of 14.7 percent.

On the issue of the Bank of Israel's policy of intervening in the foreign exchange market in an attempt to restrain the shekel's appreciation, Fischer said: "We cannot continue to do this forever".

With the shekel gaining to near 3.71 from 3.7750 at the end of 2009, the central bank has bought as much as $500 million of foreign currency the past few sessions.

Fischer partly blames the strong economy and a current account surplus in Israel's balance of payments for the shekel's strength.

Israel posted a current account surplus of 3.1 percent of GDP in 2009 and is forecast to record a surplus of 2.3 percent of GDP this year, Fischer said.

* Emerging shares hover at 17-month highs

* Icelandic debt insurance costs spike up on Icesave veto

* Romania's leu up despite rate cut; lira and rand off highs

By Sebastian Tong

LONDON, Jan 6 (Reuters) - Emerging shares eked out gains on Wednesday to hover at their highest levels in over a year but Icelandic debt premiums spiked higher after the island state's president rejected a bill to compensate British and Dutch savers for money lost from the collapse of Icelandic banks.

Most emerging currencies retreated from recent multi-week highs though Romania's leu defied a surprise interest rate cut by its central bank to advance to its strongest level in more than six months.

Risk appetite is holding ahead of the release of key U.S. jobs data on Friday, allowing the Philippines and Turkey to tap global bond markets in the first trading week of the year.

Figures showing the euro zone's services sector expanding at its fastest pace in over two years in December helped offset persistent investor concerns over Greece's parlous fiscal state. [ID:nLDE6050GG] [ID:nSGE60509G]

"Risk appetite is not very strongly entrenched...The main thing that people are looking towards is Friday's payrolls. If they are positive, we may see more risk appetite for the next few weeks. If we get a negative surprise, it could turn," said Beat Siegenthaler, chief strategist emerging markets at TD Securities.

The benchmark emerging equities index <.MSCIEF> was up 0.3 percent at 1205 GMT, staying aloft at 17-month peaks but several key bourses had slipped from the multi-month highs reached earlier in the week.

Polish <.WIG20> and Hungarian shares <.BUX> retreated after hitting 16-month peaks in the previous session while Israeli shares <.TA25> eased after reaching two-year highs on Tuesday.

Turkish shares <.XU100> slipped 0.3 percent but continued to hover at one-year highs.

However, South African stocks <.JTOPI> firmed to cling onto their highest levels in over 16 months while Romanian shares <.BETI> inched 0.5 percent up to six-week highs.

ICELAND, ROMANIA

Investors took profit on recent gains in currencies such as the lira <TRY=> and the rand <ZAR=>, knocking both currencies down from Tuesday's 10-week highs against the dollar.

The lira's weakness was also blamed on Turkey's $2 billion 30-year bond sale, which was said to renew investor doubts over the country's prospects for sealing a new loan accord with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). [ID:nLDE6050DD]

A global bond sale by the Philippines is also reportedly seeing strong investor interest. [ID:nTOE60503V]

Emerging sovereign debt spreads tightened five basis points to trade at 269 bps over U.S. Treasuries.

Israel's shekel <ILS=> was flat the central bank reportedly intervened to stop the unit from advancing past a nine-week high on Tuesday.

Romania's leu <EURRON=> rose 0.5 percent to reach its strongest level against the euro in over half a year, boosted by euro sales by local banks seeking to reduce hard-currency provisions from last year.

Despite the central bank's consensus defying move on Tuesday to cut its key interest rate by 50 bps, the unit is expected to hold firm.

"We look for another 50 bps cut next month and do not expect much pressure on the leu considering reports of M&A activity and expectations that the central bank will continue to cap the downside," said BNP Paribas in a research note. Meanwhile, the move by Iceland's president on Tuesday to force a referendum on a bill to repay Britain and the Netherlands more than $5 billion lost by the collapse of Icelandic banks continued to push up the cost of insuring the island state's sovereign debt. Credit default swaps to insure Icelandic debt for five years shot up over 30 bps from the previous close to trade at around 479 bps, according to CMA DataVision.

Fitch cut Iceland's credit rating to "junk" status while fellow ratings agency Standard & Poor's warned of a downgrade. [ID:nLDE6040YB]

"The risk now is that this whole issue will remain unresolved for another half year or full year. If the bill is refused in the referendum, Iceland will have to go back to negotiating with the UK and the Netherlands, they can forget about EU membership or the IMF programme," said TD Securities' Siegenthaler. title: UPDATE 2-Israel cbank should phase out unconventional steps-IMF
text:
(Adds Bank of Israel governor, Finance Minister comments)

JERUSALEM, Dec 14 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund on Monday called on Israel to phase out unconventional monetary policies and currency intervention gradually as interest rates rise further.

In its preliminary report on Israel's economy, the fund said policymakers had kept economic damage from the financial crisis "mild" but urged the government to cut public debt.

It said interest rate increases to stop inflation rising as the economy recovers from a recession were "appropriate".

"As the appropriate monetary stance tightens and the policy rate rises, so the role of unconventional measures in pursing monetary policy objectives should be reduced," the IMF said.

"As recommended globally, withdrawal from 'unconventional measures' -- notably foreign exchange intervention in Israel -- should be phased."

The Bank of Israel in August ended a more than one-year programme of buying $100 million of dollars a day, replacing it with a plan to buy on days of "unusual movements". It has not intervened in the local currency market since late October.

The move to "discretionary" intervention was appropriate for the transitional period since it maintains the option should it "prove necessary to secure a sufficiently accommodative stance of monetary policy", the IMF said.

But it warned this transitional phase "risks compromising the clarity of the Bank of Israel's objectives".

"To restore the free floating regime, discretionary intervention should be formally terminated when the policy rate is well above its effective floor on a sustained basis," the fund added.

The central bank in late November raised its key lending rate by a quarter-point to 1 percent, its second such move since August as inflation expectations have risen.

"We are pleased that the (IMF) mission expresses support of the monetary policy of the Bank of Israel, including the bank's activity in the foreign currency market so far, since the outbreak of the crisis," Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer said in a statement.

FISCAL POLICIES

The fund said any further sustained real rise of the shekel would remain a concern. After hitting around 3.7 per dollar, it has eased to 3.78 and has stuck to a narrow range of late.

If capital inflows surge, the central bank should not respond by buying dollars. Capital controls and taxes on inflows -- which some government officials have suggested -- would also be inappropriate, the IMF said,

The IMF recommended Israel adopt a target to reduce its debt to 70 percent of gross domestic product by the middle of the next decade and 60 percent by 2020. Debt is expected to edge up to 80 percent by the end of 2010.

"Public debt needs to come down decisively," it said, noting Israel's exposure to global and geopolitical shocks. The IMF said income tax cuts could hurt debt reduction.

The fund said the budget deficit looked to be close to 5 percent of GDP in 2009, below a target of 6 percent. It said boosting spending and breaching fiscal targets were needed during the crisis but a return to ceilings must be re-established.

"The government will continue to manage a careful and responsible exit strategy from the crisis, and will support growth and reduction of debt," said Finance Minister Yuval Steinitz. "We intend to prove, in practice, that Israel's growth potential was, and remains, high."

Israel weathered the global crisis well and avoided a financial market meltdown, the IMF said, noting it became a safe haven that attracted a sharp increase in net capital inflows.

But its medium-term potential growth rate has fallen by 0.5 percentage points to 3 to 3-1/2 percent a year after big reductions of potential output of major economies, the IMF said.

It projected 2010 economic growth of as much as 4 percent.

"The decline of the rate of potential growth ... as set forth in the report is an indication of the economy's weakness," Fischer said, noting Israel should not become "complacent".

title: Israel  cenbank  forex interventions  risk inflation -OECD
text:
PARIS, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Thursday said the Israeli central bank's foreign exchange interventions risk fuelling inflation and hurting policy credibility.

In a bid to help keep the shekel <ILS=> from strengthening too much versus the dollar and further damaging exports, the Bank of Israel began buying foreign currency in early 2008.

It scrapped a plan -- also aimed at raising foreign currency reserves -- of buying $100 million a day in August and has since intervened in the market on days of "unusual movements".

"The Bank of Israel's ... continued foreign exchange interventions risk bringing additional inflationary pressures and damaging policy credibility and coherence," the OECD said in a report.

It bought $1.27 billion of forex in October, down from $1.65 billion in September and above $4 billion in August. Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer said this week he would not stop until he was certain the market is functioning well.

The OECD in its report noted that monetary policy is more normalised following a quarter-point rate hike in August.

Israel is in the process of becoming a member of the OECD, which officials expect to be completed sometime in 2010.

On fiscal policy, the OECD said Israel was relying on short-term measures to reach deficit and spending goals and described scheduled cuts in corporate and personal taxation for 2010 as "untimely".

The OECD expects Israel to meet budget deficit targets of 6 percent of GDP in 2009 and 5.5 percent in 2010 but exceed a 3 percent target in 2011.

"The temporary tax increases are due to expire at the end of 2010, contributing to uncertainties for the budget balance in 2011," the report said.

It added that upside risks to inflation are amplified, saying standard indicators of slack may be inaccurate due to the after-effects of the recent recession on potential output.

The OECD projected Israeli GDP growth of zero this year, 2.25 percent in 2010 and 3.25 percent in 2011, with inflation at a 3.3 percent rate next year. The debt-to-GDP ratio looks to rise to 82 percent in 2010 from 78 percent in 2008 and then drop slightly in 2011, the OECD said.

"Further increases in the (central) bank's policy rate are expected with a return to more normal conditions," it said. (Reporting by Steven Scheer; Editing by Andy Bruce)

title: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Israel, Professor Stanley Fischer, to the Conference of the Business Club, Haifa and the North, November 5, 2009
text:
Release date - 05112009

In the past year Israel’s economy underwent a severe crisis that resulted from the worst global crisis since the Great Depression in the last century.

The impact on Israel was relatively slight. Although unemployment increased, it did so by less than in large economies such as the US. The feeling currently is that we-both Israel and the global economy-are starting to emerge from the crisis. The impression obtained in the bi-monthly meetings we hold with the BIS central bank governors is one of recovery. In discussions with them, however, reservations are expressed that derive from the uncertainty regarding the future.

Israel’s situation is better than the general situation abroad: no bank has failed, unemployment increased by less than had been expected, and there was renewed growth sooner than expected. We were affected less, because our economy is functioning well, and can cope with crises, as was shown in previous crises: in the last recession the then Minister of Finance and Prime Minister steered the economy out of the crisis, and their actions were essential for the economy-but the Minister of Finance resigned in August 2005. Although the markets reacted immediately with sharp drops, they corrected themselves the next day. The same occurred when Prime Minister Ariel Sharon became ill and could not function, and when the Hamas came into power in Gaza, and on other occasions.

Today we have a surplus in the current account, we do not have inflation; the 2007, pre-crisis, budget was almost a balanced one; our banking system is strong; and household debt is lower than that in other countries. These are just some of the examples that indicate the strength of Israel’s economy, and that contributed to Israel’s resilience during the crisis.

The Bank of Israel also acted to reduce the effect of the global crisis on Israel’s economy: it cut the interest rate, intervened in the foreign exchange market, and bought government bonds on the market.

1. Cutting the interest rate: we reduced the interest rate sharply. I have heard criticism about the low interest rate, with complaints from some that they have nowhere to invest their money. But that is precisely the purpose of the expansionary monetary policy, to encourage the use of money for consumption and real investments which increase production and create jobs.

2. Activity in the foreign exchange (forex) market: at the beginning of 2008 the shekel strengthened greatly, and for very good reasons. As confidence in the markets abroad eroded, Israelis discovered that the shekel was a better and safer alternative, and the repatriation of their investments strengthened the shekel. We in the Bank of Israel took into consideration that a strong shekel in a recession would make the latter more difficult to deal with. We therefore decided that this was a timely opportunity to implement an old plan to increase the size of the foreign exchange reserves. We started buying $25 million a day, and then increased the amount to $100 million a day. It should be known that the Bank does not follow the shekel/dollar exchange rate only, but closely monitors the effective exchange rate, calculated by weighting the currencies of Israel trading partners by their shares of trade with us.

3. The purchase of government bonds: this step increased liquidity in the financial system.

With regard to the situation today-in mid-November we will receive data on economic activity in the third quarter. Assessments in the Bank of Israel are that the data will indicate positive growth. The Bank’s estimates of growth are zero percent in 2009 and 2.5 percent in 2010. Some forecasters actually expect growth next year to be 3 percent. Although the unemployment rate in Israel is high, our situation is better than that in other countries.

Turning now to inflation-last month inflation, measured over the previous twelve months, was within the target range. This month it may be outside the range, above the upper limit, but we must bear in mind that government actions in the field of taxation and surcharges added more than one percentage point to the increase in the CPI; excluding that effect, inflation remains within the target range.

Regarding the budget-the government deficit this year is expected to be less than 6 percent of GDP. Government activity in countries undergoing crises increased their debt/GDP ratio; that ratio in Israel will be lower than that in other countries.

Housing prices-if someone says that there is a ‘bubble’ in housing prices I answer that what we have is not a bubble, because the low interest rate reduces the cost of mortgages and encourages purchases of apartments as an alternative investment; it is not a bubble because the prices reflect the economy’s fundamentals. That said, we are keeping a close watch on developments.

Regarding the north of Israel-one third of Israel’s GDP is produced there, so that it plays a very important part in total economic activity. During the Second Lebanon War we saw the impact on GDP. The rate of unemployment in the Northern District, however, at 9.3 percent, is higher than in the rest of the country. One of the reasons for this is the lower labor force participation rate in the north. The rate of participation in the central part of the country among those aged 15-64 years is 63 percent, whereas in the Northern District it is only about 51 percent. The gap is the result of the low participation rate among the Arab population in the area, especially Arab women. In the last two years a slight improvement in the participation rate is evident, apparently due to the economic effect of the cuts in allowances, which encourages people to find jobs.

The Prime Minister believes that improved infrastructures in the north will boost activity there. I believe that this government will invest more in infrastructures than the previous one, and this will doubtless help to develop the area. The government should play its part in the relevant spheres-infrastructures, defense and public goods-and I believe it will do so. But clearly that in itself is not enough. The continued enterprise and innovation of the people in this hall is essential. Your efforts will be augmented by the recovery of the global economy.

Questions addressed to the Governor, and his answers

Q. Is there a risk involved in holding the Bank of Israel foreign exchange reserves in dollars?

A. We hold the reserves in several currencies, not only in dollars. We manage the reserves very conservatively. The law allows us to purchase only bonds of governments and of sound banks. The managers of the reserves in the Bank of Israel are top rate professionals, and in fact in the latest crisis we did not lose money.

Q. What is the Bank of Israel’s view on the huge spread between interest to lenders and borrowers.?

A. There are various rates on interest, and one must look at all of them. Thus, for example, interest rates on mortgages are low (prime). Sound and reliable companies from the aspect of their repayment ability pay relatively low rates of interest. When we started cutting the interest rate we urged the banks to lower their interest rates, and they did, but apparently not by enough.

Q. We hear forecasts of a second round of the crisis. What is your view?

A. There are various forecasts of the future of the economy. Some relate to the letter ‘V,’ (or ‘square root sign’) with one low point, and some to the letter ‘W,’ with two. I think that it is highly probable that there will not be a second round to the crisis, but this is still a probability statement.

Q. A Prime Minister once said that ‘a drought in Israel is of less concern than a drought in the US.’ What is your opinion of the current economic situation? Should we be concerned?

A. The effect on Israel of developments in the US certainly exists, but to a lesser extent than in the past. The main question in this context is how the US will exit from its expansionary policy, and what impact will the exit process have on the players in the market. If a cautious approach is adopted, no special problems are anticipated from there.

Q. Do you intend to accept the offer to stay on as Governor for another two years?

A. The idea of another two years came from Dana Weiss, the presenter of the ‘Meet the Press’ television program. The government cannot offer a two-year term of office. My current term ends in another six months (less two days).

Q. Interest rates are expected to remain low around the world in the next few months. Will the Bank of Israel also keep the interest rate at a low level?

A. We will act according to developments in Israel’s economy. In the past we tried to transmit hints of future decisions, but because of the relatively frequent changes in the economy we saw that in all those cases the reality was already different from that on the day we sent out the hints.

title: Bank Of  Israel :  FX Intervention  Isn't Tied To Exchange Rate
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Israel doesn't have an exchange-rate target for the Israeli shekel against the U.S. dollar or any other currency, it said Monday.

This statement follows two months of accusations in the Israeli press that the central bank only intervenes in the foreign currency market when the shekel appreciates too much against the dollar.

The bank said it only intervenes in the foreign currency market when there are "unusual exchange rate movements that do not reflect fundamental economic conditions, or when disorderly conditions prevail in the foreign exchange market."

The bank added that it looks at the rate of the shekel not only in relation to the dollar but also other foreign currencies, and considers multiple macroeconomic factors, not just exchange rates, before intervening in the currency market.

The bank said Aug. 10 it had ended a program it had been carrying out for about a year of daily purchases of $100 million on the open foreign currency market in order to increase Israel's reserves.

However, the bank has continued to intervene in the market since then. At the end of July, the bank's foreign currency reserves stood at $52.4 billion; at the end of September the reserves totaled $59.97 billion.

When the bank said in August it would stop its daily $100 million purchases, the shekel was at ILS3.87 to the dollar. That rate has dropped gradually over the following months, fluctuating back up to the Aug. 10 rate only a few times. On Monday the rate was ILS3.708 against the dollar.

The bank reiterated that its purchases of $7.57 billion in foreign currency in August and September weren't related to the shekel-dollar rate. It called its intervention in the past two months "exceptional, a result of the non-yet ended global crisis."

The bank said it hadn't intervened at all in the foreign currency market from 1998 through most of 2008, and it hoped to stop intervening in the market once the global economic situation stabilizes.

-By Sara Toth Stub, contributing to Dow Jones Newswires; saratoth@gmail.com [ 19-10-09 1205GMT ]

title: Israel cenbank says no target dollar-shekel rate
text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 18 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel said on Sunday it did not target a specific dollar-shekel <ILS=> rate, and that its currency interventions were exceptional responses to the global crisis to keep the shekel in equilibrium.

Since early August, the central bank has been buying dollars on days when it deems there are unusual exchange rate movements that do not reflect fundamental economic conditions or when disorderly conditions prevail in the foreign exchange market.

That policy followed a more than year-long programme of buying $100 million a day in an attempt to slow an appreciation of the shekel, which was hurting exports, which account for nearly half of Israel's economic activity.

In recent days, the market had been expecting the central bank to intervene should the dollar slip below 3.70 shekels.

When the dollar fell below 3.70 shekels last Thursday, the Bank of Israel bought foreign currency, briefly bringing the dollar to 3.72 before moving back to 3.70.

Rather than a specific target, the central bank estimates the equilibrium exchange rate of the shekel, based on the balance of payments of the economy.

"These estimates typically change over the course of time as economic conditions change; and by their nature, there is a significant range of uncertainty around estimates of the equilibrium rate," the Bank of Israel said in a statement.

"Moreover, deviations from estimated equilibrium exchange rates are common and sometimes persistent."

Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer has declined to say when the interventions will cease and the central bank said it would continue to "follow closely" developments in the foreign exchange market.

"We regard the current period of intervention in the foreign exchange market as exceptional, a result of the not yet ended global crisis," it said.

"We expect that the market will return to a situation closer to that of 1998-2008, when the Bank of Israel did not intervene at all in the foreign exchange market -- or at least, that the need to intervene will occur only rarely, in exceptional circumstances."

The Bank of Israel noted that when it evaluates changes in the shekel, it takes into account not only the rate versus the dollar but also the euro and other currencies.

It said that since the dollar has weakened globally over the last year, the effective rate of the shekel has appreciated by less than the exchange rate of the shekel.

Over the six months ended Sept. 30, the shekel appreciated 10.6 percent against the dollar though the effective rate appreciated only by 3.2 percent, it said. (Reporting by Steven Scheer, editing by Will Waterman)

Dealers at a number of large Israeli banks said the central bank bought between $100 million and $400 million of foreign currency in various stages during the afternoon.

"They came in a few times. It wasn't in one shot," said a dealer with an Israeli bank.

The move came hours before a key inflation report is set to be published that could give the market clues on near-term interest rate policy.

It also came as the dollar briefly dipped just below 3.70 shekels.

For days, the market believed the central bank would intervene should the dollar dip below the 3.70 shekel level.

The dollar gained to 3.72 shekels after the buying but the knee-jerk rally quickly ran out of steam.

The shekel's official rate was set at 3.7180 per dollar, down 0.2 percent from Wednesday's rate of 3.7090, which was the strongest level since Dec. 18, 2008.

After the official rate was set, the shekel gained to 3.7075.

A dealer at another large Israeli bank said the intervention was not successful since it resulted in "just a 30 minute spike" for the dollar.

But with the dollar weak around the world, the Bank of Israel is just trying to keep the shekel from appreciating too fast since a strong shekel tends to hurt Israeli exports, which account for nearly half of economic activity.

Exports have already been damaged by the global recession.

The Bank of Israel last intervened in the market on Oct 6., buying an estimated $200 million of foreign currency.

In August, the central bank halted a more than year-long programme of buying $100 million a day of forex and instead said it would enter the market on days of unusual activity.

At 1630 GMT, the consumer price index for September is due. The CPI is expected to decline 0.1 percent from August and stand 3 percent higher over the past 12 months.

High inflation had prompted the central bank to raise its key short-term borrowing rate by a quarter-point to 0.75 percent in August but easing inflation pressures and inflation expectations led the Bank of Israel to keep rates steady last month.

The next monetary policy decision is slated for Oct. 26 and analysts believe another rate hike is possible should the CPI come in above expectations.

title: UPDATE 2-Israel's Fischer does 'not know' if in rate hike cycle
text:
(Adds Fischer comments, market reaction)

JERUSALEM, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer said on Thursday the interest rate increase from last month did not necessarily signal the start of a cycle of monetary tightening.

"I simply do not know if it's the start of a process of raising the interest rate. We always will watch economic developments ... and take the decisions when the time comes to do so," Fischer told Israel Radio.

The Bank of Israel on Aug. 24 became the first major central bank to raise short-term borrowing costs when it increased its key rate by a quarter-point to 0.75 percent.

Some analysts expect another rate rise to 1 percent when the Bank of Israel next decides on monetary policy next Thursday.

Fischer noted that a rate increase was deemed necessary last month since inflation remained above an annual rate of 3 percent while the economy has started to grow. Minutes of the last meeting showed officials were unanimous in backing a rate increase since the economy had moved to moderate growth, while inflation remained high.

The shekel <ILS=> barely moved against the dollar on the remarks, while stock indexes were modestly higher and bond prices were slightly lower.

The shekel on Wednesday hit a nine-month peak of 3.74 per dollar. It hovered around 3.75 all session on Thursday.

The recent appreciation has come even as the Bank of Israel has been intervening from time to time in the exchange market the past six weeks by buying dollars to try and stem the shekel's advance. In early August, it halted a programme of buying $100 million a day of forex in favour of random purchases.

Fischer said he could not say how long the central bank would continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market.

"Despite our intervention there is a lot of fluctuation in the exchange rate," Fischer said.

WEAK DOLLAR EVERYWHERE

He said the problem is the weak dollar globally, partly caused by a wide U.S. current account deficit.

"We hope that after we return to a more normal stage in the world economy, get closer to full employment, we hope and expect to resume a more normal situation in the foreign exchange market, to something more resembling what was happening the last 10 years," Fischer said.

He rejected several proposals that would impose taxes on foreign capital inflows into Israel, saying it failed in the 1990s.

Fischer said Israel's economy was starting to recover.

"We are in the initial stages of economic recovery and we're still not in a good situation. We will start to emerge from recession when growth begins ... we are on the way to exit," he said, adding Israel was not affected by the global crisis as other countries due to responsible fiscal policies.

Israel's economy grew at an annual rate of 1 percent in the second quarter and the Central Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday estimated the economy will grow 0.1 percent in 2009.

Fischer said Israel was "technically" out of recession, given the growth in the second quarter. But with Israel's annual growth rate around 1.7 percent, per capita gross domestic product is still negative.

And despite big gains in asset and real estate prices, Fischer said he did not see a bubble on both fronts.

"We raised interest rates partly in response to the rise in the inflation rate," he said.

(Additional reporting by Allyn Fisher-Ilan; Editing by Ron Askew)

JERUSALEM, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Israel's shekel <ILS=> rose to a nine-month high on Wednesday, prompting the Bank of Israel to buy as much as $200 million in foreign currency to prevent further appreciation from harming exports and economic growth.

"The Bank of Israel started intervening (in mid-afternoon), and we estimate they bought around $200 million so far," a dealer at a large Israeli bank told Reuters.

The shekel's official rate was set at 3.74 per dollar, its strongest level since Dec. 19, 2008 and a 0.6 percent increase from Tuesday.

After closing at 3.76 per dollar on Tuesday, the shekel advanced early in the day to near 3.74, a day after publication of inflation data for August that analysts said would likely prompt the central bank to hike interest rates again next week.

The dollar rose to 3.76 shekels in afternoon trading after the intervention but analysts doubt whether the Bank of Israel can slow the shekel's appreciation in the long term through interventions.

The central bank has intervened in the currency market from time to time since halting last month a programme lasting more than one year during which it bought $100 million a day in foreign currency. When it halted that programme, it said it would intervene on days of "unusual movements".

The central bank, seeking to strike a balance between unwinding an expansionary policy in order to fight inflation and avoiding a slowdown in economic recovery, raised its key lending rate by a quarter percentage point on Aug. 24 to 0.75 percent.

In data issued after the market closed on Tuesday, Israel's consumer price index rose by 0.5 percent in August, a 3.1 percent increase year-on-year, above an official target of 1 to 3 percent. Analysts said the figure could prompt another quarter-point rate hike on Sept. 24 despite the annual inflation rate falling from a 3.5 percent rate in July.

"The steep rise in the CPI and the market's expectation for inflation ... could lead to a hike of 25 basis points and bring the interest rate to 1 percent," Rafael Gozlan, economist at Leader Capital Markets, wrote in a client note.

In August the central bank bought $4.073 billion in foreign currency on the market, bringing the country's foreign currency reserves to $56.4 billion.

The Bank of Israel expanded its programme once the shekel reached close to 3.74 per dollar in early August. The shekel slumped to 3.93 but the Israeli currency over the past six weeks has gradually gained as the economy has shown signs of recovery and as the dollar has been weak globally.

Also on Wednesday, the central bank said inflation expectations for the next 12 months held steady at 2.4 percent.

title: Israel's Leon Expects  Forex  Market To Stabilize
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--Moshe Leon, director-general of the Israeli prime minister's office, views the shekel's (ILS) strengthening Friday as a sign that calm will return to the local foreign currency market this week. 

 Leon told reporters at a press conference in Tel Aviv that the "foreign currency market is heading towards stability. I expect to see a continuation of what happened Friday, that the calm will continue on Tuesday and we'll see dollar sales in the foreign currency market." 

 The shekel gained 1.2% to the dollar at its central bank fixing Friday, to ILS4.2600 from ILS4.3110 on Thursday. The market will be closed Monday for a Jewish holiday. 

 Leon's remarks followed a week of tumultuous trading on the Israeli foreign currency market, in which the shekel broke through the ILS4.000 level to the dollar for the first time ever and sparked fears the country was heading for a steep inflationary spiral. 

 Many analysts expect to see the Bank of Israel intervene in trading if the shekel's descent continues this week, although economic policymakers have pledged to stay out of the market for now. 

 The sharp and speedy depreciation - 10.8% since September alone - was touched off by the outflow of foreign investor capital and by Israeli customers seeking to cover their foreign currency debt. Most of the trading was interbank, with few business sector customers in the market due to the abbreviated work week of the Succoth holiday. 

 Foreign currency dealers and analysts said the absence of many business sector customers exacerbated the shekel's fall, since the low liquidity of trading deepened the impact of individual transactions. Individual customers are also more likely to sell dollars at such high levels against the shekel, they said.

title: FOCUS-Israel shekel fixed 1.2 pct higher on dlr.

 "It is very nervous trade at the moment. The market is bouncing around. It is small amounts that are moving the market because it is so nervous," a dealer at Bank Hapoalim said.

title: Israeli shekel rallies against dollar in afternoon.
text:
TEL AVIV, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Profit-taking by foreigners helped strengthen the battered Israeli shekel against the dollar in late afternoon trading on Thursday following publication of the representative rate, dealers said. 

 At 1415 the shekel was trading at 4.2397 against the dollar compared with Thursday's fix of 4.3110. 

 "The shekel has rebounded on a bit of profit-taking by foreigners," a dealer at Bank Leumi said. 

 But dealers said the Bank of Israel had not intervened. "There was no intervention whatsoever," a Bank Leumi dealer said. 

 Thursday marked the fourth straight session of big losses for the shekel during which it shed more than 10 percent versus the dollar. 

 Prior to the fix on Thursday, the dollar sailed through what dealers had termed a resistance level of 4.3 and quickly reached above 4.4 shekels, triggering expectations for central bank intervention. 

 Dealers said the shekel had come under pressure mostly from foreign banks, with some selling by Israeli borrowers seeking to repay foreign currency-linked loans. 

 "We are seeing foreigners selling because they are selling around the world. Because of that the Israeli private sector is getting cold feet and repaying forex loans early," said Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets. 

 Analysts said the shekel selling did not reflect a crisis of confidence in the economy but that the Bank of Israel might have to intervene at around 4.3 to signal the market that it would not tolerate a further sharp depreciation.

title: Israel central bank  cautious on  forex intervention .
text:
TEL AVIV, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Thursday that central bank intervention was "not the right way" to determine the shekel's exchange rate. 

 He made his comments after mounting speculation that the central bank would intervene after the shekel broke through what dealers had termed a resistance level of 4.3 against the dollar in trading on Thursday. 

 "The Bank of Israel of course is obligated to defend the borders of the currency band," Frenkel told Israel Radio from the International Monetary Fund conference in Washington. 

 "But in principle we have worked hard to develop a foreign currency market that is efficient enough and deep enough to avoid the need for the central bank or other authorities to intervene daily in the fixing of the exchange rate. This (intervention) is not the right way." 

 The shekel, which trades within a sloping trading band whose midpoint is about 15 percent from its edges, is currently trading close to the midpoint. 

 Frenkel attributed the sharp shekel depreciation to corporate activity. 

 "The business sector wants to cover itself...It has foreign-linked debt and now it is buying foreign currency not to be exposed to such big changes in the exchange rate," Frenkel said. 

 "Things certainly don't appear to be out of control," he said. 

 On Thursday, the shekel shed 5.0 percent against the dollar for a 10 percent loss since last Friday.

title: Analysts say Bank of Israel must defend shekel.
text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 8 (Reuters) - The tumbling shekel does not signal market concerns about the Israeli economy, but with the dollar now well above 4.3 shekels the Bank of Israel will have to intervene to prevent a free fall, analysts said on Thursday. 

 The Israeli currency has lost 10 percent against the dollar since last Friday, when it came under selling pressure mainly from foreign banks reacting to global fears over emerging markets. 

 On Thursday, the shekel was fixed 5.0 percent lower on the dollar at 4.3110. 

 "We're not seeing a speculative attack on the shekel per se. Neither foreigners nor the Israeli private sector has lost confidence in the fundamentals," said Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets. 

 But Katz and other analysts warned that if the central bank did not quickly send the market a message that it would not tolerate further sharp losses for the shekel, the floodgates could open. 

 The Israeli economy has little exposure to hot foreign capital, but domestic borrowers have as much as 83.3 billion shekels ($19.3 billion) in foreign currency and forex-denominated loans outstanding, most of it through Israeli banks. 

 "I don't see the situation as catastrophic but it could become so if companies decide all at once to pay back loans. That would show panic," said Yehuda Ben-Assayag, managing director of Koor Investment House. 

 Israelis got hooked on forex borrowing in the mid-1990s when high domestic interest rates and a stable shekel encouraged interest rate arbitrage. 

 The shekel has become more volatile, especially since the government abandoned most of its remaining currency controls last April. The shekel has lost 18 percent on the dollar so far this year, but most borrowers have held on to their loans. 

 By intervening, the Bank of Israel would be signalling that it will not let the exchange rate run wild. And, with foreign currency reserves of nearly $22 billion, the bank has the ammunition to back up its claim. 

 Analysts said the Bank of Israel would almost certainly raise interest rates, widening what has been a narrowing differential with rates abroad. Most said the rate would have to rise between one and 1.5 percentage point by the end of the year from a current base rate of 9.5 percent. 

 But they said that was less important than direct intervention for defending the shekel. 

 "Because of the panic, no one is interested in the interest rate gap. But seeing the Bank of Israel intervene would have a big effect on Israeli players (in the forex market) at least," said Adam Reuter, of the Finanical Immunities consulting firm. 

 "Israelis are much, much bigger in the market than foreigners," he said. 

 Reuter said most borrowers had little reason to repay loans and that the banks would do little to force them to repay. 

 "The banks pressured borrowers long ago to buy hedging instruments," he said. "Some are naked and might be in trouble, but the banks won't press them too far for fear that they'll go squash." 

 Reuter said Israeli banks would probably take a hit on their earnings, but he noted that they were financially sound and had little or no exposure to imploding emerging markets abroad. 

 But Ben Assayag was less sanguine. Builders and other companies will see their forex-denominated debt load balloon, he warned. 

 Banking sources said the building and property sector alone had about $3.8 billion in forex credit outstanding, and the industry is already suffering from a prolonged slump. 

 He said that even export companies are not immune, because many are now facing softer export markets, especially in Israel's key high technology sector. 

 "If the shekel reaches 4.5 to the dollar, companies will begin to fail and this will reverberate on the banks," Ben Assayag said. 

 ($1 = 4.3110 shekels) 

 ((Jerusalem newsroom, +972 2 537-0502, jerusalem.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Wrap: Israel  Forex  Market Awaits Central Bk Move On Shekel
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--If the shekel continues its dramatic plunge against the dollar - nearly 10% in just three days - the Bank of Israel should start selling dollars on the foreign currency market to check its fall, analysts said Thursday. 

 Although they differed over the timing of intervention - whether it would begin Friday or the beginning of next week - analysts agreed that a free-fall for the Israeli currency would be disastrous despite the country's oft-cited strong economic fundamentals. 

 On Thursday, the shekel lost 5.3% of its value against the dollar, plunging to a new low of ILS4.3110 from the previous day's fixing at ILS4.0960. Just one week ago, a dollar quote at ILS4.000 would have been inconceivable; yet astounded dealers saw the currency fall as far as ILS4.4700 to the dollar Thursday. 

 Meanwhile, the central bank remained silent. Trading room managers reported no intervention Thursday. 

 Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel, in an interview with Israel radio from the U.S., projected calm. 

 "One thing is clear - there is much more volatility in the financial markets," he said. "The phenomenon is a worldwide occurrence in which currencies ... are undergoing significant changes. And the shekel, which is also connected to the same system, is evidencing volatility," Frenkel said during his visit to Washington for the International Monetary Fund meeting. 

 The central bank is committed to defending the upper and lower limit of the shekel's trading band - one that allows a fluctuation of 15% on either side of a gradually depreciating midpoint. In the first half of 1997, the central bank bought $7 billion to tame an overly strong shekel. 

 Yet some analysts criticized the bank's "hands-off" approach to the foreign currency market, stressing that if Frenkel waits until the shekel nears its lower limit, it may be too late to catch up with the inflationary spiral already evident in local shops and businesses.

 Foreign currency dealers and analysts attributed the fall to global economic troubles that have led to the outflow of foreign capital and to hedging by Israeli companies especially vulnerable to exchange-rate fluctuations because of their foreign currency loans. 

 "What is happening today is effect of the great (economic) turmoil around the world," Propper said. 

 Propper said a depreciation as far as 10% was a welcome correction to the Israeli currency's value against the dollar, since the shekel's relative strength in the last two years has restricted the economy's ability to grow. 

 At the same time, Propper said, "if there is a steep slide (in the shekel) and a collapse begins, then of course I think the Bank of Israel must intervene and do everything to save this capital market. All of us need a stable basis to advance the economy."

title: Israel 's Frenkel:  Intervention  No Way To Run A Market
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel on Thursday aimed to allay fears over the shekel's 5.3% slide against the dollar, stressing that regular intervention the wasn't the right way to oversee the country's foreign exchange market. 

 "The Bank of Israel is of course obligated to defend the limits of the trading band," Frenkel told Israel radio from Washington, where he is attending a meeting of the International Monetary Fund. "We worked hard to develop an effective ... foreign currency market. To intervene daily isn't the right way." 

 Frenkel didn't say whether intervention to stem the tide of dollar purchases driving down the shekel had been ruled out as a stopgap measure. 

 The shekel is allowed to fluctuate 15% on either side of a gradually depreciating midpoint. The shekel's dive to ILS4.3110 to the dollar Thursday, the third sharp drop in as many days, placed it within 11% of its lower limit, compared to its 20% distance at the start of the week. 

 "It isn't a question of worrying (over the depreciation), but of understanding the material," Frenkel said. "The panic reflects a misunderstanding of what is happening." 

 Frenkel said heightened foreign currency risk was something market players had to take into account, and attributed the decline in large part to foreign currency loan-taking by the Israeli business sector. 

 "The foreign currency market isn't a place for amateurs. Whoever enters this market knows there is a chance to gain and a chance to lose," Frenkel said. 

 Foreign currency dealers and analysts, however, expect the central bank to intervene if the shekel continues its dramatic fall. In addition, they forecast a rise in the 9.5% discount rate is in store for November to curb the inflationary pressure of the shekel's depreciation. 

 On Thursday, Israeli legislators and economic leaders criticized Frenkel, along with Finance Minister Yaakov Neeman, for remaining in the U.S. during a sensitive time for local capital markets. 

 The central bank chief defended his sojourn, saying: "The mission we set for ourselves was to present the Israeli economy before (foreign economic and investment officials) and to stress that it's a place worth entering."

But with this change in the exchange rate, we'll probably end up in the area of 5%, which is still pretty good considering we were in double digits a couple of years ago," he said. 

 Zilberfarb said the government is optimistic that inflation will ebb to about 4% next year. 

 The shekel is allowed to trade 15% above and below a gradually depreciating midpoint, and earlier this year the Bank of Israel was forced to intervene to buy dollars and sell shekels when the local currency rose to its ceiling. 

 The central bank isn't intervening at this time to slow the shekel's fall because the currency is still close to its midpoint, he noted. 

 "(The dollar was) at the bottom of the band and what's happened is that over the last couple of months we've come close to the middle," Zilberfarb said. 

 "Most of the shift has taken place in the last few months and has a lot to do with what's happening internationally. It's more a sense of uncertainty than of pessimism," he said. 

 The shekel's prolonged strength - until it weakened abruptly in the summer - had prompted private sector investors to take out foreign currency-denominated loans in order to profit from lower interest rates. The currency weakened when these investors became nervous about the international situation. 

 That's possibly another beneficial side-effect of the shekel's weakness: that it has made private-sector investors more aware of the currency risk, and made them more cautious about their foreign exposure.

Their absence exacerbated the rise because "usually when you hit psychological (low shekel) levels, customers will sell (dollars)," and soften the declines spurred by interbank trading, said Chaim Fromowitz, head of trading at Bank Leumi. 

 Fromowitz said reasons for deep panic were absent from trading Tuesday, with little evidence of foreign banks or brokerages buying dollars or of exporters seeking to close foreign currency loans en masse. 


The Bank of Israel wouldn't comment on the shekel's sharp decline or
possible policy changes.

title: Israel interest rates seen unchanged for October.
text:
JERUSALEM, Sept 24 (Reuters) - Israeli interest rates are expected to stay unchanged for October while the Bank of Israel awaits evidence of the full inflationary impact of the shekel's recent depreciation, economists said on Thursday. 

 "If I were (Governor Jacob) Frenkel, I'd say 'Let's wait. Maybe the exchange rate will come down again and inflation won't be that high,'" said Micha Goldberg, head of research at Nessuah Zannex Securities. 

 The central bank will announce its October monetary programme, including the key monetary tender rate, on Sunday at 1430 GMT. 

 Interest rates have been coming down all this year, culminating in a surprise 1.5 percentage point cut at the start of August that put the base rate at its current level of 9.5 percent. 

 But economists said the Bank of Israel might have overshot on that last cut. The reduction, coupled with turbulence in world financial markets, caused the shekel to fall about five percent against the dollar, rekindling inflation. 

 Economists said the question was how much inflation and how long the upsurge would last. 

 The August consumer price index (CPI) was pushed higher by the depreciation, a trend which Baruch Snir, chief economist at the Federation of Israeli Chambers of Commerce, said would continue into September. But he said inflation would moderate in the last quarter of the year. 

 Full-year 1998 inflation would reach 5.0 percent, up from 4.4 percent forecast before the depreciation began, Snir estimated. 

 Goldberg said the critical factor in the future direction of inflation was the exchange rate, currently 3.84 shekels to the dollar. 

 "Expectations are that over the short term we'll be at 3.85 and then it will decline to 3.80. This will lead to short-term inflationary pressures," he said. 

 As a result, Goldberg said, the central bank would probably raise rates by 0.2-0.3 of a percentage point at the end of October. 

 But Eran Sela, economist at Israel Discount Bank, estimated there was a 50 percent chance that Frenkel would not wait that long and would raise rates by half a percentage point as soon as Sunday. 

 "Inflationary expectations are very high at about 5.5 percent, which is way above the government's (4.0 percent) target for 1999. Also money supply has been rising too quickly," he said. 

 The bond market's inflationary expectations are a key benchmark for the Bank of Israel, but Snir said the markets were likely to revise down their inflationary outlook after the September CPI is published on October 15. 

 But he warned that in coming weeks there was a 30 percent chance that the dollar would lurch higher against the shekel, which would cause the bank to boost rates sharply before the end of the year. 

 "If we see a strong depreciation, with the shekel going to 3.95-4.00, I see one of two scenarios - either the Bank of Israel will intervene in the forex market or it will raise interest rates by one percentage point," Snir said. 

 On balance, however, he said inflation could be contained even with a moderate weakening of the shekel because domestic demand remained weak and world commodity prices were falling. 

 As a result, Snir said, inflation in 1999 should fall to 4.0 percent, with the shekel losing about five percent against the dollar over the course of the year. That, he added, would enable interest rates to fall about one percentage point over the course of the year.

title: FOCUS-Israel shekel fixed 2.7 pct down on dollar.
text:
JERUSALEM, Aug 28 (Reuters) - The Israeli shekel representative rate was fixed on Friday 2.7 percent weaker against the dollar at 3.8750 in a day of panicked trading spurred by volatile world markets, dealers said. 

 Foreign banks joined the shekel selling late in the session, adding to the pressure on the Israeli currency, they said. 

 "All the (world) markets are collapsing, and people are panicking. There is a strong need to diversify portfolios, which until now have been mainly in shekels. People are now balancing their portfolios," said Yaacov Harpaz, dealing room manager at United Mizrahi Bank. 

 The shekel began depreciating in early August from a level of about 3.65 on the dollar after the Bank of Israel made a surprise 1.5 percentage point cut in interest rates. 

 The pace of depreciation gained momentum on Thursday. In the last two days, the shekel's total loss against the dollar has reached 3.7 percent. 

 A dealer at American-Israel Bank said world stock markets, especially those in East Asia, had given investors in Israel the jitters. "You had some nice falls in the Far East, and in the U.S. you'll see the same thing later in the day," the dealer said. 

 Dealers said borrowers with dollar-linked loans were seeking to repay in expectation of further dollar-shekel volatility. 

 Finance Minister Yaacov Neeman sought to calm the market by stressing that the market was free to determine the appropriate shekel rate. 

 "In the State of Israel the foreign currency rate is determined by supply and demand. This is the only way to calm investors," Neeman told Israel Army Radio. 

 The shekel easily breached what some dealers had said would be an initial resistance point at about 3.87 to the dollar. 

 The American-Israel dealer said 3.91-3.92 would constitute the next barrier and that it was a strong one. Harpaz said the shekel could weaken further before it meets serious resistance. 

 "The first resistance point should be 3.90, but it won't be a strong one. We're heading to four-double-O," he said. 

 Dealers said there was no sign of Bank of Israel intervention. Harpaz said the central bank would only intervene if the shekel breached 4.00 to the dollar. 

 The representative rate for the dollar was fixed at 3.8750 shekels, against 3.7730 on Thursday. The basket of foreign currencies, composed of the dollar, mark, pound sterling, French franc and yen, was fixed at 4.1354 shekels against 4.0142 shekels on Thursday.

 Friday's losses continued from a sharp one percent weakening of the shekel on Thursday. 

 Finance Minister Yaacov Neeman sought to calm the market by stressing that the market was free to determine the appropriate shekel rate. 

 "In the State of Israel the foreign currency rate is determined by supply and demand. This is the only way to calm investors," Neeman told Israel Army Radio. 

 Pnina Lipman, a trader at American-Israel Bank, said there was heavy interbank trading as well as trading by private investors and companies. She said much of the demand was coming from investors bailing out of the stock market and companies seeking to repay dollar-and dollar-linked loans.

title: Israeli shekel weakens against basket, dollar.

TEL AVIV, Aug 4 (Reuters) - The shekel weakened against the dollar and basket of foreign currencies in active trading on Tuesday, leaving the Israeli currency further from the edge of its trading band than on Monday. 

 "There were lots of customers in the market because (exchange rates) are still low. Now is a great opportunity to cover (forex) exposure," said a dealer at Israel Continental Bank.

 The dealer said the shekel had strengthened recently as companies sold dollars to cover end-of-the-month payments but that pressure on the dollar had now eased.

title: Israel's 1Q Short-Term External Debt Doubles At $8.45 Bln
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--Israel's net short-term external debt totaled $8.45 billion at the end of the first quarter of 1998 - double the annual average of $4.3 billion from 1990 to 1996, the Bank of Israel said Monday. 

 Most of the rise is due to an increase in the private sector's short-term external debt, which accounts for some 80% of the economy's short-term external debt, the bank said. 

 Many businesses borrow abroad and convert the money into shekels to take advantage of the difference between interest rates overseas and the high interest rates due to the Bank of Israel's tight monetary policy over the past three years. 

 The central bank also said that since the beginning of the decade, its foreign currency reserves as a proportion of the government's overall external debt have grown to 78% at the end of the first quarter of 1998 from 38% in 1990. 

Central bank reserves grew to $21.34 billion at the end of March 1998 from $6.795 billion at the end of 1994, in large part because the Bank of Israel intervened frequently in the currency market in late 1996 and 1997 to defend the shekel's trading band. 

 The Bank of Israel bought more than $7 billion in the first half of 1997 alone to weaken the shekel and keep it within its trading band.

 But Tiki Hadad of the IBI Investment House said the simultaneous rises in the dollar, CPI-linked and unlinked bonds indicated a split market opinion on what would happen next. 

 "It's very rare that these three rise together. It shows that some people aren't convinced the dollar will continue to rise," she said. 

 Hadad said she did not expect the dollar-linked bonds would continue rising because she thought the central bank would intervene to stem a continued shekel depreciation.

title: Bank Of Israel Offcial: No Promises To Avert Shekel Drop
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Israel may not intervene in foreign currency trading to moderate a sharp depreciation of the shekel if there's a speculative attack on the currency, the head of the central bank's foreign currency department said in a speech. 

 There have been concerns that the shekel could be open to speculative attack and may weaken considerably once it is declared fully convertible around May 1, the date of Israel's 50th jubilee. Many restrictions on the shekel have already been lifted in a process that began in 1985 and gathered steam in 1997 and early 1998. 

 In a copy of a speech received Monday by Dow Jones Newswires, the director of the central bank's foreign currency department, Sylvia Piterman, said: 'The Bank of Israel obviously doesn't pledge to wait until the shekel reaches the weakest point in its band before entering the market, but that possibility should be taken into account.' 

 The shekel is adjusted daily against a basket of five currencies dominated by the dollar, weighted at 60%, and including the British pound, the Deutsche mark, the French franc and the Japanese yen. It is allowed to fluctuate 15% either side of its midpoint.

title: Foreign capital imports to Israel up in 1997.
text:
TEL AVIV, Feb 17 (Reuters) - Foreign investors put $3.7 billion into the Israeli economy in 1997, an increase of $1 billion over 1996, the Bank of Israel said on Tuesday. 

 About half of the increase was the result of direct investments while the other half was from financial investments. 

 Capital inflows by foreigners in the second half totalled $2.2 billion, up from $1.5 billion in the first half. 

 The Israeli private sector imported $4.8 billion in 1997, against $2.4 billion in 1996. But the imports were concentrated in the first half, when they reached $5.4 billion. 

 In the second half Israelis exported $570 million, marking a turnaround from a huge flow of capital imports in the previous two and a half years. 

 "Israeli residents effectively stopped taking credit in foreign currency from the banking system in the second half of 1997 while increasing their deposits in foreign currency in this period by $1.3 billion," the central bank said in a statement. 

 Israelis borrowed $229 million in foreign currency from Israeli banks in the second half against $4.2 billion in the first half. 

 The inflow of capital by Israeli companies attracted to lower interest rates overseas had put upward pressure on the Israeli shekel. 

 Because of that the Bank of Israel was forced to intervene regularly in the local market to prevent the currency from appreciating outside its trading band. 

 Israeli foreign currency reforms in June and the Southeast Asian crisis increased the exchange rate risk associated with taking foreign currency loans. At the same time, the spread between domestic and foreign interest rates has narrowed. 

 Foreign financial investments in 1997 rose to $2.1 billion from $1.4 billion in 1996. Foreign investment in the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange more than doubled to $720 million from $335 million in 1996, though most of the increase was in the first half of 1997. 

 Direct investment by foreigners in 1997 rose to $1.8 billion from $1.3 billion in 1996. Much of this was the result of privatisation, such as the sale of a controlling stake in Bank Hapoalim. ((Tova Cohen, Tel Aviv newsroom, +972 3 537-2211 x238, telaviv.newsroom@reuters.com)) TCC

title: Israeli inflation-indexed bonds end down.

TEL AVIV, Feb 11 (Reuters) - Israeli inflation-linked bonds continued to drop on Wednesday, and traders were split over the possibility that prices would recover in the near term.

 * CPI-linked government bonds: -0.28 pct to 108.44

 Volume including Makams was a moderate 132 million shekels. 

 "The market is continuing to fall, but we are heading towards the end of the drop," said Roy Meir of Simodan Investments. "Yields won't go beyond five percent." 

 Meir recalled that in July 1996 the Bank of Israel intervened when yields on inflation-indexed long bonds hit 5.1 percent. Therefore, he predicted, buying support would likely develop before yields reached that level in anticipation of the central bank acting again. 

 Yields on inflation-linked long bonds rose to 4.9 percent on Wednesday, Meir said. Yields on indexed short bonds rose to 5.5 percent and to 4.7-4.8 percent on medium bonds. 

 But Yair Elek of Israel Discount Bank predicted tough times ahead for the indexed market because the Bank of Israel would maintain its strict monetary stance, therefore high real interest rates, even if the outlook is for low inflation this year. 

 "Inflation was seven percent last year, so there's no way the Bank of Israel is going to settle for anything higher," he said. 

 Unlinked bonds continued higher on Wednesday with yields falling to 12.4 percent, Meir said.

title: Bank of Israel head offers fix for unemployment.
text:
JERUSALEM, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Tuesday that Israel should spend more on infrastructure projects, especially in transport, as a short-term solution to the country's growing unemployment. 

 In a statement, the central bank quoted Frenkel as saying that to solve joblessness over the longer term, the government should be investing in "human infrastructure" and job re-training. 

 "The real and long-term solution to unemployment requires a focus on human infrastructure and professional re-training on all levels, and for the short term, investment in infrastructure, especially transport infrastructure," the bank said in a summary of Frenkel's remarks. 

 Frenkel, who was reviewing developments in the Israeli economy during 1997 before the parliamentary finance committee, has come under growing criticism for Israel's rising unemployment. 

 Critics say the Bank of Israel's restrictive monetary policy has been one of the chief factors in the country's economic slowdown. 

 "If the Israeli government and the governor continue with this policy, whose sole aim is to reduce inflation at the cost of sharply rising unemployment and slowing investment, by the end of 1998 we'll end with 9-10 percent unemployment," Abraham Shohet, finance minister in the previous Labour government, told Frenkel. 

 Israel's jobless rate reached 8.1 percent in the third quarter, the latest for which figures are available, versus 6.6 percent a year earlier. Gross domestic product grew a preliminary 2.1 percent last year, its slowest pace of the decade. 

 On Monday, the Bank of Israel said it was lowering its key rate for February by 0.5 percentage point to 12.9 percent, the first cut since the end of August. 

 However, inflation has been falling in recent months. As a result, economists estimate the real base rate will be about 5.5 percent after the reduction. 

 Frenkel said the reduction in Israeli inflation last year to 7.0 percent, its lowest in 28 years, was only an interim stage on the way to the government's stated goal of bringing Israeli inflation to European levels of the start of the next century. 

 Frenkel said the most important contribution to Israel's economic stability last year was the reduction in its current account deficit. He said the Asian crisis had demonstrated how critical it had been to cut the deficit. 

 The deficit narrowed to an estimated $3.5 billion from $5.3 billion in 1996. 

 He said the Asian crisis had also showed that it was impossible for a central bank to successfully counter trends in foreign currency markets over the long term. 

 He praised last June's decision to widen the Israeli shekel's trading band against the basket of foreign currencies to which it is linked, saying it enabled the Bank of Israel to end a long period of market intervention that occurred in the first half of last year. title: Bank of Israel:  Forex  Loan-Taking Slower Last Half '97
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--Borrowing in foreign currency slowed dramatically in the last half of 1997, to an average of $170 million per month from $710 million per month in the first half of the year, the Bank of Israel reported Monday. 

 The Bank of Israel attributed the change to customers' perception that the risk of taking credit in foreign currency had increased. 

 In the first half of 1997, customers took advantage of the differential between Israel's high discount rate and that of other countries by borrowing in foreign currency and converting it into shekels. 

 The high rate of conversions strengthened the shekel beyond the strongest point in its trading band. This forced the central bank to buy $7 billion in foreign currency in the first half of the year to defend the trading band. 

 Borrowing in foreign currency slowed after the Bank of Israel widened the shekel's trading band and cut the discount rate to 12.7% from 13.9% on June 18, reducing the rate differential. The trading band was slowly widened to allow a 15% fluctuation from a gradually depreciating midpoint, as opposed to the earlier 7% range. 

 The central bank hoped the wider band would put an end to its intervention in trading. But in September, the central bank raised the discount rate to 13.4%, making loan-taking attractive to customers again. 

 Bank of Israel intervention resumed Dec. 29, after a six-month hiatus, and has continued on an almost daily basis since then. Foreign currency dealers expected to see the central bank intervene in trading again Monday.

title: Bank of Israel Buys Foreign  Currency  Via Foreign Bank
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Israel has begun buying foreign currency via a a foreign investment house, a central bank source said Thursday. 

 This marks the first time the central bank has ever bought foreign currency through a foreign investment house as part of its intervention in trading. 

 'The reason is to introduce competition,' the source said. 'If we use more than one source, there is competition over the price.' In the past, the central bank would buy foreign currency directly through a so-called global box - a voice hookup between the trading rooms of all the Israeli banks. 

 One foreign currency dealer differed on the competition claim, saying the Bank of Israel intervenes in trading only when the shekel has reached the strongest point in its trading band and that 'it's no secret the Bank of Israel wants to turn the shekel into a convertible currency.' Using a foreign broker now increases exposure to foreign markets in advance of currency liberalization measures planned for May, he explained. 

 The government and central bank plan to make the shekel a fully convertible currency in May.
