title: Bank of  Israel intervention  was $250 mln-governor.
text:
TEL AVIV, Jan 8 (Reuters) - Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Thursday the central bank had spent some $250 million intervening in the currency market but that this did not mean a need to alter forex policy. 

 "The Bank of Israel has indeed intervened in the foreign currency market in recent days. However, interventions such as this do not necessitate a new debate on the Bank of Israel's exchange rate policy," Frenkel told reporters. 

 The central bank has been buying dollars during most of the trading sessions since last Wednesday to prevent the shekel from appreciating beyond its trading band. The band is set against a basket of foreign currencies. 

 It is the first time the Bank of Israel has intervened since last June, when foreign currency reform and a sharp interest rate cut temporarily weakened the shekel. 

 Frenkel lauded last June's reforms, saying they had enabled the central bank to stop interventions for a long stretch. 

 "There was no intervention until the end of December and the foreign currency market developed enormously in the last six months," he said. 

 "There aren't enough reserves in the world for any central bank to defend the exchange rate band where there are significant one-directional market forces for a long period. The lesson we can learn from Southeast Asia is that it was right to widen the band." 

 Frenkel also took issue with critics of foreign exchange liberalisation, who he said were seeking to slow the process in the face of rising Israeli unemployment and concerns that Asia's woes could spread to Israel. 

 "Specifically in times of slowdown, you must not strangle liberalisation. If you implement the correct policies, the financial markets will support you," he said. 

 Frenkel stressed that Israel's approach to currency liberalisation was gradual. But he promised key reforms would be carried out in the first half, among them increasing the percentage of assets provident funds may invest abroad. 

 Frenkel and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have said they are aiming to make the Israeli shekel fully convertible by the country's 50th anniversary at the end of April. 

 The Bank of Israel governor also sounded a critical note about fiscal policy. While he praised the Treasury for bringing the budget deficit for 1997 under target, he said he was discouraged by its components. 

 On Wednesday, the Treasury reported that the government deficit for 1997 was only 2.4 percent of gross domestic product, less than the targeted 2.8 percent. However, it said, the domestic deficit was wider than expected and offset by an unexpected foreign surplus. 

 "It is clear there must be a much bigger weight in future debate on the content rather than simply the size of the deficit," he said. 

 Frenkel also expressed concern that much of the reserve for the 1998 budget has reportedly been committed. 

 The markets are watching Frenkel's view on the budget carefully. 

 The Bank of Israel has not changed interest rates since the end of August, but many are hoping that with the passage of the 1998 budget in parliament last Monday he will lower rates later this month.

title: Israel / Forex  Reserves -2:  Central Bank Intervening  Again
text:
Foreign exchange reserves have been swelled by the Bank of Israel's tight monetary policy, which has tamed inflation but has also created a large differential between interest rates in Israel and interest rates on major foreign currencies abroad. 

 That differential has encouraged customers to borrow in foreign currency and convert the money into shekels, thus strengthening the shekel. 

 In the first half of the year, the Bank of Israel was forced to intervene almost daily in foreign currency trading, buying more than $7 billion to weaken the shekel and keep it within its band. 

 The intervention was staved off for half a year by the the June 18 widening of the shekel trading band and a 1.2-percentage-point cut in the discount rate to 12.7%. 

 Those two steps had the immediate effect of increasing the exchange rate risk in the minds of customers who had been borrowing in foreign currency and converting the loans into shekels. 

 But within weeks, the perception of an increased risk factor eased, and the shekel began inching back toward its ceiling. 

 After the central bank raised its key lending rate in September to 13.4% from 12.7%, with plans to keep it that high through January, the differential between Israel's interest rates and rates abroad made the shekel even more attractive, strengthening the Israeli currency and making central bank intervention just a matter of time. 

 On Tuesday and Wednesday, the Bank of Israel was back in the foreign currency market, buying an estimated $220 million to $250 million. There is no foreign currency trading Thursday because of the New Year's holiday. 

 Foreign currency dealers say they don't know what will be required to keep near-daily intervention from resuming.

title: Bank of Israel: Public Sees Greater Exchange-Rate Risk
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--The public has perceived a greater exchange-rate risk since the shekel trading band widened in June, the Bank of Israel said Tuesday, citing as evidence a doubling of demand for its shekel-dollar options. 

 The central bank widened the trading band June 18 after the shekel repeatedly strengthened to its strongest point within the band, forcing the Bank of Israel to buy more than $7 billion from the beginning of the year to weaken the shekel. 

 One of the central bank's declared reasons for widening the band was to increase the exchange-rate risk, and the shekel depreciated some 5% immediately after the band was changed. 

 But although the Bank of Israel hasn't had to intervene in foreign currency trading since June 17, the shekel has bounced back to hover just below its strongest point in the band. The discount rate is a high 13.4%, and foreign currency dealers say customers are no longer as troubled by the higher exchange rate risk. 

 Demand for shekel-dollar options from July through November more than doubled in the first half of 1997, the central bank said in a release. 

 From January through June average demand in each option auction was $9.9 million, compared with $21.1 million on average from July through November. 

 The rise in demand also led to higher prices of some 20% for three-month options and some 14% for six-month options. 

 The increased exchange-rate risk also was expressed in the slowdown in foreign currency borrowing, the central bank said. 

 The net total of foreign currency loans rose $4.8 billion in the first half of 1997, compared with a rise of $700 million from July through November, the central bank said.

title: Israel Shekel Strengthening May Force Bank Of Israel
text:
JERUSALEM (AP-Dow Jones)--The shekel is inching closer to the strongest point in its trading band, and economists expect the Bank of Israel will be forced to intervene again in the market within weeks. 

 It would be the first such intervention since June 18, when the trading band was widened at the Bank of Israel's urging to halt its near-daily intervention in foreign currency trading. 

 The widening of the band had the immediate effect of devaluing the shekel by some 5% and pushing it as far as 4.2% below the ceiling, but the impact was short-lived. By midday Monday, the shekel was trading at 3.7600 versus a basket of major foreign currencies, 0.39% below its ceiling. The central bank fixed the shekel at 3.7688 against the basket, 0.34% from the ceiling. 

 Against the dollar, the central bank fixed the shekel at 3.4950, down 0.4% from Thursday folowing the long holiday weekend. 

 And the debate that arose immediately after the trading band was modified has resurged: Was the change a real step toward reforming the Israeli foreign currency market, or did it just give the Bank of Israel some breathing room? 

 'What we know is we are being dragged almost to the (ceiling),' of the trading band, said Gad Shifron, chief economist at Israel's No. 2 bank, Bank Leumi. 

 And once the shekel hits that point, the Bank of Israel will have to intervene in foreign currency trading to defend the trading band, Shifron said. 

 The shekel could break through the ceiling of the band as early as next week, he predicted. 

 Ilan Viskin, head trader at Israel's largest bank, Bank Hapoalim, agreed the shekel was so close to its upper band that a random transaction on the Israeli market or a significant weakening of the dollar on world markets could push it above.

title: Foreign capital imports to Israel jump in quarter. [CORRECTED 22:00 GMT]
text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Foreign investors put $1.223 billion into the Israeli economy in the third quarter, marking a sharp rise from the first half, the Bank of Israel said on Sunday. 

 At the same time the Israeli private sector exported $389 million in capital, marking a turnaround from a huge flow of capital imports in the previous two-and-a-half years. In the first half alone, capital imports by Israelis reached $5.340 billion. 

 "The main change in capital movements by Israeli residents was due to a sharp drop in foreign currency credit taken by the private sector and a rise forex accounts by Israeli residents," the central bank said in a statement. 

 Israelis borrowed $200 million in foreign currency in the third quarter, compared with $4.2 billion in the first half, the Bank of Israel said. Deposits in forex accounts grew by $856 million in the quarter after falling $180 million in the first half. 

 The inflow of capital by Israeli companies engaging arbitrage between high domestic interest rates and lower overseas ones had put upward pressure on the shekel. 

 Because of that the Bank of Israel was forced to regularly intervene in the local forex market in the first half to prevent the currency from appreciating outside its trading band. 

 The rise in capital inflows by foreigners was mainly in financial investments, especially in overseas securities offerings by Israeli companies. Foreign investment in that category alone reached $531 million in the quarter, compared with $161 million (corrects from $616 million) in the second quarter. 

 Inflows from direct investments grew the most slowly, reaching $357 million in the three months from $318 million in the second quarter and $435 million in the first. 

 Total foreign capital inflows in the first nine months reached $2.606 billion, compared with $2.690 billion for all of 1996 and $2.204 billion for all of 1995.

title: Israeli shekel weakens against basket.
text:
TEL AVIV, Aug 11 (Reuter) - The Israeli shekel weakened against the basket of key foreign currencies on Monday following the sharp decline of the dollar on overseas markets on Friday, dealers said. 

 "The market was very quiet today. The session opened with slightly more conversions of shekels into dollars and the shekel rose to 3.52 shekels per dollar," said a dealer at the First International Bank of Israel. 

 "By midday the shekel started declining and it fell to 3.53 shekels per dollar. It seems that the market is stabilising in a range of 3.52 to 3.55 shekels per dollar," he said. 

 The dealer added that the basket of key foreign currencies rose following the decline of the dollar abroad on Friday. 

 "The basket is recovering and it is now trading at 0.7 percent below the higher edge of its trading band. I believe that in the near term the central bank will remain out of the market," he said. 

 The Bank of Israel stopped intervening in the forex market in mid-June, after it slashed interest rates by 1.2 percentage points following a government decision to widen the currency's trading band and lower its crawling slope. 

 The Bank of Israel will not set a representative rate on Tuesday because of the Jewish fast day of Tisha B'Av. 

 The representative rate for the dollar was fixed at 3.5300 shekels compared with 3.5330 on Friday. The basket, composed of the dollar, mark, pound sterling, French franc and yen, was fixed at 3.7586 against 3.7491 on Friday. 

 On the crosses, the shekel traded against the yen at 3.0491 shekels per 100 yen compared with 2.9862 on Friday, and against the mark at 1.9025 shekels compared with 1.8872 on Friday.

title: Shekel/ Intervention  -2: Supported By Rate Differentials
text:
The day the government voted to widen the trading band, the central bank cut the discount rate 1.2 percentage points. 

 Advocates of a rate cut hoped such a move would dampen the shekel's appeal to investors, who have taken advantage of interest-rate differentials to borrow in low-rate foreign currencies and convert the funds into shekels, increasing demand for the Israeli currency. 

 Within days of the band's widening, the shekel traded 5% below its strongest point within the band. Now it's 2% below the band's ceiling. 

 Once the currency reaches the ceiling, 'There are some that would expect the Bank of Israel to get involved,' a high-ranking dealer at a Tel Aviv bank said, after which it 'would just stay there for a while.' 

 If the Bank of Israel weren't to intervene, 'then all bets are off,' the dealer said. 'It would be uncharted waters then, and one could guess anything they want.' 

 A Bank of Israel spokesman said Monday that the central bank will continue to defend the shekel's trading band as it has in the past. 

 'We are committed to the exchange rate, and there has been no change in that commitment,' the spokesman said. 

 'And who's to say the shekel won't weaken again?' asked one central-bank source. 

 Under the new exchange-rate parameters, the shekel's trading band will widen over the next 11 months to 15% on either side of a yet-undetermined midpoint. The band's old parameters permitted a fluctuation of 7% on either side of a midpoint that depreciated 6% annually.

title: WSJ:Israel's Fischer Wins Kudos For Central Bk Role Amid Crisis
text:
TEL AVIV (Dow Jones)--Bank of Israel Gov. Stanley Fischer stepped into the global spotlight late last month when he raised interest rates, the first major central-bank chief to do so amid the global economic downturn.

Here at home, economists have been applauding the former International Monetary Fund and Citigroup Inc. (C) executive for months, crediting him with adroitly steering the Jewish state's export-driven economy into what now looks like an early rebound.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal Web site, WSJ.com).

After slowing to a near-standstill this year, Israel's economy is forecast to grow 3.3% next year, according to HSBC Holdings PLC (HBC) economists. In a recent report, the bank said Israel has shown "tremendous resilience to the global recession" and cited Fischer's active monetary policy over the last year for that performance.

In mid-2008, Israel appeared as vulnerable as any when the extent of the global downturn first started to become clear. The country's banking system and real-estate sectors appeared healthy. But exports make up about 45% of the country's economy. The prospect of sharp downturns in big consuming countries like the U.S. and Europe had Israeli industrialists bracing for a steep fall in overseas orders.

Fischer, like other central bankers around the world, slashed interest rates, cutting from 4.25% in October 2008 to 0.5% early this year. Crucially, Fischer also suspended Israel's free-floating currency policy and started intervening aggressively in foreign-exchange markets.

From May 2008 through the end of last month, Fischer spent $28.4 billion, or about 14% of Israel's gross domestic product, buying foreign currency. While the central bank never said it was acting to weaken the Israeli shekel, the purchases did just that, helping to keep Israeli exports competitively priced.

When the full force of the global downturn hit this year, Israeli exports fell. But they didn't fall as much as many had feared. Exporters praised Fischer's intervention.

The Manufacturers' Association of Israel expects exports to drop an inflation-adjusted 13% this year. But without Fischer's intervention the damage would have been worse, says Ori Yehudai, chairman of the trade group's economic committee.

"It could have been a disaster," he says, adding that Fischer "was very proactive and showed leadership." With the global economic outlook looking better more recently, the bank has slowed down its intervention.

Fischer came to Israel's top banking post in 2005. His decision to immigrate to Israel from the U.S. - where he was working as a senior executive at Citigroup - won lots of early fans here.

He arrived well prepared for crisis. As the IMF's deputy managing director in the late 1990s, he was at the forefront of efforts to stem the back-to-back Asian and Russian financial crises.

His stint at the Bank of Israel hasn't been without critics. Some economists blame the foreign-exchange intervention for stoking Israeli inflation. It was rising prices that prompted Fischer to raise interest rates by 25 basis points last month, from 0.5% to 0.75%.

Bank officials defend their actions, and say the intervention didn't stoke excessive inflation. Barry Topf, the head of the markets division at the Bank of Israel, said central bank officials realized that for a small, open economy, heavily dependent on exports, the combination of a global economic slump with an "unjustifiably" strong currency would have been too painful not to act. TEL AVIV, Sept 8 (Reuters) - The shekel weakened around 0.6 percent against the dollar on Tuesday as the Bank of Israel bought over $600 million in foreign currency, a dealer at an Israeli bank said.

"The Bank of Israel bought a lot today, over $600 million," the dealer told Reuters, adding that the central bank was in the market throughout the day.

In the morning a dealer at Israel Discount Bank estimated the Bank of Israel had bought $100 million in foreign currency.

"The central bank moved the dollar up to 3.77 shekels from 3.74," the Discount dealer told Reuters right after the intervention.

Yet despite the very heavy intervention later in the day, the shekel only depreciated a little bit more as the dollar weakened globally, dealers said.

The euro gained 1.6 percent to 5.4784 shekels per euro.

The Bank of Israel has been intervening in the currency market from time to time to prevent a further appreciation of the shekel, which would hurt exporters.

In August the central bank bought $4.073 billion in foreign currency on the market.

"It appears that massive intervention of $4 billion a month cannot continue over time," Michael Sarel, head of economic research at Harel Finance, wrote in a report on Tuesday.

Harel forecast the exchange rate against the dollar will be basically unchanged in six months at 3.76.

The Bank of Israel last month halted a more than one-year programme of buying $100 million a day in foreign currency, but said it would intervene on days of "unusual movements" in the market.

The Bank of Israel intervened late in August after it raised its key short-term borrowing rate by a quarter point to 0.75 percent. [ID:nLO650919]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Shekel up on rate hike; emerging shares down
text:
* MSCI emerging market stocks down 0.5 pct

* Israeli shekel higher after central bank rate hike

* Hungary's forint lower after rate cuts

* Weaker commodities weigh on rand, rouble

By Natsuko Waki

LONDON, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Israel's shekel currency rose on Tuesday, a day after the country's central bank surprised markets by raising interest rates, defying a broader decline in emerging currencies and stocks.

Hungary's forint inched lower after its central bank delivered a second cut in key interest rates in two months and said more cuts could come to ease a deep recession. Israel's central bank raised short-term borrowing costs by a quarter point on Monday to 0.75 percent to rein in inflation, making it the first among developed and key emerging-economy central banks to tighten monetary policy.

The shekel's rise comes despite a recent spate of foreign exchange interventions by the central bank. Dealers said the Bank of Israel stepped in again on Monday, with one saying that the bank bought $130-140 million worth of foreign currency.

"The hike in Israeli interest rates has raised the intervention risk in the shekel in the near term," said Benoit Anne, EMEA FX and debt strategist at Bank of America Securities-Merrill Lynch.

"The underlying fundamentals of the shekel are much stronger and, to compensate, the central bank will be more active in the forex market, but the shekel should continue to appreciate despite some volatility."

The shekel rose 0.3 percent to 3.7880 per dollar <ILS=>.

The forint fell 0.1 percent to 268.10 per euro <EURHUF=>. Hungary's central bank took the cost of borrowing down by half a point to 8 percent. Tuesday's data showed the country's retail sales fell 2.2 percent in June, underscoring weak personal spending.

MSCI's benchmark emerging market stocks <.MSCIEF> fell 0.5 percent, following the world index <.MIWD00000PUS> which lost 0.4 percent from Monday's 10-month high.

Chinese stocks <.SSEC> fell 2.6 percent after cautious remarks from Premier Wen Jiabao late on Monday prompted concerns about possible slowing in the country's economic recovery. Emerging Asian stocks <.MIAPJ0000PUS> fell 0.7 percent.

Oil prices <CLc1> fell 0.7 percent to $73.87 a barrel, weighing on resource currencies such as the South African rand <ZAR=> which fell one-third of a percent to 7.80 per dollar and the Russian rouble <RUS=MCX>, which fell a quarter percent against its euro-dollar basket.

CORPORATE BOND ISSUANCE UP

Emerging market bond spreads widened 1 basis point to trade 367 bps over U.S. Treasuries <11EMJ>.

Royal Bank of Canada Capital Markets said a resurgence of corporate bond issuance from emerging markets pushed the year-to-date total amount to $104 billion, exceeding the total for the whole of 2008 and approaching the historical peak of $197 billion reached in 2007 on an annualised basis.

The bank added Russian corporates, which had been locked out of external debt market since the summer of 2008, are starting to take advantage of appetite for emerging market external debt although so far the issuance has been limited to top-tier names.

A prolonged period of low interest rates would mean liquidity needs a parking slot and support high-yielding emerging market debt for several quarters, but intermediate corrections were possible, it said.

"A potential trigger for a high-yield credit correction is the beginning of the tightening cycle in the major economies, which could reduce the attractiveness of high yielders," the bank said in a note to clients.

Elsewhere, a favourable development in negotiations with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) continued to support the Turkish lira, which rose a third of a percent <TRY=> to 1.49 per dollar.

The government, locked in negotiations with the IMF over a major loan deal since the previous stand-by expired in May 2008, said on Monday there was no discord with the IMF over the content of an economic programme.

Negotiations may produce a deal by October, when the IMF and the World Bank will hold their bi-annual meeting in Istanbul. (Additional reporting by Sebastian Tong; editing by Stephen Nisbet)

* More rate hikes expected this year

* Shekel advances 0.2 percent versus dollar

* Analysts see trend to stronger shekel

(Recasts, adds details, comments)

By Steven Scheer

JERUSALEM, Aug 25 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel, trying to prevent a further appreciation of the shekel <ILS=> after its surprise rate rise, on Tuesday bought up to $100 million of foreign currency but the shekel still gained versus the dollar.

One dealer at Israel Discount Bank said the central bank bought $50 million to $70 million, while a Bank Leumi dealer said it was between $50 million and $100 million.

"It was not an aggressive intervention," said the Discount dealer.

On Monday, the Bank of Israel raised its key short-term borrowing rate by a quarter-point to 0.75 percent [ID:nLO650919] and analysts believe more increases are in the offing.

UBS's Reinhard Cluse now sees a quarter-point hike a month that will bring the key rate to 1.75 percent by the end of 2009.

To prevent the shekel from advancing and further damaging exports, the central bank bought foreign currency before and after the late afternoon rate hike.

Dealers said the market planned to keep on testing the Bank of Israel's resolve since most analysts expect the shekel to appreciate more.

"The market is still trying to check the Bank of Israel's nerves in some sense. It is trying to see how persistent the Bank of Israel will be at current levels," the Discount dealer said. "It looks like the dollar wants to go down."

The shekel's official rate was set at 3.796 per dollar, up 0.2 percent from Monday's rate of 3.8040 before the rate hike.

After closing at 3.8142, the shekel edged higher from the start of Tuesday's trade, advancing to an intraday peak of 3.7870 per dollar.

The Bank of Israel, though, has shown in recent sessions it does not want the dollar to fall below the 3.80 level and started buying dollars, although the purchases this week have been far lower than those earlier in the month when the central bought some $2.5 billion after the exchange rate hit 3.74.

Analysts predict the shekel, though, will ultimately return to a level of 3.5 to 3.7 to the dollar.

"We remain optimistic about the chances for further shekel appreciation," Citi emerging markets economist David Lubin wrote in a client note.

"We expect the shekel to end this year close to 3.7 per dollar, with risks to the downside," he added.

Goldman Sach's Ahmet Akarli said the central bank policy, aimed at stemming speculative shekel demand, was unsustainable as it would call into question the inflation targeting framework and push rates and forex in opposite directions.

"We continue to believe therefore that the Bank of Israel will let go of the forex, once external demand recovery becomes more visible," he wrote in a client note.

The Bank of Israel earlier this month halted a more than one-year programme of buying $100 million a day in foreign currency, although it said it would intervene on days of "unusual movements" in the market. (Editing by Jon Boyle)

title: POLL-Israel c.bank to hold rates but hike by end-year
text:
* What: Israeli interest rates

* When: Monday, Aug 24, 1430 GMT

* 9 of 12 economists see no rate move; 2 see quarter point hike, 1 sees half point rise

By Steven Scheer

JERUSALEM, Aug 18 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel is expected to leave short-term borrowing costs unchanged for a fifth straight month next week, but high inflation and a surprise return to economic growth has economists anticipating a rate hike by the end of 2009.

In what is expected to be a difficult call given a desire to boost economic growth while containing growing inflation pressures, the central bank will decide on rates on Monday. Nine of 12 economists polled by Reuters forecast no move from the current interest rate of 0.5 percent.

But three economists expect Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer will raise the interest rate -- two saying by a quarter percentage point and one by a half-point -- following data in recent days indicating a faster economic recovery than expected.

Like many banks, JP Morgan had forecast the start of rate hikes in the fourth quarter at the earliest but it now expects a half-point increase already next week, citing a track record of earlier than expected changes in rates.

"The risk of a deflationary depression is declining, making the case for a very easy monetary policy stance less and less compelling," said emerging markets economist Miroslav Plojhar.

Published data on Sunday showed Israel's economy grew by an annualised 1 percent in the second quarter versus forecasts for a third straight quarterly decline. The data signalled a likely end to a recession in Israel. [ID:nLG207492]

That followed a report on Friday showing the consumer price index rose a higher than expected 1.1 percent in July from June and 3.5 percent over the prior 12 months. The GDP contraction in the first quarter was revised to 3.2 percent, less severe than earlier estimates. [ID:nLAG003602]

Most economists played down both reports, saying they were filled with one-time factors such as government tax increases boosting inflation and a drop in imports helping growth.

And while that may delay rate hikes, only four of the 12 economists expected Fischer to wait until 2010. Rates are expected to rise to 2 to 4.5 percent over the next year.

TIMING UNCLEAR

Those not forecasting a hike next week are split as to the timing of a policy tightening, with some saying September, October, November or December.

"He (Fischer) will be more prudent and wait for a better view of the economy," said Alon Katz, head of research at the Maor-Luski Investment House in Tel Aviv, echoing the thoughts of other analysts who believe that raising rates now would stifle the economic recovery.

Katz said October was most likely since it will come after the September inflation report, which will not have the one-time factors from taxes seen in July and August.

The Bank of Israel forecasts a contraction of 1.5 percent for 2009. But economists now see zero growth this year.

The central bank had lowered its key rate by 3.75 points in the period from last October to March. It supplemented its easing policy with buying government bonds and foreign currency.

In announcing no rate move in July, the central bank also halted its bond purchase programme. In early August, it ended a more than one-year programme of buying $100 million a day in foreign currency as a means to weaken the shekel and boost exports.

"Both were preconditions to expect an approaching start of an interest rate hiking cycle, in our view," said Plojhar.

The Bank of Israel is still intervening in the market on days of "unsual movements".

"With unconventional policy measures removed, the timing of rate hikes has come into focus," Deutsche Bank economist Caroline Grady wrote in a client note. "We see Israel as one of the first countries to move back to a hiking cycle."

But Grady believes that won't be until 2010 since unemployment is still rising and there is "considerable slack" that should keep price pressures subdued even as the economy improves in the second half of 2010.

JERUSALEM, Aug 5 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel bought large amounts of foreign currency for a third straight day on Wednesday in an effort to weaken the shekel <ILS=> against the dollar, but central bank chief Stanley Fischer said the purchases cannot go on forever.

Dealers said the central bank had bought around $500 million on both Monday and Tuesday to weaken the shekel that had appreciated 12 percent versus the dollar since late April and worrying policymakers that exports would be damaged further.

So far, the move has been a success in weakening the shekel from a Dec. 19 peak of 3.74 shekels per dollar. It reached 3.866 on Tuesday and additional forex purchases on Wednesday sent the U.S. currency to an intraday high of 3.96 shekels.

For more than a year, the Bank of Israel had been buying $100 million a day of foreign currency for the dual purpose of boosting forex reserves and limiting the shekel's appreciation. Exports have already been hurt by low global demand and a stronger shekel would make Israeli exports less competitive.

After the shekel had appreciated by 12 percent, the Bank of Israel on Monday said it would expand its intervention in the market and buy more than $100 million a day "in the event of unusual movements in the exchange rate". [ID:nL379377]

Fischer defended the forex policy in a meeting of parliament's finance committe on Wednesday.

"I sleep much better at night ... but it's clear, we cannot continue buying foreign currency forever," Fischer said.

"Everyone understands that in the long run, the central bank cannot stand up to the market and win," he said, echoing the sentiments of analysts the past few sessions.

Fischer said that the central bank's policies of influencing the exchange rate has helped exports from being hurt more, enabling the economy to emerge from recession sooner.

title: UPDATE 2- Israel central bank  expands  FX intervention
text:
* Bank of Israel to keep buying $100 of forex a day

* Will act in event of "unusual movements"

* Shekel slides, then recovers

* Analysts say central banks can't beat the markets

(Adds analysts' comments)

By Steven Scheer

JERUSALEM, Aug 3 (Reuters) - Israel's central bank on Monday said it would widen its intervention in the foreign exchange market as the shekel <ILS=> continues to appreciate against the dollar and threatens to hurt an already battered export sector.

The move comes a week after the Bank of Israel became the first central bank to end a radical monetary easing step of buying government bonds. [ID:nLR150230]

For more than a year, the Bank of Israel has been buying $100 million of foreign currency a day, partly to try and stem the shekel's rise. It said it will continue to buy forex.

"From now on, the Bank of Israel will act in the foreign exchange market in the event of unusual movements in the exchange rate which are inconsistent with underlying economic conditions, or when conditions in the foreign exchange market are disorderly," it said in a brief statement.

Analysts said the statement was too vague since "unusual movements" are subjective and they predicted the move would ultimately backfire, since the Bank of Israel was now adding a new challenge to speculators.

"The Bank of Israel is trying to send a message they will do whatever it can to prevent an appreciation of the shekel," said Gil Bufman, chief economist at Bank Leumi in Tel Aviv.

"But what we have seen in the past ... the market is always stronger than the central bank," he said.

The shekel weakened sharply on the news to 3.83 per dollar from its official rate of 3.743, set about an hour before the announcement. The official rate was the strongest level since Dec. 19, 2008.

In late trading, shekel moved back to 3.79 per dollar.

"Once the dust settles, the shekel will recover," said Shlomo Maoz, chief economist at the Nessuah Excellence brokerage.

The Israeli currency, which gained 1.2 percent on Monday, had appreciated by about 12 percent since reaching a low of 4.25 per dollar in late April.

SPECULATORS, EXPORTS

Much of the advance came from speculators. Bufman said the central bank's announcement plays into the hands of speculators who will likely use the "artificial" weakness of the shekel to bet against it, continue to sell dollars and then buy them back at cheaper levels.

"The only way you are going to make life more difficult for currency speculators is to increase currency uncertainty," Bufman said.

As the shekel has continued to rise, exporters have appealed to politicians and Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer to act to stem its advance since they have been battered by a low global demand, the weak dollar and rising Israeli inflation.

Exports, which account for nearly half of Israel's economic activity, slumped an annualised 29 percent in the first quarter under pressure from the global economic crisis.

The economy contracted by an annualised 3.7 percent the first three months of the year. The Bank of Israel predicts a moderation in the second half of 2009.

Economists believe the shekel has no choice but to appreciate further due to a host of factors in the shekel's favour -- Israel's economy suffering less than the United States, large foreign capital inflows and a current account surplus in Israel's balance of payments.

"That creates a pretty strong set of fundamentals pointing in the direction of an appreciation of the shekel," Bufman said.

In recent days, a number of foreign banks such as Barclays, BoA Merrill Lynch and Citigroup have advised clients to buy shekels over dollars.

Maoz believes the best way to help exporters would be to raise short-term interest rates, which currently are 0.5 percent. He argued that since rates are so low, money has poured into the stock exchange, which has surged in recent months.

"Once you raise rates, the stock exchange won't go up like crazy and people will go into other assets like the dollar," he said.

title: UPDATE 1-Israel worried by shekel surge, officials eye options
text:
TEL AVIV, June 2 (Reuters) - Israeli government officials on Tuesday expressed concern that gains for the shekel <ILS=> would harm the economy, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's top economic adviser warned of possible government intervention.

"The Bank of Israel is doing a great job to keep the shekel weaker against the dollar," Ori Yogev, who advises Netanyahu as the chair of the National Economic Council's advisory committee, told a conference.

"If efforts (to weaken the shekel) do not work, the government of Israel would have to find the tools to preserve a real exchange rate," said

After weakening by some 25 percent since last July to 4.26 per dollar by late April, the shekel -- mostly due to global losses for the U.S. currency -- has rebounded about 10 percent.

It gained another 1.8 percent on Monday to a fresh four-month high, before retreating 0.6 percent on Tuesday to 3.911 per dollar.

Yogev, speaking at a business conference in Tel Aviv, did not say at what rate the government would intervene, but added: "It would be an economic catastrophe if the dollar goes back to 3.5 (shekels) or below."

To stem the shekel's run last year, the Bank of Israel in March 2008 started to buy small amounts of foreign exchange every day, raising it to $100 million a day last July when the shekel reached 3.20 per dollar. The central bank continues to buy forex every day and has not indicated when it would stop.

Exports, which account for nearly half of the country's economic activity, have been hit hard due to a very strong shekel for the first half of 2008 and then a deepening global economic crisis.

"Israeli exports are in trouble because of lower demand and the stronger shekel," Finance Minister Yuval Steinitz told the same conference.

He made no comment on the chances of intervention to weaken the currency but said the state would provide loan guarantees of up to 26 billion shekels to help minimise the damage.

RECOVERY THIS YEAR?

Exports slid more than an annualised 46 percent in the first three months of 2009, leading to a 3.6 percent contraction of Israel's economy on an annual basis in the first quarter.

The economy is forecast to contract by as much as 1.5 percent in 2009 and then grow a modest 1 percent in 2010.

"We still face months and months of negative growth but we are edging towards the end of the crisis," Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer told the conference.

He cited swift measures taken by many Western countries to counter the crisis.

"Had it not been for the global efforts from leading countries to stop the crisis we would not be sitting here talking about the possibility of recovery by the end of this year or early next year," Fischer said.

The central bank lowered its key short-term borrowing rate by 3.75 percentage points between last October and late March to a record low of 0.5 percent. It has not altered rates at its last two policy meetings, shifting its focus to buying government bonds to try and lower long-term rates.

(Writing by Steven Scheer; editing by Patrick Graham)

title: Israel shekel strength may end this yr -cenbank
text:
JERUSALEM, Aug 6 (Reuters) - The Israeli shekel's <ILS=> strength against other currencies is expected to fade and the unit may even weaken this year, the Bank of Israel said on Wednesday.

"The basic and long-term pressure strengthening the shekel is expected to moderate, and it is even possible that there will be a turnaround during the course of the year," the central bank said in its quarterly inflation report.

The Bank of Israel cited a number of factors, including an expected narrowing of the current account surplus in Israel's balance of payments, as well as daily purchases of foreign exchange by the central bank to boost its forex reserves and an outflow of capital by investors if the global financial crisis eases.

It noted, however, that the shekel's exchange rate over the next few months is still likely to experience a period of volatility.

The shekel, which stands at 3.53 per dollar, has appreciated about 8.5 percent against the U.S. currency so far in 2008 after a 10 percent gain in 2007.

But its year-to-date increase had reached more than 18 percent to a nearly 12-year peak of 3.20 last month, boosted by large foreign capital inflows, a weak dollar globally, rising Israeli short-term interest rates and a repatriation of money into shekel assets by Israeli investors.

In order to prevent a further shekel appreciation, which would hurt exporters, the Bank of Israel intervened. In March, it began buying $25 million of forex a day, raising to $100 million a day a month ago.

The central bank said its aim was to raise its forex reserves by some $10 billion.

The shekel has also appreciated against the euro this year.

title: UPDATE 3-Bank of Israel ups daily  FX  purchases, shekel dives
text:
(Updates with further shekel decline, stock market close)

JERUSALEM, July 10 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel said on Thursday it was raising the amount of foreign currency purchases to $100 million a day from $25 million, sending the shekel <ILS=> tumbling nearly 5 percent against the dollar.

The central bank said in a brief statement that the action was part of its plan to boost its reserves to $35-$40 billion, from more than $31 billion currently, and came after the shekel had surged in recent sessions to hit a nearly 12-year high against the dollar.

"The decision to increase the pace of purchases was taken after examining the programme in light of current market conditions, and the cumulative and rapid change in the exchange rate of the shekel," the central bank said in a statement.

"The Bank of Israel will continue to review the programme from time to time to take into account changing market conditions," it added.

The central bank on March 20 had embarked on what was then a two-year plan to boost its foreign currency reserves by about $10 billion through the purchase of $25 million of forex daily.

Analysts said the move to quadruple that amount was probably due to the central bank's view that the original amount was insufficient to halt the shekel's appreciation.

The shekel earlier in the session had risen to 3.2041 per dollar, its strongest level since October 1996 and brought gains in 2008 to some 17 percent. It had rallied the past four weeks from a low of 3.43.

After the announcement, the shekel slid and the central bank set the shekel's representative rate at 3.3140 to the dollar, 2.6 percent weaker than Wednesday's rate of 3.23.

But the shekel, which had been one of the world's best performing currencies the first half of the year, continued to slide after the setting of the official rate to stand around 3.36 per dollar at 1430 GMT for a 4.9 percent drop from its intraday peak.

"I don't think this will stop the appreciation of the shekel. But the shekel will appreciate at a slower pace," said Roderick Ngotho, an emerging markets forex strategist at UBS.

Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer has been under heavy pressure to deal with the shekel's strength since exporters have begun to get hit hard. A drop in exports, a key driver of growth, could threaten the overall Israeli economy, which has remained fairly robust.

In March, when the shekel had soared over a few days, the central bank intervened in the market for the first time in over a decade and bought $600 million of foreign currency.

Fischer is opposed to intervention in the belief that market forces should prevail, and the Bank of Israel has not intervened since despite speculation that the central bank would enter the market if the shekel rose too much.

Despite the daily forex purchases, the shekel has continued to gain, supported by a solid economy and Bank of Israel short-term interest rate increases aimed at curbing inflation pressures.

A third straight quarter-point rate increase is expected on July 28, a move that would bring the key rate to 4 percent.

Benchmark 10-year bond prices <ILSAHR2683=TA> shed 0.4 percent to push its yield to 5.93 percent from 5.86 percent, while key Tel Aviv share indexes closed 0.6 percent lower.

title: UPDATE 2-Israel shekel jumps to new 11-1/2-yr high vs dollar
text:
(Updates with further shekel gain, closing share indexes, analyst comment)

JERUSALEM, May 29 (Reuters) - Israel's shekel <ILS=> strengthened another 0.8 percent against the dollar in heavy trading on Thursday, boosted by heavy corporate selling of dollars.

The Bank of Israel set its official daily rate at 3.2620 shekels per dollar, its strongest level since January 14, 1997 from Wednesday's rate of 3.2880.

The shekel gained another 0.7 percent after the setting of the official rate to stand at 3.2380 to the dollar at 1450 GMT.

Dollar-shekel opened at 3.29 and remained steady until around 2 pm local time (1100 GMT), when selling intensified.

Companies typically sell dollars and buy shekels on the last few days of the months to pay salaries. But dealers said activity on Thursday was heavier than usual.

"All the companies who needed to sell dollars kept waiting for the dollar to go up. But that didn't happen," said a dealer at Israel Discount Bank. "Today we saw big volumes of dollar selling."

So far in 2008, the shekel has appreciated about 18 percent against the dollar, making it among the best performing emerging market currencies. That follows a 10 percent gain in 2007.

Part of the rise has come because of the globally weak dollar but lately, dollar-shekel has tended to decouple from euro-dollar.

Earlier this week, the Bank of Israel raised its key lending rate a quarter-point to 3.50 percent to widen the differential between Israeli and U.S. rates to 1.25 points.

With inflation soaring to an annual 4.7 percent in April from 3.7 percent in March, analysts expect the central bank to reverse all the 100 basis points of easing earlier in the year.

RATES, INTERVENTION

"We expect the shekel to remain well supported in the period ahead," Merrill Lynch analysts wrote in a report on Thursday. "At this stage, the central bank seems to have shifted its focus back onto inflation and appears less concerned about currency strength.

"Overall, monetary policy action will remain the key driver of the currency in the next few weeks, in our view," it added.

When the dollar fell sharply to 3.35 in mid-March, the central bank bought $600 million of foreign currency to halt the U.S. currency's slide. It was the first intervention in more than a decade and Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer made it clear interventions would not occur often.

The move pushed the dollar back to 3.65 in April.

Still, as the rate moved back to 3.35 shekels and below in recent days, the market expected another intervention, since a strong shekel tends to make Israeli exports less attractive and would hurt economic growth. It also helps to offset some inflation pressures since 40 percent of housing rental costs are quoted in dollars but paid in shekels.

"The Bank of Israel did not intervene at the levels the market expected them to. The market in general thought 3.33-3.34 was a line in the sand for the Bank of Israel," said Nandita Singh, an emerging markets strategist at JPMorgan Chase.

"When they didn't intervene, that emboldened investors to sell dollar-shekel," she said, adding that along with rate hikes, the central bank could now potentially use a stronger shekel to fight inflation.

Against the euro, the shekel jumped 1.6 percent to 5.0736.

Tel Aviv share indexes closed 0.9 percent higher, while the benchmark 10-year bond's price <ILSAHR2683=TA> edged up 0.1 percent.

JERUSALEM, May 27 (Reuters) - Israel's shekel <ILS=> advanced 1.4 percent to an 11-1/2 year high against the dollar on Tuesday after the Bank of Israel raised short-term interest rates for the first time in five months.

The shekel's official rate was set at 3.2850 per dollar -- its strongest level since January 21, 1997 -- from Friday's rate of 3.3330. Rates were not set on Monday due to holidays in Britain and the United States.

Late on Monday, the Bank of Israel raised its key lending rate by a quarter-point to 3.5 percent as expected in a bid to combat rising inflation pressures. It was the first rate increase since last December and another rate hike is expected next month.

The market began pricing in a rate hike in mid-May after consumer prices jumped a more than expected 1.5 percent in April on the heels of gains in food and energy costs to bring annual inflation to 4.7 percent.

"Yesterday's hike by the Bank of Israel is unlikely to be one-off given that we see inflation yet peaking at above 5 percent year-over-year in May," Silja Sepping, an emerging markets analyst at Lehman Brothers, wrote in a note.

The rate hike came after two half-point rate cuts in February and March on the central bank's view that a U.S. downturn would hurt Israel's economy and moderate inflation.

But soaring food and energy prices have fueled inflation, while Israel's economy grew at an annualised rate of 5.4 percent in the first quarter -- well above expectations.

"We think another 25 basis point hike in June seems likely," Sepping said. "Given the Bank of Israel's tightening bias and its seemingly higher tolerance of shekel strength, we stay short dollar-shekel in our model portfolio."

The shekel has appreciated by 17 percent against the shekel so far in 2008.

The Bank of Israel is opposed to such a strong shekel on the grounds that it makes Israeli exports less competitive and will ultimately dent the economy. In March, when the shekel reached 3.35 per dollar, the central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market to stem the dollar's slide.

So far, the Bank of Israel has not intervened in the current dollar slide, which has been more orderly than in March.

"Higher inflation, together with dollar-shekel having moved through previous intervention levels, suggests that the central bank is now more willing to see the shekel appreciate," wrote JP Morgan emerging markets strategist Nandita Singh.

A stronger shekel tends to offset some inflation pressures since about 40 percent of home rents are quoted in dollars but paid in shekels.

JERUSALEM, May 21 (Reuters) - Israel's shekel <ILS=> jumped more than 1 percent in late trading on Wednesday to a more than 11-year peak against the dollar, triggered by news that Israel and Syria had resumed indirect peace talks.

At 1450 GMT the shekel was at 3.33 per dollar, its strongest level since February 1997 and above its official rate at 3.3620. It had hit an intraday high of 3.32.

Key share indexes on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange rose about 1 percent and benchmark 10-year bond prices ended 0.4 percent higher.

The shekel opened around 3.38 per dollar and appreciated to 3.36 by mid-afternoon after Israel and Syria announced they had launched indirect peace talks mediated by Turkey, the first confirmation of negotiations between the long-time enemies in eight years.

The exchange rate held between 3.35 and 3.36, a key support level that was the previous high for the shekel versus the dollar in March. It was at that point, 3.35, when the Bank of Israel intervened in the market, buying $600 million of foreign currency in a bid to halt a slide in the dollar.

"There was the announcement today that Israel and Syria were starting a peace process so people started selling dollars," said Moran Yellink, a dealer at Israel Discount Bank.

"Once it got to 3.35, it (the dollar) fell like a rock. Everybody sold -- locals, banks and even foreigners."

The shekel has appreciated more than 15 percent so far this year against the dollar after a 10 percent gain in 2007.

Such a move puts Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer in a tough spot. A strong shekel helps to contain inflationary pressures since nearly half of housing costs in Israel are quoted in dollars but paid in shekels.

But a strong local currency also tends to hurt exports, which would threaten to weigh on the economy as a whole.

The shekel has moved back to its mid-March highs after a surprising 1.5 percent jump in the consumer price index in April from March, bringing inflation over the prior 12 months to a rate of 4.7 percent -- well above an official target of 1 to 3 percent.

The market had expected a monthly rise of 0.9 percent and an annual rate of 4.1 percent.

As a result, market players have factored in at least a quarter-point rate increase next week as the central bank tries to rein in inflation.

title: UPDATE 1-Bank of Israel cuts key rate by 50 bps to 3.25 pct
text:
(Adds central bank statement, shekel reaction)   

JERUSALEM, March 24 (Reuters) - Israel's central bank will cut its key lending rate by half a percentage point to a record low of 3.25 percent, it said on Monday, citing expectations that a severe global slowdown will curb Israeli growth and moderate inflation pressures.   

"The forces that served to moderate price increases last month -- mainly the higher probability of a slowdown in the global economy and the strengthening of the shekel -- continued to do so this month even more strongly," the Bank of Israel said in a statement.   

A similar move a month ago came as a surprise to the markets and was not fully supported by other central bank officials.   

However, Monday's announcement was widely expected and follows an announcement last week that the central bank would boost foreign currency reserves by about $10 billion over two years starting on March 24 through the purchase of $25 million of forex every day.   

"The global interest rate environment has fallen and is expected to continue to fall further," the central bank said.   

"Thus a reduction in the Bank of Israel interest rate is required this month too due to the moderating effect on price rises in Israel of the interest rate differentials between Israel and abroad, via the strengthening of the shekel."   

The Israeli move, which takes effect on Thursday, follows the latest U.S. rate cut last week in a series totalling three percentage points since September that has reduced the U.S. benchmark to 2.25 percent.   

The Bank of Israel intervened in the foreign exchange market on March 13 for the first time in more than a decade as the globally weak dollar threatened to hurt Israeli exports and overall economic growth.   

The Bank of Israel's moves have helped boost the dollar from an 11-year low of below 3.38 shekels <ILS=> last Wednesday to above 3.52 on Monday -- a 4 percent jump.   

The shekel strengthened by 10 percent versus the dollar in 2007 and until last week, it was up another 14 percent so far in 2008.   

"The degree of the strengthening of the shekel against other currencies since mid-December 2007 in itself acts to lower the pressures for price increases in the next few months," the Bank of Israel said, adding the link between the dollar-shekel rate and inflation was weakening.   

Inflation remains high in Israel, with consumer prices up 3.6 percent over the prior 12 months in February to exceed an official target range of 1 to 3 percent a year.   

But with the economy expected to slow in 2008 to below a 3.5 percent rate from 5.3 percent in 2007, the central bank believes inflation will be closer to 2 percent by the end of the year.   

"The half-point rate reduction is likely to support continued economic growth and employment," the central bank said. "The expected slowdown in Israel's growth reflects the decline in exports and in private spending expected to result from the slowdown in the global economy."

title: ANALYSIS-Shekel seen rising despite cbank  intervention  cloud
text:
JERUSALEM, March 19 (Reuters) - Israel's shekel <ILS=> is poised to extend its 11-year high versus the dollar in the near term, even under the threat the central bank may again buy foreign currency to stem its strength.

With the globally weak dollar tumbling to new lows versus the shekel last week -- the Bank of Israel changed its hands-off policy and intervened in the market, saying it would not rule out further forex purchases.

It bought an estimated $500 million worth of dollars last Thursday and Friday, a move that stopped the dollar's freefall against the shekel but did not stop it from weakening further.

"The central bank cannot change the direction of the market," said Leonor Terkieltaub, head of the foreign exchange department at the IBI brokerage in Tel Aviv.

Analysts are split as to whether the central bank's first intervention since late 1997 was necessary. But most believe that without it the dollar would be weaker than its current 3.3750 shekels -- its lowest level since April 1997.

Since the intervention, the dollar, which initially moved to 3.47 from 3.35 shekels, has resumed a year-long weakening trend.

"Higher (dollar) levels will be used to sell dollars again," said Terkeiltaub.

In the days before the action, the dollar slid from 3.60 shekels to 3.35 to prompt the extreme central bank move.

"The main issue right now is not dollar-shekel. It's the dollar around the world," said Ittai Ben-Zeev, head of sales and trading at Bank Leumi. "For the dollar to rise against the shekel you need it to rise around the world."

But that seems unlikely with U.S. interest rates falling, worries over the U.S. financial sector persisting, and the euro <EUR=> near a record high at $1.57.

Ben-Zeev said the dollar seemed to be holding above a key support level of 3.35 shekels for now. Should that break, "it could easily be at 3.20," he added.

EXPORTS HURT

The shekel has been one of the best performing currencies in the past year, boosted by a robust economy, strong foreign investment, higher interest rates in Israel than the United States and the weak global dollar.

"Although it may seem unwise to bet against a central bank determined to sell its own currency, we doubt the Bank of Israel will ultimately succeed in weakening the currency," Lehman Brothers wrote in a report.

"There are very strong fundamental reasons for the shekel to strengthen," it said, citing the widening Israeli-U.S. rate differential, the shekel being attractive on a trade-weighted basis, a strong economy and Israelis moving capital back to Israel. "We would look to add on shekel weakness."

The shekel rose 10 percent versus the dollar in 2007 and is up another 13 percent this year. The gains worry policymakers since exporters' troubles threaten to hurt the economy.

It remains unclear whether the intervention succeeded, despite signalling that Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer would not allow violent moves in the market.

"People who have real hedging to do need to do it regardless of what he (Fischer) is doing in the market and not be reliant on him coming to buy dollars," said Neil Corney, treasurer of Citigroup's Israel office.

"I don't think it necessarily changes the rules of trading."

But Ben-Zeev said volatility in the market has now reached 22 percent from 12 percent a month ago and 5 percent last year.

"We now have a new player who entered the game after sitting 11 years on the bench," he said. (Editing by Ron Askew)

title: RPT-UPDATE 1-'Herd' behaviour led Israel c.bank to act-Fischer
text:
(Refiles to fix typo in paragraph 12)   

(Adds comments, background)   

By Steven Scheer and Avida Landau   

JERUSALEM, March 16 (Reuters) - Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer on Sunday defended a rare intervention in the foreign currency market and stressed the central bank does not want to make a habit of buying dollars.   

The Bank of Israel bought an undisclosed amount of dollars on Thursday and Friday following a 6 percent drop in the U.S. currency against the shekel throughout the week. It was the first central bank intervention since late 1997.   

"We concluded that we saw a foreign currency market that is not anchored well and began seeing herd behaviour," Fischer told a news conference. "On the basis of this we decided to intervene in order to bring stability to the market."   

Although the dollar-shekel was weak all year, it had not moved as sharply as it did last week when it went from 3.60 per dollar early last Monday 3.35 on Thursday.   

Once the exchange rate fell below 3.40, the Bank of Israel stepped in and bought dollars. At first it didn't work and required another round on Thursday and then a third on Friday morning.   

"Initially the action was successful. The weakening of the dollar was stopped," Fischer said. "The dollar got stronger and the shekel got weaker."   

The dollar jumped from an 11-year low of 3.35 shekels to a level of 3.4740 by Friday afternoon.   

Fischer rejected the notion that the central bank was targeting a certain dollar-shekel rate.   

Trading in Israel's forex market will resume on Monday.   

Fischer declined to say how much the Bank of Israel bought but Israeli media and banks estimated the total at around $500 million.   

Fischer has been a staunch opponent of intervening in currency markets but he said that last week's freefall of the dollar against the shekel <ILS=> could no longer be ignored.   

"We have no intention of intervening on a daily basis," he said. "We will continue to trust the activities of the market except for extraordinary occurrences like we saw. We hope this intervention will be rare."   

He said that despite the action, the central bank's main mandate of keeping inflation low had not changed.   

Fischer declined to comment when asked whether he would lower short-term interest rates again at the end of the month as another way to weaken the shekel. In a surprise move, he lowered Israel's key lending rate by a half-point to 3.75 on Feb. 25.   

But the rate cut failed to halt a rally in the shekel against the dollar that has reached about 11 percent since the beginning of the year on top of a 10 percent appreciation in 2007.   

Fischer noted that in the long-term, he expected the shekel to continue to appreciating against the dollar.

title: Emerging Markets-Spreads near widest since June 05, shekel down
text:
LONDON, March 14 (Reuters) - Emerging sovereign debt spreads approached their widest levels since June 2005 on Friday as global risk aversion continued to bite, and the shekel retreated from near-11-year highs after central bank intervention.   

However local currency bond markets clawed back some recent losses triggered by a global liquidity squeeze.   

Sovereign bond spreads widened 6 basis points to 303 bps over U.S. Treasuries <11EMJ> as the dollar set new record lows against major currencies, and investors showed reluctance to hold higher-yielding assets.   

Spreads last closed above 306 bps in June 2005. Emerging debt spreads hit record tight levels below 150 bps in June 2007.   

"The basic issue under debate is the growth story and the impact of the slowing U.S. economy on different markets," said Oliver Stoenner, head of emerging asset allocation research at Cominvest in Frankfurt.   

"Latest data from India for instance gives the impression that growth is slowing and on the other side you have inflation problems, so emerging central banks have no real scope to give any stimulus to the economy. It's not a favourable mix for markets."   

India's annual growth is expected to slow in the first quarter as the economy eases towards a trend rate of 8.0-8.5 percent, the country's chief statistician said this week.   

Benchmark emerging equities dipped 0.3 percent <.MSCIEF> on Friday towards recent four-week lows.   

On currencies, the shekel slid versus the dollar <ILS=> after the central bank sold the currency to halt its run to near 11-year highs. Dealers said the bank bought about $200 million in foreign currency on Thursday, and $50 million on Friday.   

The shekel had risen over 3 percent to a high of 3.3465 per dollar on Thursday ahead of the first intervention, accelerating gains after  Moody's said it might upgrade Israel's A2 ratings.   

The shekel was trading at 3.47 at 1050 GMT, down more than 1 percent from the U.S. close.   

Hungary's forint hit a 2-1/2 week high versus the euro <EURHUF=>, as 5-year yields eased off last week's 3-1/2 year highs.   

Peripheral European bond markets had suffered ahead of the Fed's $200 billion liquidity injection this week, as investors favoured more liquid markets.   

Hungary's debt agency plans no further measures or changes to 2008 issuance plan and expects the local market turbulence to be temporary, the agency's chief executive said on Friday.   

Turkish bond yields also dropped, reversing recent sharp rises, and the lira <TRY=> steadied.   

"We see Hungary coming back a lot and performing well after the sell-off last week," said a Germany-based trader. "There is the same situation in Turkey, with yields some 10-15 bps lower."   

Ukraine's hyrvnia <UAH=> also firmed against the broadly weak dollar, heading towards the 5.0 level which marks the upper boundary of the currency's normal 5.0-5.06 trading corridor.   

The Icelandic crown steadied at 109.20 per euro <EURISK=> after a 6 percent sell-off against the euro in the past two days, to a record low beyond 111.50.   

Century Aluminum said on Friday it was starting site preparation for a 250,000 tonne aluminium smelter in Iceland, after winning approval for the project on Thursday.   

"This could be a story that would at least halt the rapid weakening in the last two days, especially if we see more developments globally and on emerging markets," said Jon Bentsson, economist at Glitnir in Reykjavik. (Additional reporting by Sujata Rao, editing by David Christian-Edwards)

title: UPDATE: Israel 's Fischer:Sees No Need To  Intervene  In  FX  -BIS
text:
(Updates with additional comments on the Israeli economy and developments in global markets)   

By Natasha Brereton   

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES   

BASEL (Dow Jones)--Israel's central bank sees no need to intervene in the foreign exchange market to adjust the value of its currency, its governor said Sunday.   

"The shekel has undergone a correction in the last few weeks, so I think the market seems to be taking care of any concerns over its valuation," Stanley Fischer told reporters on the sidelines of meetings at the Bank for International Settlements in Basel.   

With regards to intervention, Fischer said he saw "no need to do that, no desire to do that, no likelihood of its being done."   

The shekel has appreciated 4.78% against the dollar since the beginning of 2007, and 10.57% in the last year, the Bank of Israel said earlier this month.   

Fischer said that most recent data show that Israeli economic growth "is doing very well."   

The nation's gross domestic product grew at an annual rate of 6.3% in the first quarter of 2007, up from an annual expansion of 5.7% in the first quarter of 2006.   

"The indicator for May came in indicating growth in the current region of around 5%, perhaps a bit more," he said.   

There is "low inflation (and a) strong balance of payments, so all that looks fine," although of course "you have to stay on your guard," he added.   

The Israeli consumer price index was flat on the month in May and fell 1.3% on the year - well below the government target range for annual inflation of between 1% and 3%.   

Israeli interest rates currently stand at 3.5%. The central bank has cut the policy rate seven times in the past eight months, in an effort to bring annual inflation into the government's target range.   

The governor also expressed the view that a recent rise in global bond yields shouldn't have a significant negative effect on Israel or on other emerging market economies.   

"As for the interest rate correction, I think the economy is in reasonably good shape, which means for most the emerging market countries we're not going to see that having any major impact," Fischer said.   

"It may slow down a bit the capital inflows, but they have been taking place at such a rapid rate that a little slowdown isn't going to make a very big difference."

title: POLL-Bank of Israel seen cutting key rate to 3.75 pct
text:
* WHAT: Bank of Israel interest rate decision   

* WHEN: April 22, announcement due at 1530 GMT   

* Economists predict a quarter-point reduction in the key lending rate to 3.75 percent   

By Steven Scheer   

JERUSALEM, April 19 (Reuters) - Israel's central bank will probably lower rates for the sixth time in seven months next week as the shekel's continued strength against the dollar keeps inflation below zero, a Reuters poll on Thursday showed.   

All but one of the 17 economists surveyed expect a rate cut on Sunday, a decision moved up by one day due to Israel's observance of Memorial Day on Monday.   

Fourteen analysts forecast a quarter-point rate reduction, while two more predicted an even stronger half-point move, although some of those expecting a quarter-point believe there was a good chance of a half-point cut.   

"What he should do is 50 (basis points) but there was a hawkish atmosphere coming out of the most recent monetary meeting," said Jonathan Katz, economist at HSBC, referring to minutes showing the central bank was unanimous in supporting no move in late March.   

Some analysts said they believe there will be a rate cut even though there should not be one since prior rate reductions have failed to halt the shekel from strengthening. One economist said there would not be a rate move.   

After five straight monthly rate reductions totalling 1.5 percentage points, the Bank of Israel held rates steady in late March on the view that previous rate cuts and a rapidly growing economy would eventually nudge inflation back up within the official annual target range of between 1 and 3 percent.   

At the time, the shekel had been hovering around the 4.20 per dollar range and many economists believed the current monetary easing cycle was over for the time being.   

SHEKEL AT 6-YEAR PEAK VS DOLLAR   

But after the central bank's decision to hold rates, the shekel took off, rallying this week to as much as 4.05 to the dollar, its strongest level since December 2000. On Thursday, dollar-shekel was at 4.08.   

With Bank of Israel Governor Stanley Fischer rejecting calls for intervening in the foreign exchange market, analysts said the central bank is forced to use short-term interest rates as the main tool in trying to manipulate the exchange rate.   

A strong shekel typically brings inflation down since housing -- more than 20 percent of the consumer price index -- and many imported goods such as fuel are linked to the dollar.   

Those costs have more than offset price gains in food and other items in Israel not influenced by the dollar since a strong economy has led to high consumer demand and spending.   

The consumer price index for March was 0.9 percent lower than a year earlier.   

Economists have revised 2007 inflation estimates to a rate of 0 to 1 percent, with inflation reaching the target in 2008.   

"Following the recent appreciation of the shekel...the Bank of Israel will be under significant pressure to cut rates further by at least 25 basis points, perhaps even 50 basis points," Reinhard Cluse, emerging markets economist at UBS, wrote in a report.   

"Clearly, the bank is aware of the risk that additional rate cuts might cause a more serious overheating a couple quarters from now," he added.   

Fischer himself last week said the central bank was in a tough spot regarding its interest rate policy.   

"We are in a situation where we have to consider how rapidly we lower the interest rate or at all because the economy is growing so fast," Fischer said, referring to an expected growth rate of about 5 percent for the fourth straight year.   

Bucking the trend of predicting a rate cut next week was Bank Leumi economist Gil Bufman. He echoed the views of others in saying the combination of rate cuts now plus a strong economy could pose trouble for the Bank of Israel next year.   

"The Bank of Israel has been lowering the interest rate but the shekel is getting stronger," Bufman said, noting the shekel's strength was due to foreign investment flows that are not sensitive to interest rates.   

"At some stage, if he cuts more we may get into a problem like the build-vc'up of inflation pressures that may come in 2008 as well as a build-up of a financial bubble."

text:
(Adds further quotes, shekel reaction)   

JERUSALEM, April 11 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel has no intention of intervening to halt the shekel's <ILS=> appreciation, and such a drastic policy move could destabilise the currency market, Governor Stanley Fischer said on Wednesday.   

"We have no intention of intervening or entering the market," Fischer told a news conference, adding:"It will change the nature of the market completely."   

Helped by record foreign investment, the shekel has surged to a more than six-year high against the dollar, prompting calls from analysts for the central bank to buy dollars since a string of short-term interest rate reductions have so far failed to stem the shekel's rise and the disinflation trend.   

After an 8 percent appreciation in 2006, the shekel has added another 3 percent so far in 2007 versus the dollar.   

"If we intervene, people will be expecting it," Fischer said, noting he prefers that the market continue to focus mostly on economic fundamentals.   

Fischer acknowleged that the Bank of Israel, which has no tradition of intervening to influence the shekel's value, was in a difficult position regarding its interest rate policy because inflation remains below zero while the economy was growing fast.   

He said the interest rate was the sole tool the central bank uses to try and maintain price stability, defined in Israel as an annual inflation rate of between 1 and 3 percent.   

In an attempt to bring inflation back to within the official target range, Fischer lowered the bank's key lending rate five straight rate times from October through February to 4 percent from 5.5 percent.   

A belief that the economy was growing fast enough to return inflation to within the target later this year led Fischer to keep rates unchanged in late March. More cuts seemed unlikely.   

But with the shekel gaining further on the dollar -- advancing to 4.1060, its strongest level since February 2001 -- expectations have grown in the foreign exchange market that Fischer has no choice but to resume rate cuts later in April. Some economists believe a reduction of a half-point is possible.   

Fischer declined to say whether he would consider another rate reduction on April 22, the next scheduled policy decision.   

"ECONOMY GROWING SO FAST"   

"We are in a situation where we have to consider how rapidly we lower the interest rate or at all because the economy is growing so fast," Fischer said.   

He cited a contraction in the output gap that indicates "the economy is on the move".   

The Bank of Israel forecasts economic growth of 5.1 percent in 2007, which would be the fourth year in a row of growth around 5 percent.   

"The economy is in a good situation," Fischer said.   

He noted that some of what was happening in the economy and to the exchange rate was not under his control.   

"The problem is the dollar is falling all over the world," Fischer said, owing mainly to the large U.S. current account deficit. Israel has a current account surplus.   

With housing and many imported goods linked to the dollar, those costs have an immediate impact on inflation in Israel. Data show that while the overall consumer price index in February stood 0.8 percent lower than the prior 12 months, the CPI was up 0.4 percent excluding housing.   

Fischer said he would prefer to target "core" inflation, which removes much of the dollar/shekel's influence like in the United States but he doubted the Israeli public would accept it.   

"Domestic prices are rising and only imports and housing are falling," he said. "But negative inflation is not a problem.   

"We have decided to focus on the index that people understand -- the CPI -- and if we don't hit the target we try and explain it and that's what is happening today," he added.   

Fischer also said that while the economy was doing well and government was adhering to responsible budget policies, more needs to be done on reducing Israel's huge public sector debt, which is about 88 percent of gross domestic product.

title: Lebanon says  FX  reserves enough to support pound
text:
BEIRUT, July 15 (Reuters) - Lebanon's central bank governor said on Saturday the bank has enough foreign currency reserves to defend the Lebanese pound exchange rate and meet the financial markets' needs despite Israel's military offensive.  

"We have around $13 billion of foreign reserves and given the situation we are living in the financial markets have not reacted that negatively because they know the central bank's capabilities," Riad Salameh told Voice of Lebanon radio.  

The Lebanese pound <LBP=> has been trading at the weakest end of its official 1,501-1,514 band. The central bank intervened to offer dollars after Israel intensified its military campaign against Lebanon after Hizbollah guerrillas captured two Israeli soldiers on Wednesday.  

"The central bank will continue its policy to support the pound and offer liquidity with the current interest rates," Salameh said.  

The Stock Exchange also temporarily cut the daily limits set on price moves for listed securities and bonds to five percent from 10 percent on Friday for a week to bolster the markets after the military confrontation shook confidence.  

The benchmark BLOM Stock Index <.BLSI> fell 3.14 percent on Friday, for a tumble of just under 14 percent over the week.
