title: Israel's daily  forex  trade volume $1.7 bln in 2003.
text:
TEL AVIV, March 24 (Reuters) - Average daily trading volume in Israel's foreign exchange market reached $1.7 billion in 2003, up 10 percent from 2002, the Bank of Israel said on Wednesday.   

The growth is lowest since the bank of Israel changed its policy and stopped intervening in the forex market in 1997, a central bank spokesman said.   

In a statement, the central bank said the 10 percent growth rate was smaller than that of previous years. In 2002 the average daily volume grew 12 percent compared with the previous year, while in 2001 and 2000 volumes nearly doubled.   

The central bank said the lower volume growth could be explained by the fact that Israel's forex market has reached maturity and is thus growing at a slower rate than in previous years. Or alternatively, the slow development of Israel's capital and money markets is hindering additional growth in the forex market, the bank said.   

"A faster development of the local markets could have increased their attractiveness to foreign investors and encouraged a rise in their activity in the local capital markets," the central bank said.   

The foreign exchange market is highly centralised, the central bank said. Just a small number of market makers are active in this market, while 57 percent of the exchange activity is done by the three biggest Israeli banks and 83 percent by the five biggest banks.   

"Because of the high centralisation, very few market makers provide liquidity to the market, something that could hamper its development in the future," the statement said.

title: Israel shekel sinks as cease-fire seen shaky.
text:
TEL AVIV, July 8 (Reuters) - Israel's shekel  slid 1.2 percent against the dollar on Tuesday after a Palestinian suicide bombing threatened a 10-day cease-fire that may have signalled an end a strong shekel rally, traders said. 

 The shekel's representative, or official, rate was set at 4.3340, from Monday's rate of 4.2830 to the dollar - its strongest level since December 20, 2001. 

 After the setting of the rate, the shekel sank further to close to 4.37 to the dollar. 

 "Things were looking good up until today," said a dealer at United Mizrahi Bank. "After we saw that the bomb was a terrorist attack and not a mistake fear has emerged that the cease-fire may fail." 

 Earlier on Tuesday, a West Bank-based cell of the Islamic Jihad militant group took responsibility for a suicide bombing on Monday night that killed a woman in Israel. 

 Dealers said that suicide bombings have not impacted the market much in recent months because they had been so frequent. 

 "But now, things are starting to get better so any terrorist attack makes the market think we may be going back" to when they occurred more often, the Mizrahi dealer said. 

 He noted that foreign banks were the big dollar buyers today. 

 "They made profits on the (dollar's) way down so it was a good time to close," he said. "There was a bit of foreign banks closing short postions in fear the bomb may cause a new crisis in the cease-fire." 

 The shekel had jumped some 10 percent against the dollar in the past few month, buoyed by progress on Middle East peace, tighter fiscal policies and a wide interest rate gap between Israel and the United States. 

 In recent days, some dealers said the shekel could still gain further to 4.25 or more because Israel's key lending rate stands at 7.5 percent to the U.S. federal funds rate of 1 percent but Tuesday's move may have shown the shekel was still vulnerable. 

 "This might have been the trigger to closing short positions," said the dealer. 

 Although the central bank has lowered its key rate from 9.1 percent in recent months, dealers said the 6.5-point gap over the U.S.'s fed funds rate makes holding dollars difficult. 

 Prime Minister Ariel Sharon and Finance Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have urged the central bank to lower rates faster in the wake of zero inflation and the stronger shekel's impact on exports, but Bank of Israel Governor has said he has no plans to intervene in the foreign exchange market or drop rates sharply to weaken the shekel. 

 He stood firm on his policy to steer clear from intervening in the strengthening shekel, saying only the market should determine the exchange rate. 

 The basket of foreign currencies, composed of the dollar, euro, pound sterling and yen, was fixed at 4.7116 shekels against 4.6638 shekels on Monday. 

 On the crosses, the shekel traded at 3.6606 shekels per 100 yen compared with 3.6278, against the euro at 4.9018 shekels from 4.8633 and against the pound at 7.0993 versus 7.0618.

title: Israel  c.bank says won't  intervene  in  forex  market.
text:
JERUSALEM, July 3 (Reuters) - Israel's central bank chief on Thursday stood firm on his policy to steer clear from intervening in the strengthening shekel, saying only the foreign exchange market should determine the shekel's rate. 

 The shekel has jumped some 10 percent against the dollar in the past few months, prompting calls for lower short-term interest rates or direct intervention to prevent the stronger currency from curtailing exports and damaging Israel's recession-hit economy further. 

 "Attempts to intervene in trading to guide the exchange rate will fail and is an idea that is playing with fire," Bank of Israel Governor David Klein told an economic conference. 

 In recent weeks, Finance Ministry officials and those depending on exports have said the shekel - which on Thursday was at a fresh 18-month high at 4.29 to the dollar - was too strong and could hurt the economy, which has been in recession for more than 2-1/2 years due to a global slowdown and bloody Israeli-Palestinian conflict. 

 "There is no basis for arguing the shekel is either too strong or too weak," Klein said. "This is a market rate." 

 He reiterated his position that intervention usually fails since "you are working against the market" while "interest rates are not a tool for controlling the exchange rate". 

 The shekel has gained on expectations of tighter fiscal policies, the end to the Iraq war in which Israel was unscathed amd optimism over the start of a process that could lead to a peace deal with the Palestinians.

title: Israel  cbank denies reports of  forex intervention .
text:
TEL AVIV, March 10 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel on Monday denied media reports that it had intervened in foreign exchange trading on Friday to prevent banks from artificially boosting the exchange rate ahead of a dollar-linked bond redemption. 

 The central bank said it called banks as part of its management of foreign exchange dealing to check on the difference between quote prices and rates at which transactions were taking place. 

 "It would be an exaggeration to call it an intervention," said a central bank spokesman. "It was simply part of our ongoing activities and happens from time to time." 

 Israeli media reports on Monday said the central bank intervened in trading to prevent manipulation of the exchange rate ahead of Friday's redemption of 3.6 billion shekels ($742 million) of bonds. Payment to bondholders was based on Friday's representative, or official, rate which was set at 4.8490 shekels to the dollar. 

 The dollar rose against the shekel last week as institutional investors tried to prop up the dollar's rate against the shekel ahead of the bond expiration. 

 The Ha'aretz daily said the central bank intervened after it noticed the banks were offering quotes that were not in line with transaction prices. The paper said the banks were trading the dollar at 4.84 shekels but quoting it at 4.86 shekels and that foreign banks had complained that Israeli banks were manipulating the rate. 

 The bond holders were mostly institutional investors, including banks, which had an interest in seeing a high rate set ahead of the redemption, Ha'aretz said. 

 "I would not call this intervention, the (central) bank calls the banks from time to time to check the level of the market," said a dealer from a major bank who requested anonymity. 

 A dealer at another of Israel's largest banks said the banks had an interest in the official rate being set as high as possible but said the gap between the quote and transaction prices was less than cited in media reports. 

 "The bank called and asked us to check the price difference," the dealer said. "That happens sometimes, particularly when trading is volatile. It doesn't happen every day, but it's not rare either." 

 ($1 = 4.85 shekels).

title: Emerging  FX -Rand strength ebbs, shekel down after bomb.
text:
LONDON, May 8 (Reuters) - The South African rand eased off five month highs against the dollar on Wednesday after earlier exporter buying had helped it extend its six-day old bull run. 

 Elsewhere, the shekel dropped back to its weakest levels in over a week against the dollar in the wake of another suicide bomb attack in Israel, while the zloty pulled back after verbal intervention from the Polish Finance Minister. 

 The rand found upward momentum initially from exporter demand, but ran out of steam ahead of the key 10 level. However, analysts think that level will come under pressure again in coming sessions. 

 "The rand has risen on a combination of flows and fundamentals," said Callum Henderson, currency strategist at Citibank. 

 "Last year we had a loose monetary policy, and a relatively tight fiscal policy, but the mix has changed to tighter monetary policy, with a looser fiscal stance this year, and the rand has risen on that basis," said Henderson. 

 Firm commodity prices and the prospect of another rate hike from the central bank in June have underpinned the rand's recent rally. 

 South African Reserve Bank Governor further bolstered expectations of another rate hike in June on Tuesday, saying that inflation was on an upward trend. 

 "If it (inflation) is on the upside the Reserve Bank has one instrument...which is to use its monetary policy stance," said Mboweni. 

 The recent rise in bullion prices to their highest levels in over two-year have added to the rand's bull run. South Africa is the world's largest gold producer. 

 The market has also broken through some key technical levels, with the 200-day moving average around 10.3140 giving way on Tuesday. 

 At 0930 GMT, the rand traded at 10.1587 to the dollar from 10.17 late on Tuesday. 

 BOMB ATTACK HITS SHEKEL 

 The latest suicide bomb attack in Israel left 15 dead and prompted Prime Minister Ariel Sharon to cut short his trip to the U.S. He also vowed to "hit back hard" against Palestinian militants. 

 Fresh security worries undermined the shekel, which retreated close to its recent record lows against the dollar below 4.90. 

 The shekel traded at 4.9050 to the dollar from 4.8620. 

 The zloty retreated from its recent highs as Finance Minister Marek Belka intensified his efforts to talk the currency lower. 

 Belka said the strong zloty was a curse and called on the central bank to help take action to weaken it. He added that he was concerned over the central bank's misguided monetary policy. 

 Analysts said that Belka's desire for a weaker zloty was well documented, but some also noted that the zloty had risen a long way in recent days and could be ripe for a pullback. 

 "Belka has said before that he sees fair value for the zloty around 4.25 to the dollar, so this is not a great surprise," said Simon Watts, emerging markets analyst at UBS Warburg. 

 "Locals have been worried that non-residents might start pulling out of the bond market after recent signals from the central bank that the pace of monetary easing will slow, but you still get paid handsomely for taking on zloty risk," said Watts. 

 With benchmark interest rates at 9.5 percent, Poland still attracts investors in search of high yields. 

 The zloty traded at 3.6287 to the euro from 3.6197 and at 3.9839 to the dollar from 3.9642. 

 The Turkish lira climbed off recent lows against the dollar, finding support from news of strong Turkish industrial output in March. 

 Output rose 18.7 percent on the year, far in excess of the 4.3 percent predicted in a Reuters poll of analysts. 

 The lira traded at 1,372,500 to the dollar on the interbank market from 1,376,000.

title: Israeli Shekel Can Find Support In Tight Policy Stance
text:
JERUSALEM -(Dow Jones)- The Bank of Israel's decision to keep interest rates on hold is expected to have less of an impact on the shekel (ILS) than the security situation and an expected interest rate rise in May. 

 After the central bank announced Monday that it was freezing the discount rate at 4.4% for April, the shekel slipped to ILS4.68 to the dollar from its ILS4.6650 Bank of Israel fixing an hour earlier. It then edged up, and traded between ILS4.6670 and ILS4.6780 through most of Tuesday before weakening to ILS4.6830 by 1530 GMT. 

 Short-term, the decision could weaken the shekel, Ilan Zadka, head of the corporate desk at the United Mizrahi Bank trading room, said Tuesday. 

 "It's less attractive," Zadka said. "If the rate had risen, then the shekel would have been more attractive." 

 Over the coming months, sources see the shekel trading within a range of ILS4.57-4.78 to the dollar and within a narrower range of 4.63-4.70 over the next few weeks, driven mainly by political developments. 

 "If there's no cease-fire, no good outcome from the cease-fire talks, from (U.S. envoy Anthony) Zinni, or from the Arab summit, there's no reason the dollar shouldn't go much higher...the 4.75 area again," said Michael Rabinowitz, a senior dealer at Israel Discount Bank. 

 "If there's some good news on the peace front, the dollar could go back down to the 4.62 level," Rabinowitz said. 

 The shekel will also be influenced by expectations that the central bank won't maintain its neutral stance on the discount rate, analysts said. 

 "You'd think logically that the dollar would rise and the shekel would fall," said Daniel Hass, head of institutional sales at the Bank Hapoalim trading room. 

 But over the past couple of months, Bank of Israel Governor David Klein has "littered the market with verbal interventions, and he may make some comment on the future possibility of rate hikes," Hass said. 

 Such hints on the Bank of Israel's part have strengthened the shekel - most recently a Feb. 12 warning that brought the shekel up from a ILS4.78 low and foreshadowed an actual rate hike in March. 

 Klein, in fact, suggested broadly in his rate announcement that further rises may be in the offing. Though he acknowledged that price surges in the first two months of the year wouldn't heat up annual inflation, he repeated that fiscal laxity would force him to tighten credit to meet the government's 2002 inflation target range of 2%-3%. 

 "Adhering to a budget framework that ensures low long-term interest rates and a declining government debt/GDP ratio is a necessary condition for maintaining price stability in the long run," the central bank said. 

 The government is widely expected to significantly overshoot its 2002 budget deficit target of 3% of gross domestic product. 


                      Policy Reversal



The central bank raised its base lending rate by 60 basis points for
March to counteract the inflationary effect of a shekel that weakened
13% after a 200 basis point rate cut in late December.



Further rate rises are now expected to keep the shekel in check and
suppress capital outflows. Analysts and market sources see the discount
rate back up to 5%-5.5% by the end of the year.



"I think certainly if we go up to (ILS)4.75, we are going to hear Dr.
Klein threatening to raise again," Rabinowitz said.



Hass expects Klein to raise the key lending rate if the U.S. starts
hiking its own rates again as the economy recovers, reasoning that
without the differential the shekel won't be attractive. Rabinowitz said
an Israeli rate rise wouldn't necessarily follow from a U.S. hike -
unless a devaluation follows, fueling inflation.



"At the end of the day, Dr. Klein is looking where inflation is
going," he said. "And if we're overshooting inflation then he'll raise
the rates."



An illiquid currency market through the end of the Jewish Passover
holiday late next week will also leave its mark on the shekel in the
immediate term, sources noted.



"The holiday period is coming up, so no one is going to push it (the
dollar) wildly, because liquidity is going to be really low for the next
couple of days," Hass said.

title: Curb On Bk Of Israel Powers Seen Prompting Intl Backlash
text:
(This item was originally run March 10 at 1647 GMT.)



By Amy Teibel


 JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--The Finance Ministry's proposal to curb the Bank of Israel's powers threatens to unleash a harsh response by the international financial community, critics said Sunday. 

 Even those analysts who favor stripping Israel's central banker of his sole authority to set monetary policy termed the proposal misguided. 

 "This is an attempt to fully politicize the Bank of Israel, to take over fully the control of the central bank," a senior economist said on condition of anonymity. 

 "...It's a very tricky and treacherous road that the Ministry ofFinance has decided to venture into," he said. "And hopefully there will be some people from the international financial community who will be able to point out the risks of playing around with central bank independence." 

 The mainstay of the proposed amendment to the 1954 Bank of Israel Law, which the ministry submitted to Cabinet on Sunday, is formation of a nine-member monetary committee to set Israel's discount rate. 

 The committee, headed by the governor but nominated by the finance minister, would include the central banker's two deputies plus "six prominent economic figures or academics known for their monetary, financial or macroeconomic experience." 

 The ministry proposal also would give the government license to subordinate the central bank's mission of preserving price stability to growth and employment targets, and to change inflation targets mid-year. Additionally, it would let the finance minister direct the investment of foreign currency reserves, and allow the government to intervene in the foreign currency market. 

 The Bank of Israel, which supports the formation of a professional board of governors devoid of vested interests, warned of an international backlash in its attack on the proposal. 

 "The proposal does away with Israel's commitment to price stability, damages the Bank of Israel's independence, and subordinates the Bank of Israel to the directive of the finance minister," the central bank said. 

 "This proposed legislation is liable to lead to a lowering of Israel's credit rating, given the expected deviation in the government's budget deficit, the downgrade in 2002 growth forecasts, and the grave security situation," the central bank said. 

 A ratings downgrade would encourage capital outflows and thereby lead to higher domestic interest rates and financial destabilization, the central bank warned. 


          Stock Exchange Unfazed



The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange didn't react harshly to the news.
Politicians have made similar proposals before, brokers noted, even
though previous bills wouldn't have so sharply limited the central
bank's powers.



The government never did anything with a professional committee's
December 1998 proposal to overhaul the Bank of Israel Law, which
included the establishment of a monetary committee and a clear statement
of the central bank's mandate of preserving price stability.



The foreign currency market doesn't trade on Sunday.



The draft legislation, which Cabinet is to discuss next Sunday, comes
at a time when the economy is stagnating, the budget deficit is
ballooning, and the Bank of Israel is considering raising rates again
after a 200-basis-point cut fueled price rises.



Finance Minister Silvan Shalom, furious that the Dec. 25 rate cut was
negotiated behind his back, is no less happy with the notion of rate
rises, calling them a hindrance to growth and job creation.



"I think that the government, and particularly the minister of
finance, is worried that the economy is going to look bad and he's
trying to clutch some straws to avoid sinking," the economist said. "And
evidently those straws are in the form of irresponsible monetary policy
and high inflation as something that is supposed to be a magic cure for
GDP growth and unemployment."



The finance minister likely hopes the draft legislation will curb any
planned rate rises in the short term, and in the longer term, "cause the
Bank of Israel to be another department within the Ministry of Finance,"
he said.



If the government wants to administer monetary policy, "you don't need
the Bank of Israel at all," a banking source said on condition of
anonymity.



"This would very much weaken the Bank of Israel," he said. "I'm
certainly not enthusiastic about this."



- By Amy Teibel; Dow Jones Newswires; 972-2-537-6985;
amy.teibel@dowjones.com

title: Israel cbank mulls rates as CPI rises,economy dives.
text:
JERUSALEM, Feb 25 (Reuters) - Faced with a deepening recession and rising consumer prices, the Bank of Israel faces one of its toughest decisions ever on Monday on whether to raise interest rates to prevent a potential spike in inflation. 

 Analysts were unusually reluctant to predict which way central bank Governor David Klein will jump when he announces the monetary programme later on Monday. 

 He could leave rates alone, or raise them anywhere from 0.2 to 1.0 point depending on how Klein views the dive in the shekel against the dollar - which has led to higher consumer prices - analysts said. 

 "He has a big dilemma. It's almost a lose-lose situation for him," said Tal Vardi, vice president at Citibank in Tel Aviv. 

 What is known is there will be no more rate reductions. A rate cut cycle that began in late 1999 seemingly culminated in December with an emphatic two-point drop in the key lending rate to an all-time low of 3.8 percent, meant to aid an economy hit by the global downturn aggravated by the Palestinian uprising. 

 Since then, two conflicting forces have emerged in the economy: a 10 percent drop in the shekel that sent housing and other items linked to the dollar soaring - reflected in a 1.1 percent jump in the consumer price index in January - but also data showing a worsening economy and unemployment above 10 percent for the first time since 1993. 

 "There's a recession going on which we saw in unemployment and GDP (gross domestic product) numbers," said Ptachia Bar-Shavit, chief economist at Bank Hapoalim. "There are very few signs of a recovery. If there is a recovery, it is very fragile." 

 Bank Hapoalim, which initially gave even odds for a rate hike, on Sunday offered a prediction of a one percentage point increase. 

 Economists said an interest rate increase at this time would squash any rebound and counter any positive effects the economy would gain from cheaper exports. Business leaders have also urged the central bank to hold rates. 

 "Klein (shouldn't) raise interest rates when we have a 10.2 percent unemployment rate," said Shlomo Maoz, chief economist at Nessuah Zannex Securities. 

 Still, a decision to take no action could weaken the shekel further and fuel more CPI gains, since the foreign exchange market has priced in at least a half-point rate increase based on Klein's warning two weeks ago that he would not tolerate inflation. 

 SHEKEL GAINS ON RATE HIKE SPECULATION 

 On Monday morning the shekel was gaining 0.9 percent against the dollar as the market speculated the central bank could raise its key lending rate by more than a half-point. 

 The shekel's representative rate on Friday was set at 4.70 against the dollar, near its weakest ever point reached earlier this month. After the shekel depreciated by more than 10 percent in two months Klein warned of a rate hike and the shekel temporarily calmed. 

 "I really believe Klein doesn't want to hike rates because the economy is doing poorly and (a hike) would send a bad signal from the central bank that it is doing a zigzag" with rates, Vardi said. "I would wait another month at least." 

 Economists predicted a CPI rise of more than one percent in February as effects of the shekel drop continue to feed into the economy, followed by a 0.6 percent rise in March. 

 After that, many analysts believe prices will stabilise, but expect inflation to be more than four percent this year - above the government's 2-3 percent target rate. Economic growth is forecast at less than 1.0 percent after a 0.5 percent contraction in 2001 and some analysts fear stagflation. 

 "Prices are going up but it's not inflation; a one-time price adjustment is not inflation," said Vardi. 

 "But if Klein feels it's the beginning of an inflation cycle or feels there will be a run on the shekel he will raise rates," he said. "If he feels the price rises will only be in January, February and March because of the depreciation of the shekel he will not change rates." 

 Maoz, though, was confident Klein would hike rates at least a half-point even though he did not believe rate should rise. 

 "If he doesn't raise rates, the depreciation in the shekel will go to five to the dollar and people will say he is not fighting inflation," he said. "If he doesn't raise it by a half-point now, he will have to raise rates 1-1.5 points in one shot later." 

 "By March, we will be at three percent inflation," he said, adding that the central bank should directly intervene in the foreign exchange market and sell dollars rather than raise rates to stem the shekel's weakness. 

 The Bank of Israel is against intervention, citing the market is too large to fight. 

 "They have $23 billion of reserves," Maoz said. "Central banks hold foreign currency for emergency times and this is an emergency. If you don't use it in an emergency, then when will you use it?"

title: UPDATE 2-Israel shekel slide hits 10 pct vs dollar.
text:
JERUSALEM, Feb 11 (Reuters) - Israel's shekel, down 10 percent since a steep interest rate cut in late December, fell to new lows against the dollar on Monday, sparking fears of renewed inflation. 

 The shekel's representative rate was set at 4.7440, down 1.6 percent from Friday's level of 4.6670. 

 The dive in the shekel comes against the backdrop of a reeling Israeli economy that has been hit hard by a global economic downturn and a Palestinian uprising that has lasted 16 months, hurting exports and keeping tourists away. 

 Gross domestic product (GDP) growth is expected at 0.5-2.0 percent in 2002 after a 0.5 percent decline in 2001. 

 "It's a one-way market right now," said Gideon Sadeh, head of Treasury sales at HSBC in Tel Aviv. "You don't have any dollar sellers." 

 The rapid descent of the shekel, which had remained strong against the dollar since the end of 1999, has particularly raised inflation fears since housing prices are linked to the U.S. currency. Inflation, which was just 1.4 percent in 2001 is seen rising to around three percent in 2002. 

 But the shekel's fall has also given hope to exporters who have been hard hit due to the combination of a global economic slump and a resilient Israeli currency for the last three years. 

 "That will stimulate the economy, but if the shekel continues to depreciate the Bank of Israel will have no other choice but to raise interest rates," said Yacov Sheinin, president of the Economic Models consultancy. "The only way to intervene is to raise interest rates." 

 The Bank of Israel is not likely to intervene directly in the foreign exchange market by buying shekels, since it believes the global forex market is too large to fight. 

 But raising rates would be an about-face, since it was a steep rate cut in late December that ignited the shekel's dive. Bank of Israel Governor David Klein on December 23 slashed the country's key lending rate by two percentage points to an all-time low of 3.8 percent as part of a deal in which the Finance Ministry agreed to chop government spending in 2002. 

 "It's not so bad to have a weak shekel but it's the way it was done," Sheinin said, adding that Klein should have lowered rates in steps in order to monitor the effects of the cut. "Now we are paying the price. This is what we call zig-zag policy." 

 SMALL RATE CUTS 

 Since the end of 1999, the central bank had cut the lending rate in gradual increments of 0.2 to 0.3 percentage point at a time from a rate of 11.5 percent as inflation was benign. The bank repeatedly warned of a volatile reaction from financial markets if interest rates fell too fast too soon. 

 As a result, the high level of interest rates and a moderate rate differential between Israel and the United States helped support the shekel until almost the end of 2001, even as the Israeli economy entered a recession. 

 With only a 2.05 point differential in rates between Israel and the United States, analysts said more of a premium is now required to hold shekels given the upheaval in the economic and security situations and as many believe U.S. rates have bottomed out with the federal funds rate at 1.75 percent. 

 The shekel hit close to 4.40 to the dollar in late 1998 during the collapse of emerging markets. 

 But it strengthened back to near 4.0 to the dollar after the Bank of Israel raised interest rates by 4.0 percentage points in late 1998 to curb inflation and steady the shekel. 

 On Monday, the shekel was set at 3.5411 shekels per 100 yen compared with 3.4905, against the euro at 4.1690 shekels against 4.0738 and against the pound at 6.7531 shekels versus 6.5933. 

 Dealers said Monday's sharp drop in the shekel is the result of market perception that the Bank of Israel is not resisting the development. Escalating Israeli-Palestinian violence was also pressuring the shekel. 

 "The market feels that the Bank of Israel will not intervene in the market so there is a feeling of further appreciation in the dollar," said a dealer at Bank Hapoalim. 

 Dealers noted that much of the shekel's drop has come from the general public selling shekel assets through mutual funds. 

 "People have been waiting for the dollar to retrace lower so they can buy at cheaper levels," said the Hapoalim dealer. "But a lot of people missed the opportunity to buy at lower levels and now don't want to miss any further (shekel) depreciation." 

 Still, dealers are unwilling to speculate how much further the shekel will weaken since analysts had bet on a level of no more than 4.75 to the dollar by the end of the first quarter. 

 "The dollar broke through resistance levels without any difficulties," noted HSBC's Sadeh. 

 The near-term direction of the shekel depends, dealers agreed, on Friday's release of the consumer price index (CPI) for January which will indicate the impact of its slide. 

 If the CPI comes in as expected at a rise of no more than 0.8 percent and the central bank holds rates steady, "fixed players will think they have another month to play with until the February CPI and the dollar can reach higher levels," Sadeh said. "But the only thing that will derail the dollar's rise is a rate increase."

text:

title: Israel's Concern Is Shekel's Strength, Not Vulnerability
text:
By Jennifer Downey 

 OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Currencies are expected to tumble in times of political turmoil or war, but no one seems to be taking that bet with the Israeli shekel. 

 Since the beginning 14 months ago of the second intifada, or Palestinian uprising, the shekel has declined a mere five percent, despite suicide bombings, a rise in terrorist-group popularity and a shift in  the Israeli government. 

 Moreover, many analysts have expressed concern that squeezing Palestinian leader Yasir Arafat out of power will produce a void that may allow dangerous factions to gain influence. After another terrorist attack Wednesday, Israeli armed forces retaliated and the administration of Prime Minister Ariel Sharon cut off ties with Arafat. 

 But rather than fearing a currency fallout during the political crisis, some analysts are more concerned about an overly strong shekel during worldwide economic downturn. 

 Despite the deteriorating geopolitical backdrop, the dollar traded around ILS4.2250 on Wednesday and is trading only slightly stronger Thursday at ILS4.2270. 

 "If you look back two years, including terrorist attacks or other turmoil, it did nothing except provide intraday volatility" in the dollar/shekel exchange rate, said Joseph Barnea, foreign exchange trader at Bank Leumi in New York. "I have to say, it's steady like a rock." 

 The same phenomenon can be seen in Israeli bond spreads, which haven't widened much in light of the traumatic events of the past two weeks, said Assaf Gutterman, chief economist at the Israeli Ministry ofFinance's mission to New York. 

 A chief reason for predictable moves in the shekel is the "clockwork" series of month-end conversions, when Israeli companies transfer dollars and euros into shekel, Barnea said. 

 Israel is heavily reliant on foreign markets, mainly in the U.S. and Europe, and demand abroad has helped drive Israel's competitive high-technology industry. Thus the regular transactions these companies require in order to move assets from international sales back into Israel  provide a consistent source of shekel buying. 

 So far, whenever speculative traders have dabbled in the shekel, "commercial interests have somehow been able to put a lid on everything," Barnea said. "Those trying over time to sell shekels and buy dollars on political events or security issues have been smacked." 

 But companies are actually being harmed by a general propensity among Israelis to stay in the shekel instead of expanding into assets denominated in other currencies, said Joseph Morgenstern, consultant and publisher of the Israel High-Tech & Investment Report. 

 Israel's key lending rate is 5.8%, over four hundred basis points higher than the current U.S. federal funds rate. Rates offered for bank savings in Israel are around 5.5% and some Israeli government bonds yield a 9.7% tax-free return, Morgenstern said, providing strong reinforcement for citizens to keep their money in shekels. 

 This leads to "what's euphemistically called a mountain of shekels," which sounds positive but is dangerous for Israeli companies which are already suffering from the global economic slowdown, he said. 

 A high-priced shekel reduces the competitiveness of Israeli exports. The problem is exacerbated because a large amount of Israel's exports are in the high-tech sector, which has struggled after the collapse of the late 1990s bubble economy. In return, imports are cheaper, further reducing the domestic market for Israeli goods. 

 Far from fearing that political consequences will take a toll on the shekel, Morgenstern would welcome a decline in the shekel's exchange rate in order to stave off dire economic consequences. 

 "I think a country of six million people has to maximize the return on its exports. It needs to have a rational exchange rate," Morgenstern said. 

 The shekel trades within a 36% band, and each trading day the Bank of Israel assigns a "fixed" rate for the shekel against a basket of currencies, but the shekel is free to trade at any rate within the wide band. 

 The Bank of Israel follows a non-intervention policy, but as concerns over the strength of the shekel grow, it may become more difficult for the central bank to avoid intervention, Barnea said. 

 Early this week, Bank of Israel Governor David Klein sharply addressed this concern, warning that Israel's exchange rate policy could "explode in our face one day," and suggesting that the band should be scrapped in order to avoid the need for central bank intervention. 

 Like the European Central Bank, the Bank of Israel's prime concern is price stability. The Bank of Israel, like the ECB, has heard more voices calling for the Bank of Israel to make more drastic interest-rate cuts to spur growth during the global slowdown. 

 Because the interest-rate incentive is a key reason the shekel is so strong, a reduction in these rates would not only weaken the currency, but make the economic downturn less taxing on exporters and likely even boost employment, Gutterman said. 

 But in the meantime, turmoil in the Middle East is "calculated in the risk" that is inherent in the high rates that Israeli assets offer, and when people buy shekels, they already know this, Gutterman said. 

 "The international community understands the situation that Israel is in," he said. "They understand they're not buying currency of the Netherlands."

title: Bk Of Israel Head Urges Pension Reform,End To Shekel Band
text:
CAESAREA, Israel -(Dow Jones)- Bank of Israel Governor David Klein took advantage of Israel's most important economic conference Thursday to demand deep reforms to the country's pension system, and an end to the shekel trading band and the cap on treasury bill sales. 

 Klein urged that the pension system be forced off its diet of non-tradable government bonds and gradually move to market instruments, to help the domestic capital market. 

 "Without a deep and fluid bond market, the stock market can't develop either, and that clearly hurts the economy's ability to grow," Klein told a conference of leading figures in government and the private sector. 

 Conceding that it would be unrealistic to undertake a wholesale reform of the pension sector, Klein urged a partial reform that would bar new members to the funds from having their pensions financed by non-traded bonds. 

 He said tax benefits accruing to pension holders should be awarded according to the taxpayer's income level rather than across the board. 

 The governor, facing off against the resistant Finance Ministry, repeated his call to eliminate the shekel trading band. He said hyperinflation and other conditions that once made it necessary no longer exist, and warned that the central bank could one day be forced either to jack up interest rates to defend the band or intervene in the currency market. 

 "If we are forced to defend (the band), then we will ultimately be forced to eliminate it, after paying a high and unnecessary price," Klein cautioned. "Better to do it at our own initiative and not under market pressure." 

 The last time the Bank of Israel intervened heavily in the market, between 1995 and 1997, it bought $16.5 billion, he noted. 

 The Finance Ministry objects to eliminating the shekel band, on the grounds that a free-floating currency would depreciate. 

 Klein also took the Finance Ministry to task for capping sales of treasury bills, saying it prevents the central bank from using them as a monetary tool. Left only with interest rates, Klein said the bank was compelled to keep them slightly higher than necessary. 

 He said stability of asset prices, like securities and real estate, were a key concern of policy-makers. But he warned that without reform of the pension system, the trading band and T-bill sales, the central bank was in a poor position to ensure stability of asset prices. 

 "Only after these constraints are lifted and the culture of price stability becomes firmly rooted, can the Bank of Israel turn its attention to the financial markets, in an effort to contribute to the preservation of their stability," Klein said.

title: Israel June Discount Rate Cut Again, Dn 20 BPs To 6.8%
text:
JERUSALEM -(Dow Jones)- Making up for a skipped rate cut in May, the Bank of Israel said Monday it will cut the discount rate for a second time in June, to 6.8% from 7%, effective Thursday. 

 Governor David Klein canceled the May rate announcement because of labor unrest at the central bank, saying he was denied data critical to setting policy. But when the bank announced the first June discount rate cut of 20 basis points in late May, it signaled that another reduction would follow if the unrest stopped, as it did last week. 

 Klein plans an announcement on the July discount rate in one week, resuming the central bank's regular once-a-month decision making process. He's expected to cut the July rate some 20 basis points. 

 The stock and foreign currency markets were unaffected by the expected modest credit softening. 

 Klein told Israel radio the rate reduction was designed to help stimulate growth without heating up inflation. Inflation expectations two years out aren't far below government targets, so "it is best to act prudently" when lowering rates, he said, signaling an intention to maintain his policy of small cuts. 

 In a release announcing the cut, Klein said rate changes to meet the inflation target won't offset the recessionary influence of the U.S. economic slowdown and renewed political violence at home, nor structural problems. 

 He urged the government to spend more on programs promoting economic growth, while maintaining a commitment to the diminishing budget deficit targets set through 2003. 

 Economists forecast 2001 inflation at 2% or less, below the government's target range of 2.5%-3.5%. The economy is expected to grow only 1%-2% in 2001, entrenching unemployment of close to 9%. 

 Political pressure now compounds the economic data in favour of a cut, with Prime Minister Ariel Sharon telling a business forum last week that rates "should and will come down." 

 Klein deflected an Israel radio question on how long he could withstand the political pressure for deeper cuts. 

 The Bank of Israel has cut the discount rate by a total of 1.4 percentage points over the past five months. 

 In the release, Klein also cautioned that failure to jettison the shekel trading band is liable to set off "a financial crisis of inestimable proportions," and "uncalled-for and distorted intervention in the markets by the Bank of Israel." 

 The Finance Ministry, which would have to approve such a move, opposes eliminating the band for fear that a free-floating shekel would depreciate sharply.

title: Bank of Israel says no need to impact shekel trade.
text:
JERUSALEM, March 25 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel sees no need to intervene in or influence shekel trade despite a recent depreciation, as long as the weakening does not translate into higher inflation, the spokesman for the central bank said on Sunday. 

 The spokesman's office confirmed remarks by central bank Governor David Klein published Sunday in the Maariv newspaper. 

 "The Bank of Israel will not intervene in the foreign currency market as long as the depreciation does not threaten meeting the inflation targets and price stability," Klein said. "The shekel's depreciation is positive as long as it is not accompanied by higher prices." 

 The central bank spokesman's office said Klein's remarks did not refer to direct intervention but to the use of monetary policy as an influence on shekel trade. 

 The shekel has slipped more than 4 percent against the dollar since the start of 2001 as international markets have been rattled by a Wall Street purge and Israeli high-tech companies find their resources for importing capital are drying up. 

 At the same time, Israeli inflation is forecast at 1.5-2 percent for 2001, well below a government target of 2.5-3.5 percent for the year and matching a long-term goal to stay in a range of 1-3 percent inflation in line with Western economies. 

 Klein reiterated his view that the shekel's trading band - a mechanism that defines limits for the currency's depreciation or appreciation before the central bank must defend it - should be removed. 

 "The trading band ... is artificial and unnecessary, and no one would feel it if we got rid of it," he told Maariv. 

 Israel's Finance Ministry has opposed removing the band, fearing the lack of a defined limit could encourage too rapid a rise or fall in the shekel's value. 

 The central bank maintains that the shekel's value should be determined by the market alone and that monetary policy is the proper tool for influencing the market.

title: Israel Shekel Topping 4-to-Dlr; Grazing Strong Pt In Band
text:
JERUSALEM -(Dow Jones)- The shekel peaked above four to the dollar early Thursday for the first time since late March, grazing the strongest point in its trading band and taunting the Bank of Israel to intervene. 

 All this is happening amid a fierce dispute between the Finance Ministry and the Bank of Israel over whether to abolish the shekel trading band. 

 At 0545 GMT, the average between ask and bid prices at several Israeli banks reached ILS3.9990. The currency is about 1.5% below the strongest point in its trading band. Should it strengthen beyond that point, then the central bank is committed to buy foreign currency to weaken the shekel and force it back within the confines of its band. 

Central Bank governor David Klein has been pushing since his appointment in January for the elimination of the band, arguing that it is no longer needed given Israel's low inflation and liberalized foreign currency market. Inflation for all of 2000 is projected at some 1.6%. 

 But the band can't be jettisoned without the support of the Finance Ministry, which argues that instead of a freely floating shekel, the central bank should cut the discount rate instead. The discount rate for September has been cut 20 basis points to 8.9%, but inflation-adjusted rates continue to hover in the 8% range. 

 Lower rates would make foreign inflows less attractive and ease upward pressure on the shekel, the ministry reasons. They would also help old economy sectors that are largely responsible for Israel's 8.5% unemployment rate, and whose exports struggle to compete when the shekel is strong. 

 The Ha'aretz newspaper reported Thursday that the Finance Ministry has proposed that the trading band be phased out by 2003, but the central bank said it didn't know of any such plan. 

 The shekel is adjusted daily against a basket of four currencies dominated by the dollar, and including the British pound, the euro and the Japanese yen. It is allowed to fluctuate 15% on either side of its midpoint. 

 The currency has been strengthening steadily throughout August because of large capital inflows to Israeli high-tech companies, export growth and foreign investment in infrastructure projects. Political instability has also strengthened the shekel by delaying progress on a proposed tax overhaul that eliminates tax disincentives for investing in foreign assets. 

 Some economists say the band should be scuttled when Israel implements the tax reforms. The reforms would encourage capital outflows, easing the upward pressure on the shekel allaying Finance Ministry fears that the shekel could continue to strengthen if the band is jettisoned, they said.

title: Bank of  Israel  head says will  intervene  if needed.
text:
JERUSALEM, Aug 23 (Reuters) - Bank of Israel Governor David Klein said on Wednesday that the central bank would intervene in foreign currency trade if the shekel hit the strongest limit in its trading band. 

 "If and when the exchange rate will hit the bottom part of the band, we will intervene because this is our obligation," Klein told Israel's Army Radio. 

 Klein called on the government this week to eliminate the trading band - a mechanism that allows the shekel to fluctuate 17 percent above and below a gradually depreciating midpoint - before intervention was necessary. 

 Klein said that although the exact timing depends on the market, "the moment will definitely come in which the exchange rate hits the lower limit of the trading band. And so it will be necessary to intervene and such intervention will needlessly embroil the economy." 

 The shekel is currently 2 percent away from its strongest point in the band, but Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak's government has yet to show support for abolishing it.

foreign currency policy has been significantly liberalized.



But the band can't be scuttled without the support of the Finance
Ministry, which argues that the central bank should cut interest rates
instead. Lower rates would make foreign inflows less attractive and ease
upward pressure on the shekel, the ministry reasons. They would also
help 'old economy' sectors that are the major contributors to Israel's
8.5% unemployment rate, and whose exports are hard-pressed to compete
when the shekel is strong.



"One reason the shekel is approaching the ceiling of its trading band
is that interest rates are high relative to those in Western economies,"
the Finance Ministry said in a release Wednesday. "Measured and prudent
discount rate cuts would halt the appreciation of the shekel and
eliminate the need (for Bank of Israel) intervention in foreign currency
trading."



The central bank is committed to intervene in the foreign currency
market to defend the trading band.



Some economists say the band should be dumped when Israel implements
the tax reforms, which eliminate the tax disincentives for investing in
foreign assets. This would ease the upward pressure on the shekel and
encourage capital outflows, allaying Finance Ministry fears that the
shekel could continue to strengthen if the band is jettisoned, they say.



The Israel Discount Bank economists see the currency strengthening to
ILS4 to the dollar in coming weeks. Katz believes it could go even
higher if there is a breakthrough in Mideast peacemaking. But he sees it
weakening to ILS4.10 or ILS4.15 in 2001 on the back of continued Israeli
rate cuts and U.S. rate rises.

title: Israeli shekel at four-month high to dollar.
text:
TEL AVIV, Aug 21 (Reuters) - The Israeli shekel forged another four-month high against the dollar on Monday spurred by the Bank of Israel's renewed call to remove the currency's trading band, dealers said. 

 With the shekel less than 3.0 percent away from the strongest point of the band - a mechanism that allows the shekel to fluctuate some 17 percent above and below a gradually depreciating midpoint - it may not be long before the central bank has to defend the currency by intervening in the market, Bank of Israel Governor David Klein told Reuters on Sunday. 

 But buying foreign currency would necessitate printing more shekels, thereby putting in danger the country's inflation target, he said. 

 "The market is jumpy on the back of Klein's comments, but it seems some people are looking at it as a good buying opportunity and that may be holding (the exchange rate) at these levels," said a dealer at Bank Hapoalim. 

 "There's some support at 4.03, but it's at a level where if that breaks (the dollar) could go much lower," he said. 

 Klein's call for abolishing the band has not been supported by the government in the past and a government source said on Monday that the issue was not currently on the agenda. 

 The shekel's representative rate against the dollar was set at 4.0310 from 4.0400 on Friday. 

 Corporate sector customers were more involved in buying dollars while banks led sales on thin volumes, a dealer at Eurotrust said. 

 "If (Klein) gets rid of the band he will do it with a rate cut, because otherwise it will push the shekel stronger," the dealer said. "The market is ripe to head to 4.0 but the question is what will happen there." 

 The basket of foreign currencies, comprising the dollar, euro, pound sterling and yen, was fixed at 4.1494 compared with 4.1705 on Friday. 

 On the crosses, the shekel traded at 3.7250 shekels per 100 yen compared with 3.7093, against the euro at 3.6394 shekels compared with 3.6988, and against the pound at 6.0141 shekels compared with 6.0434 on Friday.

title: UPDATE 1-Israel Bank head says shekel band an impediment.
text:
JERUSALEM, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Bank of Israel Governor David Klein said on Sunday that the shekel's eight-year-old trading band could endanger the country's inflation target and called for its elimination while the foreign currency market is calm. 

 Israel's shekel is allowed to trade some 17 percent above and below a gradually depreciating midpoint, with the central bank committed to defending the currency once it reaches the upper or lower limits of the band. 

 In his first interview with the international media since taking office in January, Klein told Reuters that Israel's approach towards Western inflation levels could bring the shekel to its strongest point of the band. The shekel is currently less than three percentage points away from that strongpoint. 

 "A day will come, and I don't think it's very far away, where the actual exchange rate will reach the limit of the band just because we don't have any more inflation differentials" with other major currencies, he said. 

 The shekel has strengthened to a level of 4.04 to the dollar compared with 4.15 at the beginning of the year, largely due to an influx of foreign currency invested in Israeli high-tech companies and accelerated economic growth. 

 In addition, the shekel's strongpoint on the trading band is built to depreciate at a rate of two percent annually to account for the inflation differential between Israel and developed countries. 

 But with Israeli inflation expected to finish below 3 percent in 2000, that differential is becoming insignificant and could bring the shekel even closer to its limit, he said. 

 Once that happens, the Bank of Israel would have to buy foreign currency to protect the shekel and as a result, "pour shekels into the economy, increase the means of payment and endanger the inflation target," he said. 

 Furthermore, "in order to absorb those shekels, we will have to raise interest rates" to stave off the inflationary pressures, he said. "This is why I think the band is really an impediment now." 

 FOREIGNERS TO LOOK ASKANCE AT CENBANK INTERVENTION

 Klein said that for the past three years Israel has had an opportunity to abolish the trading band and he most recently called on the government to do so last week during a vote on the 2001 national budget. 

 "We should do it when the foreign currency market is calm," Klein said. "It's not any particular day or month. It's whenever we are within the band and we don't have to defend it - this is a good opportunity." 

 Klein does not expect the band's abolition under such circumstances would shake up the foreign currency market which has been determining the shekel's exchange rate according to its own needs for several years. 

 However, if the Bank of Israel were to intervene again in trading - something not seen since late 1997 - the move could have a negative effect on foreign investors active in the market. 

 "They are not going to understand if we start entering as a central bank...the market in order to protect artificially a given trend of exchange rates," he said. 

 "This is going to change all their views of the Israeli market. This is also a reason why we should be a lot more careful about moving away this threat of the existing band."

title: ANALYSIS-Lebanese gloomy as Israeli withdrawal nears.
text:
BEIRUT, April 18 (Reuters) - A sense of foreboding is settling over Lebanon as a long-sought end to Israel's occupation of the south threatens to bring war rather than peace. 

 "Anyone who really believes that an Israeli pullback will automatically herald the end of Lebanon's problems is in for a rude awakening," The Daily Star newspaper said in an editorial on Tuesday. 

 That pullback - and the unpredictable consequences it will unleash - took on a feeling of inevitability with Israel's formal notification to the United Nations on Monday that it would end its 22-year occupation by July. 

 But Lebanese are already showing deepening unease that they will be caught up in a power struggle between Syria and Israel. 

 The central bank intervened in foreign exchange markets last week to support the Lebanese pound for the first time in a year. People in south Lebanon, nearest the conflict, report some shops are running down their stocks. 

 The security problem is compounding already deep economic trouble. Earlier this month the Beirut stock exchange, shrinking since 1997, sank to a daily volume of a mere 1,046 shares worth $5,843. 

 Investment, such as a Four Seasons Hotel to be built by Prince Alwaleed bin Talal, the Saudi investor, has apparently been put on hold. Bankers say even heavy discounting cannot attract buyers for real estate acquired as collateral. 

 The atmosphere is more of resignation than panic; people still hope to avoid a major conflict and talk of Lebanon's resilience. But for a country rising from the ashes of the 1975-90 civil war, the prospect of an indefinite delay in Arab-Israeli peace and the investment that would bring is suffocating. 

 Lebanon and its dominant partner Syria have warned Israel that a withdrawal that is not part of a broad peace agreement returning Syria's Golan Heights will not give security to Israel, implying that attacks over the border will follow. 

 Israel has responded with threats of massive retaliation on Lebanon, which has served as the battleground between its more powerful neighbours for the past two decades. 

 JUSTIFYING FIGHTING 

 Both sides appear to be laying the groundwork for justifying fighting after a withdrawal. 

 Lebanon and Syria continue - despite Israel saying it will withdraw to borders recognised by the United Nations - to suggest that Israel will occupy small parts of Lebanon, which would be a cause for continued guerrilla attacks. 

 Lebanese Prime Minister Selim al-Hoss told members of parliament on Monday night, immediately after Israel's withdrawal announcement, that Lebanon could not be held responsible for border incidents. 

 But it will be. Israel has spent the weeks before the formal withdrawal announcement ensuring there will be no criticism from Washington and most other governments if it launches intense attacks on Lebanon in reprisal for even minor cross-border incidents. 

 A diplomatic source close to the process expected that Israel would quickly escalate any incident, hitting Lebanese infrastructure and even some of the 35,000 Syrian forces inside Lebanon. It is not to the advantage of Israel, with overwhelming military superiority in the region, to be drawn into a protracted conflict along the border. 

 Either conflict - short and highly destructive, or continuous clashes inflicting a steady toll - would be disastrous for Lebanon's fragile economy. 

 Only strong economic growth can save the government from disappearing into a debt trap; debt servicing takes more than 80 percent of revenues and public debt is growing about 1.5 percent a month. The economy was stagnant last year and hopes for any substantial improvement depend on peace. 

 Increasingly, Lebanese professionals who returned to their country after the chaos of the civil war are questioning their prospects in a country where the hopes of the mid-1990s are now seen to be a mirage. 

 "I have a young family and I have to wonder what future there is for them here," said a professor who returned to help restore the American University of Beirut but is now contemplating leaving. 

 The government was swift to deny a report in As Safir newspaper this month of alarming levels of emigration. But the fact that the issue has moved on to the frontpages was a sure sign of the public mood. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 2000.

title: Israel  industry official urges cenbank  intervention .
text:
JERUSALEM, April 10 (Reuters) - Israeli industry official Rimon Ben-Shaoul called on Monday for the Bank of Israel to intervene in foreign currency trading and stem the tide of capital inflows strengthening the shekel. Ben-Shaoul is head of the economic division at the Manufacturers Association of Israel and president of Clal Industries & Investments, the investment arm of one of Israel's largest conglomerates, Clal Israel. Ben-Shaoul said capital inflows surged to an annual rate of $7.6 billion in the first quarter versus some $4.5 billion in 1999, fuelled by funds raised and repatriated by the country's high-tech sector. 

 "There is an unusual situation of one-sided foreign currency flows leading to a real (shekel) appreciation, harming export profitability and unemployment," Ben-Shaoul told reporters. 

 "I think the Bank of Israel must intervene in the foreign currency market and stabilise it because this trend will continue and worsen," he said, estimating the central bank would need to buy several billion dollars of foreign currency annually "in excess of the market's equilibrium." 

 Left untouched, a too-strong shekel would push unemployment as high as 9.8 percent in 2001 from 8.9 percent in 1999 and keep economic growth on a low burner at 3.2 percent annually, he said. A shekel-dollar rate of 4.2-4.25, as seen in 1999, would better serve Israeli exporters, he said. 

 The Bank of Israel is committed to intervening when the shekel hits the upper or lower limit of its trading band, which allows the currency to fluctuate 18 percent above and below a gradually depreciating midpoint. 

 Ben-Shaoul advocated abolishing the band altogether, calling on the central bank to intervene strategically. 

 "The Bank of Israel is supposed to intervene if we reach the (shekel's strongest) limit, but by the time we get there we'll have 250,000 unemployed people," he said. 

 The central bank's monetary policy has become ineffective against the appreciation because the market already factored in rate cuts, he said, adding "the Bank of Israel doesn't have a lot more room to cut rates - 1.5 to 2.0 percent." 

 Ben-Shaoul also called on the government to increase growth inducing investment and said he supported a reduced tax burden "which can only be accomplished with a tax on capital", among other measures. 

 ($1 = 4.03 shekels). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 2000.

title: Israel Ctrl Bk Must Cap Shekel, Say Manufacturers
text:
JERUSALEM -(Dow Jones)- Israel's manufacturers urged the central bank Monday buy billions of dollars to reverse the shekel's rising trend, which it says is damaging exports and jobs. 

 Rimon Ben-Shaoul, chairman of the economics panel of the Manufacturers Association of Israel, blamed upward pressure on the shekel on capital inflows. 

 He also urged the government to more than double its infrastructure investments to $2 billion annually, and to cut taxes to the point that the budget deficit will widen. 

 Bank of Israel policy is to intervene in foreign currency trading only to defend the trading band. It last intervened in early 1998. 

 The shekel (ILS) has strengthened to some ILS4.03 to the dollar from some ILS4.2800 at the end of September, largely on the back of capital inflows in search of high-tech investments. 

 The central bank refused to comment on Ben-Shaoul's proposal. 

 Ben-Shaoul, who is chief executive of Clal Industries and Investments Ltd., acknowledged that his call for central bank intervention in foreign currency trading was "unmodern and anachronistic." But he projected that foreigners attracted by Israeli high-tech industries would invest $7.6 billion in the country's industry in 2000, a rise of $3 billion over 1999. 

 These inflows cause the shekel to appreciate, making exports less profitable and causing unemployment to rise, he said. If the Bank of Israel were to eliminate the shekel trading band and intervene in foreign currency trading, he said, then the economy could grow between 4% and 5%. 

 Without intervention, the economy will expand 3.2% in 2001 and unemployment will rise to 9.8%, he said. Joblessness in January was 9.3%. 

 The large capital inflows aren't "a natural economic development," and the central bank should act now to offset its effects, he said. 

 Ben-Shaoul said he didn't know exactly how much foreign currency the Bank of Israel should buy, but said it should be "several billions." He said he'd like to see the shekel trading around ILS4.20 to ILS4.25 to the dollar. 


On lower taxes, Ben-Shaoul said studies in the U.S. have shown that
even if tax cuts aren't balanced in the budget, they still stimulate
growth by themselves, thereby
narrowing the deficit.   Ben-Shaoul also called for the introduction of
capital gains tax on Israeli securities, which at present are not
taxed. Previous efforts to impose a tax have failed.



A Finance Ministry-appointed panel is to submit a tax reform program
in May.

title: Israeli  forex  hedging instruments rise to $12 bln.
text:
JERUSALEM, April 5 (Reuters) - The value of hedging instruments against foreign exchange rate risk in Israel rose to $12 billion in the beginning of 2000 from $8.5 billion in 1998, the Bank of Israel said on Wednesday. 

 The 2000 estimate represents an average of January and February figures. 

 The instruments include options and futures transactions, reflecting the total value of all contracts that have yet to expire expressed in dollars. 

 The central bank attributed the rise "to the public's increased awareness to (exchange rate risk), due to the process of easing the exchange rate policy and the Bank of Israel's non-intervention policy in the foreign currency market." 

 Exchange rate risk in Israel has increased with greater volatility in the foreign currency market seen in recent years, especially with a gradual liberalisation of trade. 

 In late 1998, a shekel depreciation was deepened by customers with foreign currency loans who were forced to buy dollars on the spot to cover their positions. 

 Commercial banks hold the vast majority of hedging instruments while 22 percent are traded on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, the central bank said. 

 ((Jerusalem newsroom, +972-2-537-0502, jerusalem.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Israeli Use Of Exchange Rate Hedges On The Increase
text:
JERUSALEM -(Dow Jones)- The use of exchange rate hedges is on the increase in Israel as the public becomes more aware of risk due to the June 1997 widening of the shekel trading band and the Bank of Israel's policy of not intervening in the foreign currency market, the Bank of Israel said Wednesday. 

 Options and futures contracts on the shekel exchange rate totaled an average $12.4 billion in the first two months of 2000, up 12% from an average $11.1 billion in 1999. The 1999 figure was 30% higher than the year-earlier figure of $8.56 billion, the central bank said.

title: FOCUS - Israel's Frenkel mum on report he will top IMF.
text:
JERUSALEM, Jan 9 (Reuters) - Jacob Frenkel declined to say on Sunday, his last day as Bank of Israel governor, whether he had been tipped by European diplomats to replace Michel Camdessus as head of the International Monetary Fund. 

 A spokesman for the Bank of Israel said neither Frenkel, 56, nor the central bank would comment on the speculation he would succeed Camdessus who steps down in a month. 

 Frenkel's departure as Bank of Israel governor, after more than eight years in office, left a void pending cabinet approval of David Klein, a senior central bank director, chosen by Prime Minister Ehud Barak to take Frenkel's place. 

 Frenkel announced in mid-November he would resign on January 2, but postponed his departure at the request of Barak who asked for one more week to name a successor. 

 Barak is in the United States for peace talks with Syria and a spokeswoman in his office could not say when the government would vote on Klein's appointment, announced on Friday. 

 Klein, like Frenkel, is thought to hold a tight monetary policy aimed at curbing inflation. But some politicians, including Finance Minister Abraham Shohat, had hoped for a loosening of the reins that would jump-start economic growth. 

 In his first comment on the choice of Klein, Shohat told Israel's Channel Two Television: "It is no secret that I thought there were nominees more suitable for the matter. 

 "I am not saying it on the personal level against David Klein. I have no complaints against him. I think conceptually a different governor should have been appointed." 

 Israeli markets hailed news of Klein's appointment, with the shekel strengthening against the dollar slightly on Friday and major stock indices gaining over three percent on Sunday. 

 PARLIAMENT TO REVIEW MONETARY POLICY COUNCIL 

 Lawmaker Elie Goldschmidt of Barak's One Israel faction said the parliamentary finance committee which he heads would review on Monday a bill to dilute the powers of the central bank governor. 

 The bill, introduced several years ago by Shohat and other lawmakers, would establish a monetary policy council that would make interest rate decisions. Currently the central bank chief has final authority over interest rate adjustments. 

 "I suggest we do not interpret this initiative as a lack of faith in the incoming Bank of Israel governor," Goldschmidt told Israel Radio. 

 "We are creating a wider platform for taking such critical decisions for the future of the economy without hurting the character, standing or importance of the governor," he said. 

 NO DECISION-MAKER IN THE INTERIM 

 In the intervening days until Klein is voted in, Israel will be left without a central bank chief for the first time since the institution was established. 

 The Bank of Israel law only allows a previously appointed deputy governor to step into the number one post once a central banker leaves, but the deputy position has not been filled for more than a decade. 

 While routine central bank decisions can still be carried out without a chief, the choice to adjust interest rates or to intervene in the foreign currency market ultimately rests with the Bank of Israel governor. 

 "If there is some kind of sudden shock to the markets there is no one to take decisions (until Klein takes office), but there is little chance that will happen," a banking source said. 

 At the same time, "the situation is much better now than if Frenkel had left a week ago," the source said. 

 "The markets already know that the next governor will continue in (Frenkel's) line and are calm, so there is less likelihood that there will need to be a response" in the form of monetary policymaking, the source said. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 2000.

title: Israeli Ctrl Banker: Politics Won't Dictate Monetary Policy
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Israel will pursue a monetary policy that is dictated by economic considerations and not domestic politics, Governor Jacob Frenkel told a delegation from the Institute of International Finance Sunday. 

 Given the uncertainty on global financial markets and parliament's failure to approve a 1999 budget, "the Bank of Israel will continue to take action to preserve and guarantee economic stability as defined by government targets," a central bank release cited Frenkel telling the delegation. 

 "Interest rate policy therefore will continue to be administered according to the dictates of the economic agenda, irrespective of political schedules," he said. 

 Parliament recently voted to dissolve itself over deep divisions within the governing coalition which led among other things to a failure to pass a budget for 1999. Early elections have been called for May 17. 

 Frenkel also defended his decision to raise the discount rate to 13.5% from 9.5% in November, and not to intervene on foreign exchange markets when the shekel dropped sharply against the dollar in October. 

 The central bank's tight monetary policy has been criticized by many Israeli economists as well as some foreign economic experts. In its annual report on Israel in December, the International Monetary Fund seemed to fault the Bank of Israel for not intervening in October, when the shekel lost 11% of its value against the dollar. The shekel has since regained much of the ground it lost. 

 The delegation from the Institute of International Finance, an organization made up of leading financial institutions, is in Israel preparing its annual report on the Israeli economy. 

 (END) Dow Jones Newswires 24-01-99

title: Legislators warm to Bank of Israel oversight bill.
text:
JERUSALEM, Dec 8 (Reuters) - Israel's parliamentary finance committee voted on Tuesday to move forward with opposition-sponsored legislation that would create a board to oversee Bank of Israel monetary policy-making, currently concentrated in its governor's hands. 

 The bill, which is not supported by the government, will now be presented to the plenum for the first of three readings before it becomes law. 

 After lying in abeyance for more than a year, the bill gained new momentum after the Bank of Israel came under attack from politicians and many business leaders for its handling of the shekel's sharp depreciation in October. 

 The Bank of Israel refused to intervene in the forex market and in a bid to curb resulting inflation its governor, Jacob Frenkel, raised interest rates sharply. 

 The hike was seen by many politicians and manufacturers as excessive and at the expense of economic growth. Under the current law, the central bank's governor has sole authority to set interest rates. 

 "Monetary decisions cannot be in the hands of one person," said Likud legislator Zeev Boim. "Frenkel is top notch but something as serious as monetary policy can't be left to one person." 

 But some legislators warned a board of governors could hurt the central bank's independence. 

 "This bill is dangerous (because) it ties the hands of the governor and affects the independence of the central Bank," said Michael Kleiner, a member of the finance committee who voted against the proposal. 

 "There will be a chain reaction that will lead to a lowering of Israel's credit rating, a drop in investment and thousands of people losing their jobs." 

 Frenkel has said he would support a council of governors so long as the governor appointed its members and the change was part of a larger revision of the Bank of Israel Law. 

 A government-appointed committee is currently evaluating a revised law, proposed by the Bank of Israel, that would define the bank's goals and objectives. 

 The committee is expected to present its recommendations toward the end of the month. ((Jerusalem newsroom, +972 2 537-0502, jerusalem.newsroom@reuters.com)).

 It could also "facilitate a gradual reduction in the exposure of Israel residents to foreign currency risk, and thereby lower the potential vulnerability of the Israeli economy to contagion effects from shocks that might hit other countries with weaker fundamentals," the report said.

title: IMF Report Urges Israel To Ease Monetary Policy
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--The International Monetary Fund urged Israeli economic authorities to establish conditions to gradually ease Israel's monetary policy and appeared to criticize the Bank of Israel for not intervening in foreign currency trading to calm market volatility. 

 The IMF also cautioned authorities against raising the government's 1999 inflation target of 4.0% and widening the 1999 budget deficit target of 2.0% of gross domestic product. 

 "A protracted period of high real interest rates would further weaken domestic demand," the IMF wrote in its preliminary annual report on the Israeli economy, published Wednesday. "Thus, economic policies in the next few months should strive to establish the conditions for a gradual easing of the monetary stance, without risking a rekindling of inflation or the re-emergence of pressure for a depreciation of the shekel." 

 The Bank of Israel raised its key lending rate by four percentage points in November to 13.5% to curb higher inflation expectations stemming from the shekel's 17% depreciation between early August and late October. Annual 1998 inflation, which had appeared to be heading for just 4.0%, may be as high as 7.0% to 9.0% because the shekel weakened so sharply amid turmoil in international financial markets. 

 The central bank was widely criticized in Israel for not selling dollars in early October to calm the volatile market. The IMF report appeared to contain a veiled criticism of that stance. 

 "In pursuing monetary policy goals, it is desirable to avoid as far as possible abrupt changes in monetary conditions," the report said. "In this context, it would be useful to continue to explore whether limited intervention in the foreign exchange market can be undertaken without unduly encouraging risky behavior."

title: FOCUS-IMF report favours Bank of  Israel intervention .
text:
JERUSALEM, Dec 2 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel should consider limited intervention in the foreign currency market, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in a report obtained by Reuters on Wednesday. 

 "It is desirable to avoid as far as possible abrupt changes in monetary conditions. In this context, it would be useful to continue to explore whether limited intervention ... can be undertaken without unduly encouraging risky behaviour," the IMF said in its interim report on the Israeli economy. 

 The report also urged the Israeli government to keep to its 4-percent inflation target for 1999, saying a revision upward would raise inflationary expectations, unsettle financial markets and coax wages higher. 

 The report came a day after the cabinet agreed to defer a decision until the second half of January on whether to raise next year's inflation target. 

 The IMF report appeared to be critical of the Bank of Israel, which did not intervene in the local forex market in early October when the shekel lost nearly 10 percent of its value against the dollar. 

Central bank Governor Jacob Frenkel has said repeatedly that the bank's policy is ordinarily not to intervene. But the depreciation caused inflation to surge higher in October, forcing the Bank of Israel to raise interest rates 4.0 percentage points over late October and early November. 

 The IMF said the rate hike had been successful in curbing inflationary expectations but it said the government should now focus on bringing rates down. 

 "Economic policies in the next few months should strive to establish conditions for a gradual easing of the monetary stance, without risking a rekindling of inflation or the re-emergence of pressure for a depreciation of the shekel," the IMF said. 

 The report also urged policymakers to continue efforts to lower the degree of concentration in the Israeli financial system. 

 It said Israeli banks should be divested of their smaller banking units. The government should also "encourage additional break-ups of financial conglomerates" and "facilitate entry by foreign banks." 

 The report also suggested some technical changes, among them for the government to set its inflation target according to underlying inflation. It said that would insulate policy from much of the volatility in headline inflation. 

 The IMF said the central bank should consider stepping up financial requirements for the banking system by raising minimum capital requirements, requiring larger provisions and discouraging high dividend payouts. 

 "While there is no reason to be concerned about the soundness of the banking system, the increased volatility in financial markets and asset prices and the large share of credit in - or linked to - foreign currency justify heightened vigilance," the report said. 

 The IMF conceded that its positive outlook for the economy a year ago had not been realised. 

 It said, however, that Israel now stood to benefit from the weaker shekel, which should make the country's exports more competitive, so long as policy makers could prevent the depreciation from creating long-term inflation. 

 ((Jerusalem newsroom, +972 2 537-0502, jerusalem.newsroom@reuters.com)).
