title: Israel/Fin Min -2: Zilberfarb Criticizes Rate Rises
text:
At the same cabinet session, Finance Ministry director-general Ben-Zion Zilberfarb criticized the Bank of Israel for relying only on higher interest rates to stabilize the foreign currency market. 

 Frenkel has been criticized widely in Israel for raising interest rates instead of intervening in foreign currency markets in early October, when the shekel fell sharply against the dollar. Critics say the high interest rates will only deepen Israel's economic slowdown, now in its third year. 

 "The Bank of Israel's involvement as a market maker would have prevented big jumps in the exchange rate," added liquidity to the market and raised long-term stability, Zilberfarb said. If the central bank had intervened as the Finance Ministry had asked it to, then the price rises that followed the shekel's depreciation would have been more moderate, he said. 

 Although the Finance Ministry agrees that routine Bank of Israelintervention in the foreign currency market is undesirable, neither is total abstinence from market involvement, which carries an economic price by failing to restore stability to the financial market, Zilberfarb said. 

 Zilberfarb concluded his speech with an appeal to the cabinet not to expand spending in the 1999 draft state budget and to sign "responsible" public sector wage agreements. 

 Frenkel told the cabinet that the Israeli economy's primary challenge is to stimulate economic growth. The only way to do that is to cap spending at the level set out in the 1999 draft state budget and reaffirm a commitment to low inflation, he said. 

 The governor advocates maintaining the 1999 inflation target of 4.0%. 

 Frenkel cautioned that if interest rates are cut too rapidly or the Bank of Israel's autonomy is undermined, Israel's financial stability and economic growth could be hurt. 

 He once again defended his decision to raise the key lending rate as an effort to prevent the recent surge in prices from becoming entrenched.

title: Israel 's Frenkel: Ctrl Bk Didn't  Intervene  In  Forex  Trade
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel Wednesday defended his decision not to intervene in foreign currency trade, preferring to raise domestic interest rates to tame an inflationary upsurge. 

 "What I can say after the fact is that we didn't intervene" in foreign currency trade, Frenkel said of the period in which the shekel ($1=ILS4.1630) lost more than 11% of its value against the dollar in early October. 

 The shekel's swift decline has doubled inflation estimates for 1998 to as high as 10% and called into question the government's ability to meet its 1999 target of 4.0% inflation. The government inflation target for 1998 is 7.0% to 10%. 

 Some foreign currency dealers said the central bank may have intervened once or twice, selling dollars on the market in early October, but didn't choose to make it public. 

 Frenkel stressed that the central bank's view of intervention was pragmatic, not dogmatic. 

 "If I reach the conclusion with my colleagues that (intervention) will be effective it will be done," Frenkel said. 

 At the same time, he and Finance Minister Yaakov Neeman decided against intervening in shekel trading, even during the most dramatic shekel declines in early October, to prevent a possible speculative attack on the Israeli currency, Frenkel said. 

 Frenkel made the remarks Wednesday at a Knesset Finance Committee meeting and was subject to harsh criticism by lawmakers on his policy moves. The Knesset committee was to discuss a bill that calls for diluting Frenkel's sole authority to set interest rates and advocates reinforcing the powers of an advisory council on monetary policy.

title: Bank of Israel head under attack from old allies.
text:
JERUSALEM, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The head of Israel's central bank, Jacob Frenkel, is coming under heavy fire from old allies in the government and financial markets for his handling of the shekel's slide and resulting inflation in the last seven weeks. 

 "I don't think we needed to have three percent inflation and a 22 percent depreciation. He should have taken drastic steps earlier on," said Micha Goldberg, head of research at Nessuah Zannex Securities. 

 The Bank of Israel governor was widely criticised for refusing to intervene directly in the forex market in early October, when the shekel tumbled against the dollar. After recovering some of its losses, it is down nearly 19 percent against the U.S. currency this year. 

 Now he is being attacked for raising interest rates excessively. In less than three weeks, the Bank of Israel has raised the base monetary tender rate by four percentage points to an annual 13.5 percent in response to surging inflation. 

 October's consumer price index jumped 3.0 percent on the back of the shekel depreciation, the highest monthly index in more than seven years. But most economists say inflation will retreat to its pre-depreciation levels very quickly. 

 Frenkel's stubborn drive to bring down Israeli inflation to Western levels long ago earned him the disapproval of many business leaders and legislators. They blame the central bank's tight monetary policy for the slowing economy and rising joblessness. 

 Earlier this week, the head of the leading business lobby, the Manufacturers Association, called for the state comptroller to investigate monetary policy. In parliament, legislators said they were reviving efforts to create a board to oversee the central bank. 

 Those critics have been joined some of Frenkel's old supporters. 

 On Sunday, Finance Minister Yaacov Neeman said for the first time he has differences of opinion with Frenkel, although he refused to detail them. 

 Newspaper reports have said Neeman viewed Frenkel's last boost in interest rates - a two percentage point hike announced last Thursday - as wrong, as was the bank's refusal to intervene in the forex market. 

 Neeman is expected to come back to the cabinet next week with plans to raise the government's inflation target for next year, a move Frenkel has opposed. 

 Ministers are seeking to boost the target, on the basis of which the Bank of Israel sets interest rates, to a range of four to six percent. The target is now at four percent. 

 "I think the party responsible for monetary policy must do some soul-searching with regard to the policy it is implementing," Treasury director-general Ben-Zion Zilberfarb told reporters on Monday. 

 Market economists have also been mainly critical of the central bank. 

 Victor Shohet, chief economist at Ofek Securities, said Frenkel's orginal sin was cutting rates 1.5 points last August, a move that contributed to the shekel's first losses. 

 When the currency began plunging in October, he acted too cautiously and then moved precipitously with two unscheduled rate hike announcements. 

 "He should have acted earlier (during the depreciation), but he tried to convey business as usual. Then he panicked," said Shohet, who said he nevertheless thought Frenkel had no choice but to jack up rates sharply. 

 Ed Butchart, an economist for Merrill Lynch in London, said the central bank had erred in not selling dollars to moderate the shekel's losses in October, thereby causing dollar-denominated housing prices to soar and raising inflation. 

 "I find it a little bit difficult to understand when you have a CPI so influenced by housing prices, to try to get inflation down without managing the exchange rate," he said. 

 Ironically, the markets have been positive since last Thursday when Frenkel announced his latest rate hike. 

 The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange's benchmark Tel Aviv-100 index has advanced about four percent, which analysts attributed to the strengthening shekel. The currency has also gained about four percent against the dollar. 

 "He certainly accomplished part of that," said Goldberg. "But the question is whether he could have done it at a lower price." 

 ((Jerusalem newsroom, +972 2 537-0502, jerusalem.newsroom@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Israeli Shekel Up Vs Dlr In Late Trade: Fixing At ILS4.1520
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--The shekel (ILS) is higher against the dollar for the seventh consecutive trading day Tuesday as a newly widened gap between local and foreign interest rates is making dollar sales attractive for customers. 

 The Bank of Israel fixed the shekel at ILS4.1520 to the dollar, up 0.2% from Monday's fixing at ILS4.1600. 

 The shekel traded within a range of ILS4.1200 to ILS4.1700 to the dollar. Shortly after the 1315 GMT fixing, the shekel was trading at ILS4.1500. 

 The central bank raised its key lending rate in November to 13.5% in two separate increases of 200 basis points each. Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said the second surprise increase was meant to stem a wave of dollar buying on the foreign currency market and halt accelerating inflation. 

 "It was an hysterical response to the market coupled with (the Bank of Israel's) determination not to intervene in trading" to strengthen the shekel, one foreign currency dealer said. 

 The consequent rise in real interest rates had customers selling dollars Tuesday, pushing the shekel as high as ILS4.1200 to the U.S. currency. Trading volumes were moderate, dealers said. 

 The Bank of Israel is scheduled to announce the December key lending rate on Monday. A Tel Aviv-based dealer said the market "isn't ruling out another rate rise, but at this point it's at the back of their minds." 

 Customers see another rate rise likely only in the event of the shekel weakening considerably against the dollar in the next week, to levels of ILS4.3000 or lower, dealers said.

title: Israel finmin says will review inflation target.
text:
JERUSALEM, Nov 15 (Reuters) - Israeli Finance Minister Yaacov Neeman told a cabinet meeting on Sunday he would reexamine the government's 1999 inflation target, a Treasury spokesman. 

 "The finance minister thinks...there is reason to examine the need to change the inflation target in light of what has happened over the past month and a half," the spokesman said after the meeting. 

 Neeman agreed to study the matter after several ministers called for raising the target to between four and six percent after the shekel's slide against the dollar last month, which has led to higher inflation and a sharp hike in interest rates. 

 The government is currently committed to a 4.0 percent inflation rate next year, down from a 1998 target of seven to 10 percent. 

 The year-end surge in inflation is expected to lift the full-year 1998 inflation rate to close to 10 percent. It was running at a four percent rate in the first eight months. 

 Sunday's cabinet meeting followed the Bank of Israel's surprise announcement on Thursday that it would hike the base lending rate by two percentage points for the second time in less than three weeks. The latest increase, effective on Sunday, brings the key lending rate to an annual 13.5 percent. 

 Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said the move was aimed at bringing inflation in line with the government's 1999 target of four percent. 

 Frenkel's tightening of monetary policy has led to an uproar in both the public and private sector and some leaders of the business sector have called for his resignation. 

 According to the Treasury spokesman, Neeman told the cabinet the Treasury had differences of opinion with the Bank of Israel but said it was inappropriate to make personal attacks on the governor because it challenged the authority of the central bank. 

 The spokesman declined to detail the nature of these disagreements. But he said Neeman would elaborate on them during a special cabinet meeting later this week or next. 

 A senior Treasury source said the key dispute between the Finance Ministry and the central bank is over the Bank of Israel's failure to intervene in the foreign exchange market. 

 The Treasury believes intervention should have taken place already to stem the shekel's decline. 

 Later on Sunday the government is due to publish October's consumer price index, which is expected to show a surge of three to four percent reflecting the brunt of a nearly 10 percent drop in the shekel against the dollar over the month. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Israel/Inflation -3: Recession To Buffer Price Rises
text:
Most economists agree with Central Bank and Finance Ministry assessments that the worst of the shekel's decline is now over. 

 "We believe this was a one-time wave and that we'll return to lower inflation rates of 5.0% to 6.0% in 1999 if the depreciation comes to an end," said Eyal Kolka, head of economic research at Sigma P.C.M. Capital Markets Ltd. in Tel Aviv. 

 Victor Shohet, chief economist at Ofek Securities and Investments Ltd. in Tel Aviv, said Israel's 2 1/2-year-old economic slowdown should also prevent recent price markups from translating into a permanent inflation trend. 

 "The recession is actually going to create a situation where the price increases we see are only price adjustments to the new exchange rates," Shohet said. 

 Analysts and investors are anxiously awaiting the scheduled announcement Sunday of the October consumer price index and the announcement of the December interest rate, expected to follow eight days later. 

 Consumer prices are expected to have risen 3.5% to 4.0%, and market players foresee a 150- to 200-basis-point rate rise in store for December. 

 "I won't be surprised if we see interest rates rise an additional 400 basis points by the end of the year," Katznelson said. 

 For all that, he said he would prefer if the Bank of Israel were to restore calm to financial markets with other tools "and rely as little as possible on rate rises because under the current slowdown, it comes with a price," he said. 

 Economic growth has slowed to a forecast 1.5% in 1998, from 1.9% in 1997 and 4.5% in 1996. Unemployment has risen as high as 9.5% for the year, from 7.7% in 1997 and 6.7% in 1996. 

 Some analysts said the central bank should have sold dollars on the foreign currency market to calm trade, especially during the shekel's most rapid decline in the first week of October. The Bank of Israel isn't known to have intervened in trade during the period. 

 Another option would be to abolish the shekel's trading band - a mechanism that allows the Israeli currency to fluctuate 15% on either side of a gradually depreciating midpoint. Media reports have said the central bank was seriously considering such a move but was meeting opposition from the Finance Ministry. A Bank of Israel spokesman refused to comment on the reports.

title: Israeli Treasury says no plan to end shekel band.
text:
JERUSALEM, Nov 11 (Reuters) - The Israeli Treasury on Wednesday denied press reports that it was in talks with the Bank of Israel to eliminate the shekel trading band following the currency's recent sharp depreciation. 

 "There is no intention of changing the trading band - not at this stage," Treasury spokesman Moti Sherf told Reuters. "I don't want to discuss this because, if I do, it's as though it's on the agenda." 

 Israeli newspapers on Wednesday reported that Treasury officials had held talks with the Bank of Israel over the last few weeks over a central bank proposal to eliminate the band. 

 The Ha'aretz newspaper said the central bank believed removing the band would make it easier for it to intervene in the forex market if it came under further pressure. 

 The Bank of Israel declined to comment on the reports. 

 "We are not saying anything about this," a spokesman for the Bank of Israel said. 

 The shekel trades within a band set against a basket of foreign currencies and straddles two sides of a sloping mid-point. The band has a width of 31.25 percent. 

 Since the end of 1996, the shekel has traded close to the bottom, or stronger edge of the band. But in the last six weeks the Israeli currency has tumbled against the dollar and basket of currencies, pushing it towards the mid-point. 

 The shekel's slide and continued volatility has triggered calls for central bank intervene in the local forex market. The Bank of Israel has repeatedly said it will not ordinarily intervene in the forex market. 

 The central bank in the past has only intervened to defend the trading band. 

 At midday on Wednesday, the shekel had strengthened to about 4.27 to the dollar from Monday's 4.301 fix. ((Jerusalem newsroom, +972 2 537-0502, jerusalem.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Israel Finance Ministry:Not Planning To Abolish Shekel Band
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--The Finance Ministry denied Tuesday that Israel's economic policymakers are discussing plans to abolish the shekel's trading band ($1=ILS4.3010). 

 "The Finance Ministry states that changing the exchange-rate policy isn't on the agenda. In light of the fact that the exchange rate now falls in the middle of the trading band, there is no need to change the band's limits," the ministry said in a statement. 

 The shekel is allowed to fluctuate 15% on either side of a gradually depreciating midpoint. The Bank of Israel is committed to defending the upper and lower limits of the band. 

 The statement followed a report in the Yediot Ahronoth newspaper that said Finance Ministry officials are more likely to accept widening or even abolishing the trading band since the shekel lost more than 10.5% of its value against the dollar in October. 

 In addition, the report said, central bank officials are stepping up discussions on abolishing the band to allow for more freedom of intervention in the foreign-currency market. 

 The Bank of Israel isn't known to have intervened in trade in the last two months, and central bank officials have repeatedly opposed regular intervention that could invite speculative attacks on the Israeli market. 

 Removing the band, however, would allow the central bank to intervene when necessary to calm market volatility without significantly reducing market risk. Critics of the central bank have called for some intervention in trade to halt the shekel's slide and prevent an inflationary spiral. 

 Inflation estimates for 1998 have doubled since the depreciation occurred, with estimates running at around 9.0%, compared with earlier forecasts of 4.0% to 5.0%. 

 The Bank of Israel refused to comment on the report. 

 The Finance Ministry said it doesn't rule out using any tools necessary to adjust to developments on the foreign currency market, but stressed "the authority to intervene in foreign-currency trade rests solely with the Bank of Israel."

title: Bank of  Israel  official defends  intervention  policy.
text:
JERUSALEM, Nov 2 (Reuters) - A senior Bank of Israel official on Monday defended the central bank's decision not to intervene in the foreign exchange market last month but left open the possibility it might act to moderate market volatility. 

 "There are situations when central bank intervention in the market can be considered as a way of moderating sharp daily fluctuations, but not in order to reverse the trend," David Klein, head of bank's monetary division, said in an article released to the press. 

 The Bank of Israel has come under fire for failing to support the shekel during volatile trading in October when the currency shed some 10.5 percent against the dollar. 

 In response, the Bank of Israel last Monday announced a 2.0 percentage point hike in the base lending rate to 11.5 percent. In addition, the Treasury has stepped up auctions of dollar-linked bonds to try to soak up demand for the currency. 

 Klein cited the Bank of Israel's support of bond prices when the market collapsed in the summer of 1996 as an example of successful intervention. 

 "The Bank of Israel...helped the market to arrive at a new level of equilibrium that allowed it to stop intervening," the report said. 

 "This was a successful measure because we were careful to allow the bond prices to drop in line with the market trend. The market knew that there was no absolute level at which we would bring the decline to a complete halt." 

 Klein ruled out intervening to reverse trends or to intervene on the sly. 

 "Those who recommend that the Bank of Israel secretly sell foreign currency would perhaps also recommend... doing this via futures contracts, without reporting them, which was done by the central bank of Thailand in 1997, before it broke its neck." 

 Klein warned that measuring the extent of demand for foreign currency was difficult and the central bank risked increasing demand by intervening. ((Jerusalem newsroom, +972 2 537-0502, jerusalem.newsroom@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: FOCUS-Bank of Israel raises interest rate to 11.5 pct.
text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The Bank of Israel raised its key monetary tender rate for November to 11.5 percent on Monday, hiking it by a full two percentage points in response to a slump in the value of the shekel and a sudden surge in inflation. 

 "This is an exceptional rise in the interest rate and the circumstances are exceptional," Central bank governor Jacob Frenkel told a news conference. 

 He said the move was designed to help ensure that the government would meet its 1999 inflation target of four percent and again ruled out repeated foreign exchange intervention by the Bank of Israel, calling it inefficient. 

 Frenkel blamed "dramatic" global conditions for sparking the first interest rate rise in more than a year and said the increase was intended as a "cure for the illness and to restore stability so that for 1999 we will return to inflation equal to four percent as determined by the government". 

 The decision was announced at 8.30 a.m. (0630 GMT), eight hours earlier than is normally the case, so that markets would be able to trade on the basis of the new figure. 

 The shekel strengthened against the dollar in very early trading in Tel Aviv but then pulled back on profit taking following the central bank announcement. 

 At 0705 GMT, the shekel was at 4.2201 to the dollar, compared with its 4.2490 fix on Friday. 

 "The market basically opened lower for the dollar. We traded around 4.16 before the announcement from the governor of the central bank," said Yaacov Harpaz, currency dealer at United Mizrahi Bank. 

 Harpaz said the interest rate differential between the shekel and dollar had widened. He said the rate hike, which was at the higher end of analysts' expectations, would help steady the Israeli currency. 

 "I think it will be stabilising in the range in 4.10-4.25," he said. 

 The shekel has been falling against the dollar since August. The pace quickened in an increasingly volatile market during October and then last Thursday, the currency hit a record low against the dollar of 4.367. 

 The shekel's losses have quickly upset expectations that annual inflation would fall below four percent this year and there are fears it could cause further damage in 1999 unless checked. 

 Some analysts expect the consumer price index in October alone to rise by about 3.5 percent. 

 Amir Haik, chief analyst at Israel Union Bank, said on Sunday that even if the shekel stabilised at between 4.1 and 4.2 to the dollar, 1999 inflation would be five to six percent, well above the government's 4.0 percent target. 

 In the last three years, the Bank of Israel has changed the direction of interest rates three times. It had cut the base rate a total of 3.9 points in the first eight months of this year. The last rate rise was in August 1997. 

 Economists are divided about the preference for raising rates over direct intervention, a mechanism Frenkel reiterated on Monday was not on the cards. 

 "In current conditions, intervention by the Bank of Israel in the forex market on a daily and sustained basis...in order to preserve the exchange rate is inefficient and cannot substitute for an interest rate policy," Frenkel said. 

 ((Jerusalem newsroom, +972 2 537-0502, jerusalem.newsroom@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: WRAP: Israel Rate Rise -3: Will Hit 1999 Growth
text:
The government approved the 4.0% inflation target after inflation expectations for the first half of 1999 had dropped to a low of 3.5% to 4.5% by the end of July. But following the depreciation, analysts now forecast 1998 inflation between 6.0% and 9.0%, and project a 5.0% to 7.0% increase for 1999. 

 Analysts said strategic and discrete intervention in the foreign currency market may have served the Bank of Israel, and the economy, better. But a declared intervention might have increased a sense of panic in the market and invited speculative dollar-buying, Gutman said. 

Central bank critics said the 200 basis point increase will only deepen the country's slowdown and worsen unemployment, forecast between 9.0% and 9.5% for 1998. 

 "The discount rate rise ruins any chance to renew growth at the start of 1999," said Doron Tamir, vice president of the Manufacturer's Association of Israel. Growth in 1998 is forecast at 1.5%, while 1999 projections have been lowered to a range of 2.0% to 2.5% from 2.5%. 

 "I don't think we need to give priority to another decline in inflation over a decline in unemployment at this time," Ben-Bassat said. "The drop to 4.0% inflation was to a certain degree unsustainable," because it was kept down through artificial exchange rate levels that resulted from the high interest rate policy, he said. 

 "A decline to 7.0% inflation is a little more convincing (for 1999)," he said.

title: Analysts see sharp rise in Israeli interest rates.
text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Faced with a sudden surge in inflation and continued selling pressure on the shekel, the Bank of Israel will raise interest rates sharply this week, analysts forecast on Sunday. 

 "I see a 1.5 percentage point hike, possibly more...The higher the better," said Victor Shohat, chief economist at Ofek Securities & Investments. 

 Other economists said the Bank of Israel could raise rates as little as one point or as much as two points when it announces its November monetary programme on Monday. The base monetary tender rate is currently 9.5 percent. 

 The bank said on Sunday it was moving up the announcement to 0630 GMT from the originally scheduled 1430 GMT so that the markets would be able to trade on the basis of the new rate. 

 Economists said the Bank of Israel faced the twin task of taming inflation quickly and helping to stabilise the currency. 

 The shekel has slid some 14 percent against the dollar over the last 11 weeks, going into a sharp decline at the start of October. Trading remains nervous and volatile, leaving the outlook for the currency cloudy. 

 Economists said the central bank was hoping a sharp rate hike would obviate the need for direct intervention in the forex market. 

 The Treasury has been absorbing some of the demand for dollars by stepping up the issue of Gilboa dollar-linked convertible bonds. But the Bank of Israel has not intervened and has indicated a reluctance to do so. 

 "The Bank of Israel wants to send a signal to the market that it will not intervene," said Amir Haik, chief analyst at Israel Union Bank. 

 He stressed however that would not necessarily be the final word. "If it doesn't work, they'll intervene." 

 The shekel's losses have quickly upset expectations that annual inflation would fall below four percent this year and could cause further damage in 1999. 

 Haik said that in October alone the consumer price index would rise about 3.5 percent. He said that even if the shekel stablised between 4.1-4.2 to the dollar, 1999 inflation would be 5-6 percent, well above the government's 4.0 percent target. 

 Haik said he was looking for a hike of 1.5-2 points. 

 In addition, economists noted, the rate of money supply growth was too rapid. It expanded 15.9 percent in the 12 months through September. 

 Shohat said the rate hike should prevent a one-off spike in the CPI from becoming long-term inflation. 

 Expectations of higher inflation were already prompting calls from labour unions for wage increases, he said. Meanwhile, retailers were now testing whether consumers would accept sharp price rises for imports. 

 "We're seeing the rush into shops, so they (retailers) may get the impression that they can keep raising prices," Shohat said. 

 Shohat said that if the currency settled at 4.0-4.1 to the dollar inflation could hold at four percent for 1999 while at 4.3 the CPI would be about six percent. 

 Economists were divided about the preference for raising rates over direct intervention, especially as a rate hike would mark another about-face for the central bank. 

 In the last three years, the Bank of Israel has changed the direction of interest rates three times, most recently cutting the base rate a total of 3.9 points in the first eight months of the year. 

 "We believe that greater intervention in the forex market...would help the central bank avoid such a stop-start approach to interest rate setting," said Merrill Lynch in a report. 

 Merrill, which said a one-point rate hike looked to be in the offing, warned that a sharp rate hike would also undermine Israel's tepid economic recovery in 1999. 

 But Shohat was more optimistic, saying the shekel depreciation was good for export competitiveness as long as the rate stabilised at current levels or better. ((Jerusalem newsroom, +972 2 537-0502, jerusalem.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Israeli Shekel/Rate Rise -3:  Intervention  Preferred
text:
Sheinen and others argue the Bank of Israel should intervene in support of the shekel, even though it's still some 11.4% from the floor of its trading band. The currency is allowed to fluctuate in a band of plus or minus 15% from a gradually depreciating midpoint. 

 "It's not like Southeast Asia or Russia because the Israeli economy isn't in a state that requires such a depreciation," Sheinen said. "It's leading to upheavals we don't need." 

 Because Israel is a small, import-reliant market, it's vulnerable to swings in exchange rates, he said. 

 "We need a central bank that will moderate the fluctuations," Sheinen said. 

 The shekel had been kept artificially strong over the last four years as the Bank of Israel kept interest rates high in an effort to tame inflation. 

 But the shekel's over valuation was only in the range of 10% to 15%, not the 20% by which it has fallen since August, said Sheinen. If the Bank of Israel doesn't stabilize the market, inflation in 1998 could surge above 10%, he cautioned. 

 A dealer at a major Israeli trading room said he thought the Bank of Israel should have intervened in the market first in words, then in deed. 

 "They should have said 4.2 shekels to the dollar is a good level for the Israeli economy, and then if needed, added some liquidity to the market" by selling dollars, he said on condition of anonymity.

title: Analysts split on reasons for Israeli shekel's fall.
text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 21 (Reuters) - The battered Israeli shekel has been careering lower for some three weeks, but analysts still can't agree on who is in the driver's seat. 

 Some dealers point to foreign banks for the 13 percent slide in the shekel against the dollar since the start of October. But others insist it is nervous Israelis. 

 On Wednesday the shekel was fixed at a record low against the U.S. currency of 4.355. 

 A senior dealer at Israel Continental Bank said overseas institutions were testing the Israeli forex market with the knowledge that they would be losing trading opportunities when the single European currency is introduced on January 1. 

 "With the euro taking away a lot of business, foreigners are looking for business," the dealer said. 

 "They are looking to see how much money they can make in this market, if they can do a little bit of manipulating and how much of a multiplier effect they can have." 

 But Nadine Baudot-Trajtenberg, of Bank Hapoalim's securities research and international marketing division, said domestic players had triggered the recent round of losses. 

 She said the atmosphere of uncertainty was causing domestic investors to pile into dollar-linked investments, while Israeli companies were seeking to refinance forex-linked loans. 

 Global economic uncertainty had turned foreigners off from speculating in the Israeli forex market, she argued. 

 "Given the dramatic turn in the world crisis, a lot of companies are scared of playing the shekel," Baudot-Trajtenberg said. "They thought they could play Russia and they learned they couldn't." 

 Despite the lack of consensus on reasons for the shekel's recent weakness several analysts said the time had come for the Bank of Israel to intervene. 

 "I don't really understand why the Bank of Israel hasn't intervened in order not to have to change the interest rates," said Ed Butchart, an economist and market strategist for Merrill Lynch in London. 

 He said a steep increase in interest rates would hurt investment but that intervention in the forex market could help offset inflationary pressure resulting from the shekel depreciation. 

 Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel has indicated several times this month that he would not intervene in the market unless the shekel reached the edge of its trading band against a basket of foreign currencies. The shekel is currently at about the mid-point. 

 That means the shekel would have to weaken a further 15 percent before the central bank intervened. 

 Butchart said that before the shekel's most recent drops he expected the central bank to raise interest rates by 0.5 percentage point when it announces November rates on Monday, but he would have to reassess that forecast after the shekel's recent losses. 

 The Bank of Israel's base monetary tender rate is now 9.5 percent. 

 Pinchas Landau, head of Euro Strategies Ltd, said the Bank of Israel should launch a "pre-emptive attack" in order to defend the shekel. 

 "Because of the very uncertain situation, right now is the time to do it (intervene), before things get out of control," Landau said. ((Jerusalem newsroom, +972 2 537-0502, jerusalem.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Israel's Frenkel, Neeman Predict Slowing Inflation
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--Israel's top economic policymakers expressed optimism Monday that the rate of inflation will turn lower, despite the shekel's 10% depreciation against the dollar since the end of September. 

 Finance Minister Yaakov Neeman and Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel made the remarks to Israel radio after speaking to the Knesset Finance Committee on the effects of the depreciation. 

 Both have blamed the shekel's fall on world economic troubles taking a toll on Israel's foreign currency and stock markets. However they said the country's economic fundamentals will allow it to weather the storm. 

 "It's a situation that requires us to keep our fingers on the gauge," Neeman said. "When the market calms down, and I assume that will take some time...we should return to the same level of inflation we saw at the beginning of the year." 

 Consumer prices rose 1.4% in September, following a 1.3% shekel depreciation that month. Analysts forecast an inflation increase of about 2.5% in October due to the sharper depreciation seen so far. The figures have raised 1998 inflation estimates to as high as 8.0%, compared with forecasts of 4.0% to 5.0% that had been held through the end of August. 

 Frenkel said that it would still be possible to reach the government's 1999 inflation target of 4.0%. 

 "There's no doubt that if we implement the correct policy measures we will be able to reach this target," he said. 

 The Bank of Israel didn't intervene in trading to soften the shekel's fall even during the swiftest period of depreciation in the first week of October. Analysts expect the central bank will raise the 9.5% discount rate by as much as 100 basis points in November to tame the upsurge in inflation.

title: Israel says no change is planned in  forex  regime.
text:
TEL AVIV, Feb 4 (Reuter) - Finance Minister Dan Meridor and Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Tuesday that they planned no changes in the foreign currency system. 

 "There is no change in the exchange rate system," Meridor said after a meeting with Frenkel. 

 Frenkel vowed to continue to defend the exchange rate even though that has forced the central bank to inject more than an estimated $1 billion during January intervening in the market. 

 "The Bank of Israel will continue to defend the system," he said. "We have all the tools required to do this and we will continue to do so. Every dollar the Bank of Israel buys and the shekels we consequently sell we are absorbing immediately." 

 The shekel traded quietly on Tuesday and the Bank of Israel did not intervene in the local foreign currency market. 

 Since mid-January, the shekel has been trading at the bottom end of its trading band against the basket of foreign currencies to which it is pegged. To prevent it from sliding under the band, the Bank of Israel has been intervening heavily in the local currency market. 

 The financial daily Globes quoted senior central bank officials as saying they were considering various measures to alleviate pressure on the Bank of Israel to support the exchange rate and absorb the liquidity created by intervention. 

 Among them was a special tax on short-term foreign currency borrowing; widening the trading band, which now allows the shekel to deviate up to seven percent above or below a sloping rate to as much as 12 percent; suspending further government borrowing overseas; and increasing the reserve requirement by five percentage points. 

 Frenkel expressed concern about the unexpectedly wide budget deficit in January, which reached 1.28 billion shekels. 

 "When in January the budget figures are so worrisome following so great an effort by the government (to approve the 1997 budget), it is very important that the budget cut which was decided upon is in fact implemented," Frenkel said. 

 "What happened in January is a result that troubles us very much," he said.

title: Israel: Shekel Trading Band System Under Fire
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)-- Israeli economists are engaged in a intense debate about the future of the country's rate of exchange regime, as the Bank of Israel, the central bank, is forced to intervene daily to prevent a strong appreciation of the shekel. 

 According to unofficial calculations the central bank was forced during the past four weeks to purchase about $1.3 bn in currency trading. To prevent a major increase in money supply, the central bank has had to increase deposits of commercial banks. The Bank of Israel has also asked the Finance Ministry to allow it to sell a larger amounts of Treasury Bills, but the ministry has refused to help the central bank of this matter, according to government official talking on the basis of anonymity. 

 ``The Bank should not do away with the trading band system. Instead it should devalue the currency administratively and announce that it will do the same in the future. That would introduce risk into the markets and prevent selling of foreign currency'', said Ptahia Bar Shavit, chief economist at Bank Hapoalim. He added that the system of a trading band had served the economy very well and should be kept. 

 Other economists were critical of the trading band system. According to Sauli Katznelson, chief economist at Israel Discount Bank the solution the the problem would be to do away with the trading band. Officialy there would be a free floating shekel, but in practice there would be incrased risk, and much smaller speculative import of short term capital, he said.

title: Israel/Discount Rate -4: Critics Demand Deeper Cut

The president of the Manufacturers Association of Israel, Dan Propper, urged the central bank to abandon its "wrong-headed monetary policy" and to lower the key interest by about two percentage points.

 But the cost to the economy has been high. Business profits and exports have suffered because of the strong shekel.  The government has projected that gross domestic product grew 4.4% in 1996, a sharp drop from 7.1% in 1995 and an average of 6% annually from 1990 to 1995. 

 Finance Ministry economists have fovecast a 4% GDP growth in 1997, but other economists have projected that the economy will grow around 3%.

title: Bank of Israel lowers interest rates 0.5 point.

TEL AVIV, Jan 27 (Reuter) - The Bank of Israel said on Monday it would lower its key lending rate for February, but analysts and traders said the 0.5 percentage point cut was cautious and would do little to ease pressure on the shekel exchange rate. 

 The cut, which takes effect on Thursday, brings the base lending rate to 14.2 percent. The rate is the one charged commercial banks at daily and weekly monetary tenders. 

 The central bank said it had cut rates 2.8 percentage points since August from a peak of 17 percent. But inflation has fallen from a 14.6 percent annualised rate in the first-half of 1996 to less than half that in the second, according to Bank Hapoalim estimates. 

 "It was (the reduction) expected, no surprises. They put a lot of pressure on (Bank of Israel Governor Jacob) Frenkel to lower more but he was very cautious. It won't influence shares or the forex market," said Tzvi Hoffman of Meitav Securities and Investments. 

 Analysts said the bank faces pressure to keep lowering rates to prevent the shekel from strengthening too much against the basket of currencies to which it is officially linked. The bank sees the currency band as a key facet in achieving monetary stability. 

 The shekel on Monday fell to an all-time low against the dollar. However, the weakness of other currencies in the basket has caused the basket rate to fall over the last two weeks to the bottom end of its official trading band. 

 The Bank of Israel has been forced to intervene heavily in the local foreign exchange market, injecting what currency traders estimated was about $500 million into the economy. 

 Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets, said the lower inflationary trend and a slowing economy were also encouraging the bank to ease rates. 

 The slowing trend has recently grown worse, with the Bank of Israel's "S" index of economic performance falling one percent over November and December. 

 Katz is now forecasting that the economy will grow three percent this year, down from the 3.7 percent he had earlier forecast. 

 However, the central bank must also contend with the budget deficit, which analysts said was making it cautious. Although the official budget aims to keep the deficit to 2.8 percent of gross domestic product, analysts said January spending was probably running ahead of projections.

title: Bank of Israel expected to cut rates 0.3-0.5 pct.
text:
TEL AVIV, Jan 27 (Reuter) - The Bank of Israel is expected to announce an interest rate cut of 0.3 to 0.5 percentage point from a rate of 14.7 percent, analysts said on Monday. 

 The Bank of Israel is scheduled to announce its February monetary programme at 1430 GMT today. 

 "My forecast was previously for an 0.3 point decrease based on the consumer price index," said Jonathan Katz, chief economist for Solid Financial Markets. "Now part of me is leaning towards 0.5 point because of the economic indicators released in recent days." 

 Katz cited the drop in the "S" index of economic performance for November and December, lower industrial production and weak trade figures. 

 "The whole trend in interest rates is now more downward than previously expected," he said. "You're now looking at negative growth, not just a slowdown." 

 Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel also faces exchange rate pressures. The shekel has been strong and its currency-basket rate has been near the bottom of the trading band for more than a week, which has forced the Bank of Israel to intervene heavily in the local forex market and inject an estimated $500 million of liquidity into the economy. 

 Eli Nahum, head of research at Zannex Securities, said the market was also looking for a cut of 0.3 to 0.5 point. 

 But he and other analysts said the market is focused less on interest rates than on the unfolding government crisis, declining share prices on Wall Street and concerns that the market is overbought after a nearly uninterrupted rise in share prices since the start of November. 

 Worries about an overbought situation were alleviated by a 3.61 percent plunge in the Mishtanim index of top 100 shares on Sunday. Today the index was up 1.22 percent to 234.75 points in midday trading. 

 The government crisis, however, may continue to shadow the market, Nahum said. 

 The crisis stems from allegations of high-level corruption in the appointment of an attorney-general earlier this month. On Sunday, Israeli police launched an investigation into the matter. 

 Nahum said the affair has sparked worries that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government could fall. 

 "I personally think that (is the reason for the market's nervousness), but a lot of players don't," he said. "Really, the market was looking for a reason to take profits." 

 He said the market might be driven by interest rates if the central bank opted to hold rates or to cut them by more than 0.5 point.

title: Israel Shekel Strengthens Against  Currency  Basket
text:
JERUSALEM (AP-Dow Jones)--The shekel strengthened slightly against a basket of major international currencies at the Bank of Israel fixing on Wednesday. 

 The shekel briefly exceeded its strongest point within the trading band set by the Central Bank, but the Bank of Israel didn't intervene to weaken it, traders said. 

 The currency basket was valued at 3.6145 shekels, a drop of 0.132% compared to Tuesday's close of 3.6193 shekels. 

 The dollar, which dominates the basket, rose 0.92% at the fixing to 3.2470 shekels from Tuesday's close of 3.2440 shekels. 

 'Most of the day the dollar strengthened against the mark, and it strengthened against the shekel at the same time,' said a foreign currency dealer at the First International Bank of Israel. Volume was moderate, he said. 

 Tal Zindorf, an economist at Bank Hapoalim, said the trading session was 'nothing special,' adding that she doesn't expect any sharp changes because Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel has made it clear that he won't cut the discount rate until he sees the budget deficit shrink.' 

 The 14.7% discount rate is so high relative to those for other major currencies that customers are still borrowing in foreign currencies and converting them to shekels. 

 Maybe the foreign currency market will be more interesting toward the end of the month, when Frenkel announces the February discount rate, she said. 

 Zindorf also suggested that the capital market's attention may have been diverted to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, which has been enjoying sharp rises on large volumes.

title: Israel  forex  reserves rise to record $10.262 bln.
text:
TEL AVIV, Oct 1 (Reuter) - Israel's foreign currency reserves at the end of September rose by $739 million to a record $10.262 billion, the Bank of Israel said. 


		 (In millions of dollars)
		 Sept 96     Aug 96	 Sept 95
Reserves     10,262	9,523	  8,839


 The Bank of Israel attributed the rise to its market interventions during the month as well as to government transfers of foreign currency from abroad. 

 The central bank bought foreign currency in September to prevent the shekel from appreciating beyond the band in which it is allowed to trade. 

 The bank said in a statement that the sale of foreign currency by the private sector was mainly the result of an increase in loans of foreign currency loans taken by the private sector from Israeli commercial banks. 

 The Bank of Israel said it used other monetary tools to offset the interventions and prevent money supply from expanding.

title: Israel's Foreign  Currency  Reserves Up to $10.26 Bln
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--Israel's foreign currency reserves rose $740 million to $10.262 billion at the end of September, in part because of foreign currency purchases the Bank of Israel made to protect its exchange rate policy. 

 The other factor contributing to the rise from $9.523 billion at the end of August were transfers of government money from overseas, the Central Bank said in a release. 

 The bank gave no breakdown of its purchases versus transfers of money from overseas accounts, and a spokesman was not immediately available. 

 The Bank of Israel said its intervention in the foreign currency market did not add liquidity to the market "because every influence that contributes to the undesirable increase in the amount of money is completely offset by the variety of monetary tools the bank has at its disposal." 

 The statement did not elaborate. 

 In late August, the Central Bank intervened in foreign currency trading for the first time since February, after its currency basket exchange rate dipped below the lowest point that the Bank of Israel has said it will permit. The Central Bank continued to intervene throughout September to prop up the exchange rate. 

 To moderate cycles of foreign currency speculation that were fueled by expectations of devaluation, Israel linked the shekel to a basket of five currencies in 1986. The dollar is weighted heaviest, accouting for about 60% of the basket.

title: Dollar Weakens Against Israeli Shekel After Two-Day Rise
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--The dollar lost steam against the shekel on Tuesday, after rising 1.5% in the previous two days. Analysts said the drop was a correction of an extraordinary rise on Monday that appeared to have been a combined reaction to deadly Palestinian-Israeli clashes and the strengthening of the dollar around the world late last week. 

 Trading in the dollar opened with a decline of 0.67%, which drove down the dollar exchange rate to 3.19832 shekels, from 3.22 shekels on Monday. 

 About half an hour later it was down 0.9% to 3.1916, and at the end of a trading day shortened because of the Sukkot holiday, the Bank of Israel fixed the exchange rate at 3.1920, a drop of 0.87%. 

 Trading was much quieter than on Monday, when large morning purchases by banks and the commercial sector set off panicked buying that temporarily drove up the exchange rate to 3.24 shekels to the dollar, said Aviad Bar-Sella, a foreign currency trader at Israel Discount Bank. 

 Monday's volatile trading was a delayed reaction to the violence that engulfed the West Bank and Gaza Strip last week, and Tuesday's drop in the dollar exchange rate was a return to business as usual, Bar-Sella said. 

 "There was profit-taking, and the Bank of Israel didn't intervene, so rates went down," he said. 

 The Central Bank has bought foreign currency in recent weeks to keep the currency basket exchange rate from dipping below the lowest point the Bank of Israel has set.

title: Israeli shekel weakens, unaffected by violence.
text:
TEL AVIV, Sept 26 (Reuter) - The Israeli shekel on Thursday weakened against the dollar and basket of foreign currencies following the dollar's rise abroad and trade was not affected by the political unrest, dealers said. 

 "The market did not react to the political events and the shekel weakened after the dollar rose abroad," said Ilan Raviv at Israel Discount Bank. 

 In two days of bloody clashes between Israeli troops and Palestinians 33 Palestinians and five Israelis were killed. 

 "The Bank of Israel had to intervene on a relatively high scale in the market, buying more than $50 million to support the basket. The market will be influenced by the political unrest between Israel and the Palestinians only if foreign investors decide to leave Israel," Raviv said. 

 The shekel can trade in a band of seven percent above or below a slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency at six percent a year against a basket of currencies representing Israel's main trading partners. 

 If the shekel-basket exchange rate reaches the lower trading band the central bank intervenes by buying foreign currency. 

 The representative rate for the dollar was 3.1800 against 3.1710 on Wednesday. The basket, composed of the dollar, mark, pound sterling, French franc and yen, closed at 3.5567 shekels against 3.5541 on Wednesday. 

 On the crosses the shekel traded against the yen at 2.8795 shekels per 100 yen against 2.8774 on Wednesday and against the mark at 2.0920 shekels per mark against 2.1019 on Wednesday. 

 In late afternoon the dollar was trading at 3.1800 shekels.

title: Israel/News-2: Discount Rate Cut Is Front Page News
text:
--Another front page item was the Bank of Israel's decision to cut the discount rate by three-tenths of a percentage point next month to 15.5%. 

 The Central Bank said the government budget deficit was one factor that prevented a deeper cut. Ha'aretz reported that government economic sources are weighing cutting the 1997 budget by 5.9 billion shekels rather than the originally proposed 4.9 billion shekels. 

 Globes, in its front-page commentary, said the Central Bank may have cut the rate less than expected to give itself leeway to continue cuts in coming months. The commentary also suggested that the Bank of Israel may be trying to postpone the day when people will prefer to invest in dollars rather than shekels. Because interest is rising abroad and falling here, shekel accounts are becoming less attractive, Globes said. 

 Bank Governor Jacob Frenkel is going to the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund in a few days and prefers to appear at international forums as someone who is keeping the monetary reins short and not buckling under to pressure to quickly lower the interest rate, the commentary said. 

 --The Bank of Israel intervened more heavily than usual in foreign currency trading on Tuesday to prop up the currency basket exchange rate after it fell below the Central Bank's appointed lower band. The bank bought tens of millions of dollars, Globes reported. 

 -- Economists at Israel Discount Bank expect the budget deficit to reach 12 billion shekels to 13 billion shekels, or 4% of gross domestic product. The original budget shortfall was targeted at 7.6 billion shekels; the deficit currently stands at 8.6 billion shekels.

title: Israel/Discount Cut-3: Tight Policy to Continue?
text:
Ptachia Bar Shavit, the chief economist at Bank Hapoalim, said the ``minor reduction'' reinforces the conclusion that monetary policy will continue to be very tight through most of 1997. 

 ``A substantial interest rate cut is not expected in the near future'' - even if the parliament decides to slash the 1997 budget by the proposed 4.9 billion shekels, because Frenkel will wait to see to what extent the cuts are implemented, Bar Shavit said. 

 The relatively low rise in the consumer price index in August and the 0.1% rise in the M1 supply in August had created expectations of a deeper rate cut. So too had the appreciation of the shekel, which several weeks ago forced the Bank of Israel to intervene in foreign currency trading to keep the currency basket exchange rate above the bank's appointed lowest level. 

 But Bufman, one of the lone voices to predict a three-tenths of a percentage point cut, said the low CPI increase in August was not an indicator of good things to come because the elements that contributed to the low rise will not carry over in the coming months. 

 The August CPI figure was low in part because the shekel appreciated very sharply from early June to late August, reaching the limit of appreciation the central bank set and forcing the bank to intervene in foreign currency trading, Bufman said. Because the shekel cannot appreciate any further, that factor will not affect prices for the next few months, Bufman said. 

 Furthermore, seasonal elements (such as lower produce and clothing prices) slowed down inflation during the summer and those elements are not going to continue to do so in the coming months, he said.

title: Bank of  Israel interventions  not inflationary.
text:
TEL AVIV, Sept 24 (Reuter) - Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said the central bank's recent interventions in the foreign currency markets were not inflationary as other monetary measures were being taken. 

 "All injections are being sterilised. There is no single shekel in the market beyond what we want," Frenkel told Reuters on Tuesday. 

 The central bank has been buying foreign currency frequently in the past month to prevent the shekel from strengthening beyond its permitted trading band. 

 Israeli banks estimate the central bank has injected more than a billion shekels through its interventions. 

 "Daily (monetary) auctions and other monetary instruments are being used to ensure that the interventions are not allowed to alter the base of monetary expansion beyond what we in the bank think is warranted," Frenkel said. 

 "To date (the interventions) are fully sterilised." 

 On September 2 the central bank suspended its daily auctions for loans to commercial banks in light of excess liquidity. The auctions were resumed on September 17. 

 Frenkel blamed pressures in the foreign exchange market on the government's widening budget deficit and not on interest rates.

title: Israel News: Renewed Israel-Syria Talks On Washington Agenda
text:
TEL AVIV (Dow Jones)--The following news summary is based on Tuesday editions of the Ha'aretz, Yediot Ahronot, Ma'ariv and Jerusalem Post national dailies and the Globes financial gazette: 

 -- Efforts to renew negotiations between Syria and Israel received prominent converage. Breaking the months-old stalemate is the focus of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's talks with U.S. officials in Washington this week. Ha'aretz reported that Syria's greater flexibility is likely to permit the renewal of talks before the U.S. presidential election; the Jerusalem Post cited Netanyahu as saying that he was not sure Syria wanted to talk. 

 -- Papers also gave prominent play to Ehud Barak's announcement that he will stand for Labor Party leader. Current party leader Shimon Peres was defeated by Netanyahu in the May elections. Barak is a former military commander and foreign minister and currently serves as a parliament member from the Labor Party. 

 -- An organizer of the Cairo regional economic summit, World Economic Forum director Gregory Blatt, says Egypt will give the go-ahead for the conference within a week. Egypt has threatened to call off the Nov.12-14 conference if Israel does not move faster on peacemaking. 

 -- Provident fund holders withdrew a record 2.2 billion shekels in August -- a 140% jump over July, the Finance Ministry reported on Monday. In the first eight months of the year, holders of the long-term savings plans have withdrawn 7.4 billion shekels. 

 -- The Bank of Israel intervened again in foreign currency trading on Monday to keep the currency basket exchange rate from remaining below its lowest set value. According to Ha'aretz, the central bank bought tens of millions of dollars, the largest sum it has purchased since it first began intervening in the foreign currency market two weeks ago. 

 -- A committee on promoting capital investments will weigh the possibility of continuing to let U.S. pension funds enjoy tax breaks, Ha'aretz reported. The panel had recommended that Israel rescind the tax breaks it gives foreign investors.

text:

title: Bank of Israel won't change shekel trading bands.
text:
JERUSALEM, Aug 29 (Reuter) - The Bank of Israel has no intention of changing the present trading band within which the shekel is allowed to fluctuate, sources at the central bank said. 

 The officials said that at this stage there is no intention of enlarging or abolishing the trading band. 

 "There are no talks about this and for sure this won't happen tomorrow, the day after, in another week or in another month," one official said. "Of course we have thoughts about the long term, but there is nothing on the agenda at the moment." 

 The shekel can fluctuate in a trading band of 7.0 percent above or below a slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency at six percent a year against a basket of key currencies. 

 If the shekel-basket exchange rate reaches the lower trading band the central bank intervenes by buying foreign currency. 

 The Bank of Israel intervened in trading on Tuesday and Wednesday by buying small amounts of dollars to stop the shekel-basket exchange rate from falling below the bottom of the band. 

 The officials said the central bank wanted only to preserve the band and had no intention of depreciating the shekel by making massive interventions in foreign exchange trading. 

 They said that all changes in the parameters of the band need to be done with the approval of the Treasury and they doubted the Treasury would approve such a move with the rate being so close to the bottom of the band. 

 Widening the trading band would allow the shekel to appreciate further, if the current trend continues, and cause even further damage to exporters, they said. 

 At the end of May last year, Treasury heads decided to enlarge the band from 5.0 percent above and below the slope to 7.0 percent. But when they did this the shekel-basket exchange rate was at the middle of the band and not at its bottom, the officials said.

title: Israel's  Central Bank / Forex  -2:  Currency  Basket Dips
text:
TEL AVIV (Dow Jones) --The Bank of Israel intervened in foreign currency trading for the second straight day Wednesday, after the currency basket exchange rate dipped below the lowest point the Central Bank has said it would allow. 

 The rate had hovered around the red line throughout the day, and the Central Bank began buying foreign currency in the late afternoon. 

 "The intervention was very light, as it was yesterday," said Sandrine Finkelstein, a foreign exchange dealer at United Mizrahi Bank. 

 To moderate cycles of foreign currency speculation that were fueled by expectations of devaluation, Israel linked the shekel to a basket of five currencies in 1986. The dollar is weighted heaviest, accounting for about 60% of the basket. 

 The other currencies in the basket are the German mark (weighted about 20%), the British pound (about 9%), the Japanese yen (about 6%) and the French franc, (about 6%). 

 The currency basket exchange rate is allowed to fluctuate by 7% in each direction from the given midpoint rate. The midpoint rate will depreciate this year by 6% --  which is the difference between Israel's inflation rate and the rate of inflation in the countries whose currencies are in the basket. 

 The basket had been inching toward the low point for weeks, as the shekel remained strong because of high shekel interest rates. Then on Tuesday, for the first time since the exchange rate policy was set in 1991, the basket dipped below the red line. 

 A few minutes before trading closed on Tuesday, the Bank of Israel bought small amounts of foreign currency to boost the basket back within the exchange rate range.

title: Shekel's Rise Raises  Intervention  Expectations In  Israel
text:
JERUSALEM (AP-Dow Jones)--The shekel's recent strengthening has sparked expectations that the Bank of Israel may have to buy dollars again soon to force the currency back within its trading band. 

 The central bank purchased more than $6 billion in foreign currency between the beginning of the year and June 18, when it widened the shekel's trading band and ended the immediate need to intervene in trading. 

 The foreign-exchange market's immediate response to the wider band was to buy dollars, and the shekel fell 4.9% against the U.S. currency between June 18 and June 30. 

 But recent statistics indicating stronger-than-expected inflationary pressures have bolstered the Israeli currency by damping expectations that the central bank might cut the discount rate next month from the current 12.7%. 

 The shekel has been gaining ground for four consecutive sessions, a dealer in the Tel Aviv trading room of The First International Bank of Israel noted. The dollar traded at about 3.5220 shekels at 1045 GMT, compared with Friday's fixing of 3.5320 shekels and Wednesday's fixing of 3.5560 shekels. 

 The Israeli currency also traded at 3.7950 shekels against its basket, compared with Friday's fixing of 3.8066 shekels and Wednesday's fixing of 3.8337 shekels. The shekel is adjusted daily against a basket of major international monies dominated by the dollar. 

 'People don't think the discount rate will go down - either it will stay where it is or it will go up - so they can continue borrowing in foreign currency,' the First International Bank of Israel dealer said.

title: Israel Shekel Up Again, Allaying Depreciation Fears
text:
JERUSALEM (AP-Dow Jones)--The shekel strengthened against the dollar for a third straight day Wednesday, easing fears of a steep depreciation that had been fueled by the recent widening of the trading band. 

 The central bank fixed the shekel at 3.5050 to the dollar, a rise of 1.24% from Tuesday's close of 3.5490 shekels. 

 The shekel traded within a range of 3.4950 to 3.53 to the dollar, foreign currency dealers said. About half an hour after the 1230 fixing the shekel was trading within a range of 3.5170 to 3.5270 shekels. 

 Trading volume was moderate, dealers said. 

 The shekel slid some 5% in the week after the trading band was widened June 18, generating fears of a much bigger depreciation that would feed inflation and lead to a rise in the 12.7% discount rate. 

 But the shekel's slide came to a halt Monday, and so far this week the shekel has regained nearly half of the value it lost last week.

title: Analysts see quiet after the storm for shekel.
text:
JERUSALEM, June 30 (Reuter) - Analysts say they are still waiting for the dust to clear after the Israeli government reformed the exchange rate mechanism and the Bank of Israel slashed interest rates two weeks ago. 

 Since the cabinet decision, which widened the Israeli currency's trading band and lowered its crawling slope, the Israeli shekel has lost some five percent against the dollar to 3.587 on Monday. The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange's Mishtanim index of 100 leading has fallen 3.5 percent. 

 "Both the stock and currency markets have been reacting to the uncertainty, not to the fundamentals," said Nadine Baudot-Trajtenberg, senior economist in the securities division of Israel's Bank Hapoalim. 

 Like most other analysts, she discounts the long-term significance of the changes. 

 "We believe the shekel rate will stabilise in the short run," said Vikas Nath, emerging markets strategist at UBS in London. "We are shooting for 3.47 or 3.48 once the short cover gives way." 

 By year end, he sees the dollar at 3.55-3.6 shekels, not far off from the 3.5 shekels he forecast before the eruption. 

 The shekel's current slide marks a reversal for the currency, which had been riding high on the back of big capital inflows into the country. Some of the inflow was due to stepped-up foreign investment, but most was due to Israelis' taking advantage of lower overseas interest rates. 

 That is why Baudot-Trajtenberg says the shekel's weakening is a short-term trend. 

 "The people who've forced the depreciation are mostly the business sector here," she said. "But you don't get a sense that they want to get out of their dollar loans." 

 She expects the shekel to experience periodic waves of speculation but settle near the lower end of its trading band against the basket of foreign currencies to which it is linked. As of Sunday, the shekel was 4.6 percent above the lower band. 

 But Hezy Gutman, chief economist at First International Bank of Israel, warns that each day the shekel falls further the odds of a significant rebound grow slimmer. Gutman said he is not confident that the shekel will appreciate enough to again reach the lower end of the band. 

 Gutman said he could still see the shekel falling far enough for the Bank of Israel to intervene in the forex market. "There are situations where you have no choice," he said. "If the depreciation reaches 10 percent, (the central bank) can create a balance with just a little intervention." 

 However, a top Bank of Israel official indicated on Sunday that the bank would be more inclined to raise interest rates than intervene. 

 The exchange rate has an outsized impact on the trade-oriented Israeli economy. A weaker shekel could give a boost to the country's sluggish exports but also feed into inflation by raising the price of imports and housing. Israeli home prices are customarily linked to the dollar. 

 But economists are cautious in assessing its impact. 

 Nath said even a moderate weakening of the shekel over then long run would improve export prospects. But Gutman said the continued uncertainty overhanging the exchange rate would moderate any export growth. 

 Israel's sluggish growth and rising unemployment would discourage importers and builders from passing along the higher prices created by the weaker shekel, economists say. As a result, inflation is unlikely to accelerate. 

 But Gutman said interest rates are unlikely to fall either, after the Bank of Israel lowered rates 1.2 percentage point to 12.7 percent two weeks ago. 

 "My forecast is that we won't see a further fall in the nominal interest rate," said Baudot-Trajtenberg. "I think we might see a rise towards the end of the year." 

 She warned that the budget may come under pressure in the second half of the year at the same time that the Bank of Israel begins orienting monetary policy towards the government's 1998 inflation target. She said the target could be as low as six percent.

title: Bank of  Israel  wary of  forex  market  intervention .
text:
JERUSALEM, June 29 (Reuter) - The director of the Bank of Israel's research department said on Sunday the central bank preferred not to intervene in the forex market to stem a further depreciation in the shekel. 

 "We are following what is happening in the market and now our preference is not to intervene," Leo Leiderman told reporters. 

 "First of all we have to see how the exchange rate is behaving and then we have to see how the location of the exchange rate within the band affects the inflation environment," he said. 

 "Not every acceleration of depreciation has to be translated into inflation, especially when we are in a period of economic slowdown and unemployment," Leiderman said. 

 He said the Bank of Israel would continue to focus on achieving the government's 1997 inflation target of seven to 10 percent. "Our estimate is that the inflation environment right now is at about nine percent," Leiderman said. 

 The Bank of Israel will recommend next year's target be set at six to nine percent, he added. 

 Leiderman hinted that if the central bank decides it must take steps to control inflation it would prefer to raise interest rates rather sell foreign currency. 

 "Our policy is to let the market forces set the exchange rate," he said. 

 Leiderman said he believes that calm will return to the Israeli forex market soon. 

 "Our assessment is that...following a certain learning period we'll see fewer fluctuations than what we have seen in the past week," he said. "But we hope there will still be more fluctuations than what we were used to before the change in the exchange rate regime." 

 The shekel plunged five percent last week after the Israeli cabinet approved exchange rate reform that widened the diagonal band in which the currency may trade, creating more room for a depreciation. 

 The reform was followed by an interest rate cut of 1.2 percentage points, bringing the central bank's key lending rate to 12.7 percent. 

 Leiderman said the central bank was committed to defending the upper and lower limit of the band, though market analysts say they believe the central bank will intervene well before the shekel depreciates so far that it reaches the upper band. 

 "It's still too early to judge the exact level the exchange rate will reach within the band and it's not reasonable to draw conclusions on the basis of developments over one particular day or week. What's more, we are also seeing technical adjustments," Leiderman said. 

 Many people had sold dollars in advance of the exchange rate measures on expectations of an appreciation of the shekel. Now they are buying back dollars to close positions. 

 Dealers also said some companies are paying off foreign currency loans to cut their losses. High Israeli interest rates over the past two years had led many in the private sector to take foreign currency loans. 

 "In our assessment, there are now conditions and potential for a significant drop in short-term capital imports to Israel," Leiderman said, noting domestic interest rates are now well below rates of a year ago and that the trend abroad is towards higher interest rates.

title: Bank of Israel chief discounts inflation worries.
text:
TEL AVIV, June 26 (Reuter) - Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Thursday that the weakening of the shekel over the past week would not necessarily lead to higher inflation. 

 "There are circumstances that exchange rate changes translate themselves relatively quickly to prices and there are circumstances under which this translation is not as quick," Frenkel told Reuters. 

 "It depends very much on the state of the economy, it depends very much on budgetary circumstances and it depends very much on monetary policy," he said. 

 The shekel has fallen sharply since last Friday, shortly after the government announced a reform of the exchange rate regime and the Bank of Israel lowered the base rate by a steep 1.2 percentage points to 12.7 percent. 

 In early trading on Thursday, the dollar was up 1.5 percent against the Israeli currency to about 3.58 shekels. Since last Friday, the dollar has gained about 4.7 percent against the shekel. 

 Israeli inflation has been slowing since April. But the economy has been slowing, too, and this year is expected to show its lowest rate of growth in seven years. 

 Frenkel, who was attending the annual general meeting of the Manufacturers Association trade group, said he did not believe the shekel would continue weakening. "I would not necessarily argue that a depreciation of a few days must continue with further depreciation," he said. 

 Nevertheless, he indicated that unlike most economists, the bank had not been surprised by the shekel's movement. 

 "Most commentators, politicians and others had fears of a strong appreciation of the currency. The Bank of Israel had argued that that's not a necessary presumption," Frenkel said. "As a matter of fact, there are good economic reasons for a depreciation." 

 Frenkel would not say whether the Bank of Israel would consider intervening in the forex market to stem a further depreciation. 

 "There are various assessments," he said. "We at the central bank will continue following very carefully the markets. I can assure you that no abrupt measures will be taken - the idea is steady as you go."

title: Israel's Frenkel Will Weigh Rate Rise If Inflation Rises
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel says he'll weigh a rise in the discount rate if inflation rises.

 Frenkel told Israel radio he wasn't worried by the storm in the foreign currency market. While the central bank is monitoring events, it wants to let market forces "express themselves," he said. 

 The public mustn't be fooled into thinking that the central bank serves as an insurance policy against market forces, he said, referring to the possibility of Bank of Israel intervention to stop the shekel's slide. 

 The central bank must let people internalize the risks involved in foreign currency trading, Frenkel said. 

 "There are no red lines for depreciation, whereas there are red lines for inflation," Frenkel said. 

 "If inflation continues to drop, then we will consider lowering the discount rate," he said. "If inflation rises, then we will consider raising the discount rate."

title: Bank of Israel denies rate cut linked to politics.
text:
JERUSALEM, June 22 (Reuter) - Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel on Sunday denied political considerations influenced his decision to lower interest rates sharply after the cabinet approved changes in the exchange rate regime. 

 "There had been a long period of uncertainty, which created a lot of sensitivity in the money and capital markets. It was very important to end it," Frenkel said, explaining his surprise decision to cut the central bank's key lending rate by 1.2 percentage points last Wednesday to 12.7 percent. 

 He said the central bank's only considerations were falling inflation and inflationary expectations and the slowing economy. He also cited the measures taken by the cabinet at an emergency meeting on Wednesday to ease foreign currency controls and adjust the exchange rate system. 

 "The decision was made only with these factors taken into account -- period," Frenkel said. 

 Frenkel's remarks come amid charges that he had a hand in bringing about Finance Minister Dan Meridor's abrupt resignation last Wednesday. 

 The Bank of Israel said in a statement the state comptroller had made enquiries about Frenkel's role in the affair. 

 Meridor, a political rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has charged that the timing and method Netanyahu used to bring the decision to the cabinet was meant to embarrass him, leaving him no choice but to resign. 

 Meridor has not specifically charged Frenkel with involvement, but media commentators have suggested the governor aided Netanyahu. 

 In a commentary on Sunday, the daily newspaper Maariv recalled that Frenkel had been a candidate for finance minister in the Netanyahu government and was supposed to head a planned council of economic advisers. 

 "We expected to continue seeing close cooperation between the prime minister's and the governor's office....That reached a peak in the 'Diagonol Affair,' in which the governor joined with the prime minister in helping him to indirectly force out the finance minister," the newspaper said. 

 A spokeswoman for the government watchdog office would not confirm or deny the report. 

 The Bank of Israel was originally due to make its monthly interest rate announcement this Monday, at which time economists had expected only a mild cut of about 0.5 percentage point. Interest rates had been unchanged since the end of February. 

 Early last week, however, speculation the central bank would succeed in its long-running campaign to widen the diagonal currency band created huge speculative pressure on the shekel, forcing the Bank of Israel to intervene heavily. 

 Since the start of the year, the shekel has pressed the lower limit of its trading band against the basket of foreign currencies to which it is pegged. The market assumed that if the band was widened the shekel would be free to appreciate. 

 The exchange rate adjustments approved by the cabinet did not affect the lower end of the band but reduced the incline of the slope, enabling the currency to strengthen more than it would have under the previous system. 

 In Friday trading, the dollar unexpectedly gained ground on the shekel, with the representative rate set at 3.437 shekels, up 0.53 percent from Thursday. The currency basket also strengthened against the shekel, rising 0.57 percent to 3.7343. 

 There is no foreign currency trading in Israel on Sunday.
