title: Shekel weakens in roller-coaster trading.
text:
TEL AVIV, June 18 (Reuter) - The shekel representative rate was fixed slightly lower against the dollar on Wednesday in very volatile trading following a cabinet decision to widen the Israeli currency's trading band, dealers said. 

 After the government approved foreign currency reforms, a move that triggered the resignation of Finance Minister Dan Meridor, the Bank of Israel lowered its key lending rate by 1.2 percentage points to an annual 12.7 percent. 

 It was the first rate cut since February. 

 "During early trading the shekel weakened sharply as the market awaited the rate decision. The dollar was traded in a wide spread of about 3.4200/4800 as the rumour was that the Bank of Israel would lower its key lending rate by three percentage points," said Ilan Zadka at United Mizrahi Bank. 

 Zadka said that after the rate announcement the shekel recovered. 

 Meridor strongly opposed widening the shekel's trading bands, fearing it would lead to a further appreciation of the Israeli currency, hurt exports and cause the economy to slow. 

 "Trading was very volatile today and investors were confused. Volume was relatively low as investors remained on the sidelines trying to figure out what was going on," said Guy Levi at Bank Leumi. 

 Levi said the market was looking for direction. 

 "There are still some missing pieces as for instance who is going to be the next finance minister," he said. Meridor's resignation goes into effect on Friday. 

 The shekel had been allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope designed to devalue it by six percent a year. 

 But high interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the Bank of Israel to buy massive amounts of dollars to prevent the shekel from strengthening beyond its band. 

 Under the new plan the lower band remains the same while the upper band rises to 21 percent. The spread between the top and bottom band, therefore, will be 28 percent. 

 The central bank hopes it will no longer need to intervene constantly in the currency market. 

 But Zadka said he believed that the Bank of Israel would have to intervene again in trading on Thursday as the shekel might appreciate beyond its trading band. 

 "People do not realize that from an economic point of view Meridor is the main winner. The Bank of Israel had to cut the (interest) rate, and the lower diagonal limit remained unchanged, which will force the central bank to continue to buy dollars if the shekel rises," he said.

title: Benefits Of Israel Shekel Band Change Unclear: Amplifier
text:
JERUSALEM (Dow Jones)--Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel won his battle Wednesday against Finance Minister Dan Meridor for a wider shekel trading band, but analysts aren't convinced the move will help the Israeli economy much. 

 Within a year's time, the shekel will gradually be allowed to fluctuate 15% in either direction from an as-yet undetermined midpoint. 

 Under the abandoned system, the shekel was allowed to fluctuate plus or minus 7% from a midpoint that depreciated 6% annually. 

 Immediately, the central bank dropped the floor by 15%, which it will continue to depreciate at a 6% annual rate. The ceiling was left unchanged, but it will depreciate at a rate of 4% rather than 6% previously. Eventually, that will allow the upper half of the band to widen to 15%. The central bank left the midpoint unchanged for now and didn't say when it will adjust the midpoint again or by how much. 

 According to Frenkel, in the coming year, foreign currency restrictions will also be lifted except those on institutional investors that are also imposed abroad. 

 Frenkel touted the change as a means of reducing Bank of Israelintervention in the foreign currency market. The central bank has bought billions of dollars in foreign currency since the beginning of the year to weaken the shekel, which has been bloated by the high discount rate.

title: FOCUS - Shekel dispute may bring new cabinet row.
text:
TEL AVIV, June 17 (Reuter) - Talks on expanding the range in which the Israeli shekel can fluctuate threatened on Tuesday to erupt into a power struggle between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Finance Minister Dan Meridor. 

 Meridor opposes an expansion of the bands while interest rates are high, fearing the currency will appreciate, hurting exports. He has locked horns over the issue with the central bank which is pushing for wider bands to allow the market a greater say in setting the rate. Netanyahu has not taken a clear position on the issue, but has set a goal of eventually making the shekel fully convertible in world markets. 

 It will be up to the prime minister to make the final decision if Meridor and Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel cannot resolve their dispute. Some analysts speculate Meridor would resign if Netanyahu backed the central bank's stand. 

 Netanyahu met the two warring sides on Monday but a marathon all-night meeting failed to resolve the issue, fuelling uncertainty on the foreign exchange market. 

 The Bank of Israel intervened early in the day, buying dollars to prevent the shekel from appreciating beyond its trading band, a forex dealer at Bank Hapoalim said. 

 Political analyst Hanan Crystal said Netanyahu might be using the economic talks to move on a government shake-up. 

 "He has in essence begun the great battle for the whole kitty," Crystal told Israel Radio. 

 Israel's media have speculated that Netanyahu intended to juggle his ministers, moving Ariel Sharon from infrastructure to the finance post. 

 Crystal said such a plan would leave young Likud leaders like Meridor, who might challenge Netanyahu for party leadership, outside the government circle. 

 Netanyahu announced after the all-night meeting that a budget cut and foreign currency reform, including increasing the amount institutional investors and companies can invest abroad, had been agreed. 

 But talks will continue on Tuesday afternoon in Jerusalem on the main issue outstanding -- the shekel's trading bands. 

 The shekel strengthened in early trading. Turnover was low and spreads were very wide, reflecting the uncertainty. 

 "The market doesn't know what will happen," a forex dealer at Bank Hapoalim said. 

 Frenkel has pushed for expanding the bands, which would give the central bank some relief from the need to constantly intervene in the currency market as the currency would find its own equilibrium. 

 High interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the central bank to buy massive amounts of dollars to prevent the shekel from strengthening beyond its band. 

 But Dan Propper, head of the Manufacturers Association, echoed Meridor's concerns that an appreciating exchange rate would hurt the economy. 

 "If the trading band is expanded, we'll see higher unemployment and I'm not sure from a social perspective we'll be able to deal with this phenomenon," he told Israel Television. 

 The shekel, pegged to a basket of foreign currencies, is allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency by six percent a year. 

 Netanyahu dismissed media speculation that Meridor would quit were the bands widened. 

 When asked by reporters whether Meridor would continue as finance minister, Netanyahu replied: "It is not on the agenda."

title: Uncertainty prevails in Israel markets, shekel up.

 Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced after an all-night meeting with Finance Minister Dan Meridor and Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel that a foreign currency reform and budget cut had been agreed. 

 But talks were to continue on Tuesday afternoon on the main issue outstanding -- the shekel's trading bands. 

 The stock market posted early morning supply of 80 million shekels against only seven million in demand. 

 Traders said the weakness was due in part to a closing of positions by options players on Monday afteroon. 

 But the market, which is heavily export-oriented, was also strongly influenced by the currency market. 

 "The decision on the bands will be a major decision," Danniella Finn of Batucha Securities said. 

 Frenkel has pushed for a widening of the bands, which would give the central bank some relief from the need to constantly intervene in the currency market. 

 High interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the central bank to buy huge amounts of dollars to prevent the shekel from strengthening beyond its band. 

 Meridor strongly opposes a widening of the band, fearing it will lead to a further appreciation of the shekel, causing the economy to slow. 

 Traders said the issue has now turned into a political battle that may require a resolution by the entire cabinet. 

 Netanyahu has dismissed media speculation that Meridor could resign if the prime minister decided to widen the bands. 

 "It shouldn't be a political issue, it should be an economic one. What does the justice minister or the labour minister have to do with it. They are making a political decision on a purely economic issue," Finn said. 

 The shekel, pegged to a basket of foreign currencies, is allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency by six percent a year.

title: Netanyahu in  forex  talks with Treasury, Cent Bank.
text:
CAESAREA, Israel, June 16 (Reuter) - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will meet the country's Finance Minister and the Governor of the Central Bank on Monday in a bid to hammer out a foreign currency liberalisation plan, a government source said. 

 The discussions are also expected to look at widening the Israeli shekel's trading bands. 

 The source said that Netanyahu aimed to take a decisive role in a long running dispute between the Treasury and the Central Bank on these two issues. He said he doubted the three would reach a decision tonight but expected a resolution over the next few days. 

 "We've had numerous discussions about the subject. Both sides have voiced their positions but a decision must be made," Netanyahu told reporters. 

 The meeting is scheduled for 1700 GMT. 

 The source said that the absence of any decision had made the local forex markets extremely nervous. 

 The Bank of Israel, which has been pressing to widen the shekel's currency bands, bought almost $150 million during intervention in the forex market on Monday in an attempt to keep the shekel down, traders said. 

 The currency is pegged to a basket of foreign currencies and is allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal line designed to devalue it by six percent a year. 

 An influx of foreign currency has forced the Bank of Israel to intervene heavily to prevent the shekel from strengthening beyond the seven percent limit. 

 The Treasury has refused to countenance a widening of the band for fear that it would cause a further appreciation of the shekel, which it regards as being overvalued.

 Netanyahu is due to speak this evening at an economic conference in the seaside town of Caesarea.

 High interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the central bank to intervene heavily in recent months to prevent the currency from appreciating beyond its trading band.

title: Israel's Netanyahu to decide on  currency  reform.
text:
JERUSALEM, May 27 (Reuter) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will intervene in a dispute between the Bank of Israel and the Treasury to advance a programme of foreign currency liberalisation, government sources said on Tuesday. 

 The central bank and the Treasury disagree on details of the liberalisation, especially with regard to investments by Israeli provident funds abroad. 

 Netanyahu will summon central bank Governor Jacob Frenkel and Finance Minister Dan Meridor for a meeting soon to resolve the differences, the sources said. No date has been set for the meeting. 

 The Bank of Israel would like to lift foreign currency controls over a number of years until the shekel becomes fully convertible. 

 Among the steps the central bank recommends: 

 - Allowing provident funds and institutional investors to invest up to five percent of their assets in foreign securities against two percent currently; 

 - Allowing companies to invest in foreign securities with no limitation; currently they may invest 10 percent of their capital or five percent of their turnover; 

 - Allowing Israelis to buy dollars freely from banks and open dollar accounts. 

 Talks on the programme began more than a year ago but were halted two months ago after the central bank rejected the Treasury's proposal to gradually increase the amount provident funds may invest abroad. 

 The Treasury's proposal sought to control fluctuations in the level of foreign investment at individual funds, which the central bank said was not viable.

title: Bank of Israel official slams exchange rate regime.
text:
JERUSALEM, May 6 (Reuter) - A top Bank of Israel official said in a paper released on Tuesday the current exchange rate system, featuring a fixed trading band to control shekel movement, hurts the economy. 

 "We are telling anyone who will listen: the present situation whereby the Bank of Israel buys large amounts of foreign currency because of the commitment placed on it to maintain the (shekel) trading band, hurts market mechanisms and the economy," David Klein wrote. 

 Klein, director of the central bank's monetary division, called for a more flexible exchange rate regime. 

 "Exchange rate regimes are not inscribed in the Ten Commandments...but man-made and must be adapted to changing circumstances." 

 Current exchange rate policy allows the shekel to fluctuate in a trading band of seven percent above or below a sloping mid-point designed to devalue the Israeli currency at a rate of six percent a year against a basket of key foreign currencies. 

 The Bank of Israel said recently it had been forced to intervene heavily in the currency market, buying $5 billion this year to prevent the shekel from appreciating above the trading band. 

 "As long as this (need for such intervention)...continues, the damage and price the economy will pay will increase and the way out will be more costly," Klein wrote. 

 Klein suggested loosening foreign currency regulations for Israelis by allowing private individuals to hold foreign currency accounts in local banks. 

 "As for the business sector, it is possible to cancel all remaining remnants of exchange control," he said. "There is no reason the Israeli economy cannot by the end of the decade be like all the developed markets and have a completely convertible currency." 

 The Bank of Israel and the Treasury have been discussing a foreign currency liberalisation programme but officials said final proposals have been delayed by differences mainly over rules for investment abroad by Israeli financial institutions. - Jerusalem newsroom, 972-2-5370502

title: Bank of Israel pays price for inflation stance.
text:
JERUSALEM, April 3 (Reuter) - The Bank of Israel is paying a heavy price in the foreign currency market in its battle to contain inflation, but the market is convinced the bank will not back down, dealers said on Thursday. 

 The bank is soaking up dollars flooding into the economy as Israelis increasingly borrow overseas to take advantage of lower comparative interest rates. 

 The foreign loans are prompted by high domestic interest rates imposed by the central bank to fight inflation and offset excess government spending. 

 In recent weeks, the central bank has been forced to intervene almost daily in the local forex market to offset massive demand for shekels. On Wednesday alone, dealers said, it bought more than $200 million. 

 "The Bank of Israel can continue, but it can't go on forever," said Ilan Raviv, manager of Israel Discount Bank's forex dealing. "The amounts aren't sustainable from the shekel point of view. You can't keep printing money." 

 But, he and other dealers said, the market thinks the central bank will continue on its path for the foreseeable future. 

 "It doesn't frighten people because the Bank of Israel governor says if he had to choose between (defending) the exchange rate and inflation, he'd choose (fighting) inflation," said Raviv. 

 The intervention is aimed at supporting the foreign currency basket rate, to which the shekel is officially linked. The rate trades in a band seven percent above or below its midpoint. 

 However since mid-January, the rate has been scraping along at the bottom of the band, forcing the central bank to intervene to prevent it from falling through the bottom. 

 The demand for shekels is due to a renewed surge of foreign currency borrowing by the Israeli business sector to take advantage of lower foreign interest rates, said Michal Rotlevy, a dealer United Mizrahi Bank. Israel's prime rate is currently 15.4 percent in nominal terms. 

 Borrowers are converting the foreign currency into shekels creating huge demand for the Israeli currency. The central bank soaks up the shekels through currency swaps and by luring deposits from the commercial banks with high interest rates. 

 On Wednesday, media reports said the pressure was due to a big foreign exchange loan Israel Corp took to finance its 667 million shekel purchase of an Israel Chemicals Ltd stake. "We see a lot of big deals in the economy being financed by forex loans," said Raviv. 

 Rotlevy said the demand for foreign currency loans began at the end of last year, when the market concluded that the Treasury's 1997 budget cuts were insufficient to prompt the Bank of Israel to lower interest rates significantly. 

 She added that the recent acceleration of inflation has strengthened that view. "Everyone is expecting high (consumer price index figures) so the Bank of Israel won't lower interest rates," she said. 

 Borrowers reason that without a cut, the interest rate differential between Israel and abroad will remain wide and the prospects for a significant depreciation of the shekel will be slim. 

 The Bank of Israel has not yet published figures on the extent of capital imports in the first quarter and it will not comment on the extent of its market intervention. 

 But foreign currency reserves, which central bank officials said is a rough indicator for both figures, have risen $3.8 billion this year to record $15.3 billion at the end of March. 

 Dealers said the Bank of Israel wants to resolve the problem without having to make concessions on interest rates. 

 "The Bank of Israel wants to move towards full currency liberalisation and stop all intervention," said Rotlevy. 

 Governor Jacob Frenkel reiterated his call for liberalisation earlier this week, but the Treasury is reportedly blocking any such move in hopes of jawboning the central bank into lowering interest rates. 

 In the meantime, the market is betting an an interim move to widen the currency band, which would alleviate the pressure to intervene, said Rotlevy. 

 "The Bank of Israel may widen the currency band by seven, 10 or even 12 percent -- this is the market's reasonable expectation," she said.

title: Bank of Israel seen cutting rates nil to 0.3 pct.
text:
TEL AVIV, Feb 23 (Reuter) - Analysts said that the Bank of Israel would either leave interest rates unchanged or else cut them by up to 0.3 percentage points when it announces its March monetary programme on Monday. 

 The analysts on Sunday said the central bank faces contradictory signals, ranging from a low January consumer price index (CPI) to a widening budget deficit. The daily newspaper Maariv on Sunday said Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel is under pressure from the prime minister's office and the Treasury to make a big cut. 

 "I think Frenkel is very resistant to this kind of pressure," said Danniella Finn, a vice president at Betucha Securities. "The estimates are for 0.0-0.3 percentage point cut in interest rates....I feel comfortable with those estimates." 

 The Bank of Israel has cut the base rate 0.5 percentage point in each of the last two months, capping a total reduction of 2.8 points since the middle of last year. The base rate is currently 14.2 percent. 

 Adam Reuter, managing director of Financial Immunities, a financial consulting firm, predicted Frenkel would lower the rate 0.3 point. 

 "First they (the Bank of Israel) absorbed the liquidity they injected into the economy, second the CPI was low and finally the state of the economy," he said citing reasons for making a relatively sharp cut. 

 In a bid to defend the currency basket rate against the Israeli shekel, the Bank of Israel has been routinely intervening in the local currency market since mid-January. But the central bank has said it is successfully absorbing the resulting liquidity. 

 Although, M1 money supply rose a sharp 3.4 percent in January, analysts have dismissed any connection with the forex market intervention. 

 Meanwhile, consumer prices rose a moderate 0.4 percent in January, while the economy remains in a slowdown. 

 Roy Meir, of Simodan brokerage house, said he thought the central bank would hold rates this month. 

 "The January budget deficit was a lot bigger than expected," he said. "Even though there was a low January consumer price index, that's history. The deficit is still an issue." 

 He said it was unlikely that rates would come down until the Treasury was able to put spending back on course, which he said would not occur before the end of March. 

 Reuter said he also doubted rates would continue coming down after this month. 

 "I think we've reached the end of a trend," he said. "We'll see higher CPIs in March and April because of the strength of the dollar."

title: Shekel weakens on Bank of  Israel intervention .
text:
TEL AVIV, Feb 6 (Reuter) - The shekel weakened mildly against the dollar and basket of foreign currencies after the Bank of Israel intervened more aggressively than usual to support the dollar, dealers said. 

 Operators continued to convert dollars into shekels to take advantage of high domestic interest rates. 

 "Trading volume was average but today was different because of the aggressive nature of the central bank's intervention," said Ron Bedny of Bank Discount. 

 "The bank was not merely acting to keep the shekel-dollar balanced but actively sought to bring the shekel exchange rate to 3.0210 per dollar by buying up excess dollars. The central bank even created a shortage of dollars in the morning," he said. 

 The shekel closed the daily tender at 3.0210 shekels per dollar against Friday's rate of 3.0110. The basket closed at 3.3813 shekels per basket unit against 3.3802 on Friday.

title: Bank of Israel buys dollars to slow shekel rise.
text:
TEL AVIV, Jan 18 (Reuter) - The shekel gained against the dollar and the yen and the Bank of Israel intervened, buying dollars to moderate the rise, dealers said. 

 "Trade volumes were high today as the private sector continued to sell dollars," said Ilan Raviv of Bank Discount. 

 "The Bank of Israel is evidently determined not to let the basket fall below 3.37 shekels per basket unit. Whenever the exchange rate dips below that point and the shekel becomes too strong, the central bank starts buying dollars."

title: Shekel strengthens, Bank of  Israel intervenes .
text:
TEL AVIV, Jan 5 (Reuter) - The Israeli shekel strengthened against the dollar, which weakened around the world, and the Bank of Israel intervened several times to prop up the basket of foreign currencies, traders said. 

 The shekel closed the daily tender at 3.0240 shekels per dollar against Wednesday's rate of 3.0280. The basket closed at 3.3641 shekels per basket unit aginst 3.3651 on Wednesday. 

 Trade was characterised by a large supply of dollars and foreign currency and volume was high. 

 Dealers said investors were attracted to high interest rates on shekel holdings. 

 "The trend will probably continue until the shekel is devalued," a dealer at First International Bank said. The central bank has said it will not devalue the shekel. 

 On the crosses the shekel traded against the yen at 2.9901 shekels per 100 yen against 2.9911 on Wednesday and against the mark at 1.9427 shekels per mark from 1.9402 on Wednesday.
